At that time, the sheriff said investigators focused on two violent gangs in Fort Pierce, the 10th Street gang and the 23rd Street gang. That operation resulted in more than five dozen arrests and 50 guns seized.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie grandmother grateful after flood rescue from van swept into canal - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie grandmother grateful after flood rescue from van swept into canal    WPEC
entry.article_text: Maria Andrade-Vasquez of Port St. Lucie has overcome plenty of challenges in her life. The mother of four, grandmother of 10, cancer survivor and dialysis patient never imagined a routine ride home from treatment would turn into a fight for survival. On Monday, Andrade-Vasquez was riding home from dialysis when floodwaters swept the transport van she was in off the road near Lakehurst Drive and into a canal in Port St. Lucie's Swan Park community. Speaking with CBS12 News through her son, Raul Morales, who translated from Spanish, Andrade-Vasquez said she feared she would not survive. "Yes, very, very scared," she said. Morales said as floodwaters rose around the van, his mother thought she might be living her final moments. Also see: Officer, firefighters rescue two from vehicle swept into Port St. Lucie canal "Seeing all the water go up, she was thinking, what's going to happen? Is this it?" Morales said. Police body camera video released this week shows how quickly first responders reacted. Lucie police said Officer Peterson arrived just 100 seconds after being dispatched to reports of a transport van that had gone into a canal off Southwest Hogan Street. Video captured the officer rushing into the water and rescuing the driver first before learning another passenger was still trapped inside. That passenger was Andrade-Vasquez. As water surrounded the vehicle, rescuers say the van tilted into the canal, leaving her trapped in the back. Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said the same wheelchair equipment used to help Andrade-Vasquez after dialysis treatments was now blocking her escape. "She's wheelchair bound, so the equipment that came out of the back of the van was up in place blocking her in," Niemczyk said. "They had to get her out of the wheelchair and pull her up over the equipment to get her out of the van." According to police, firefighters with St. Lucie County Fire District joined the officer at the scene and worked together to free Andrade-Vasquez from the vehicle. Morales said his mother still struggles to understand how rescuers were able to get her out so quickly. "She said, 'I don't know how they did it, but they quickly released her,'" Morales said. "To me it was amazing to see how quick they did what they did." Both Andrade-Vasquez and the driver were rescued safely. Her rescue was one of dozens of flood-related emergencies first responders handled as rainfall inundated roads and neighborhoods across Port St. Now recovering at home with her family, Andrade-Vasquez remains grateful to the first responders who helped save her life. The way I see it, you guys went the extra mile," Morales said. So thank you." Morales said his mother is still processing the trauma of the rescue but plans to continue her dialysis treatments three times a week as she focuses on her recovery.

entry.title: Viral video of student swimming home raises safety concerns in Port St. Lucie - WPBF
entry.summary: Viral video of student swimming home raises safety concerns in Port St. Lucie    WPBF
entry.article_text: A viral video showing a student swimming home from a school bus in flooded Port St. Lucie streets has raised questions about why schools opened during Monday’s severe weather. The video, filmed in a neighborhood where water has since receded, shows the student navigating deep floodwaters after exiting the bus. "He literally almost went completely underwater," said Lucinda Lopez, a Port St. Another neighbor, Ariel Abel, described the scene: "We watched the school bus get stuck over in that turn area, and then we watched the kid get off, and he sunk straight into the water." The incident has left parents questioning why schools opened on Monday despite the flooding. Concerns include why buses were sent into severely flooded streets and whether students should have sheltered in place at school until conditions improved. "Seeing the danger that all of the kids were put in is not okay," Lopez said. Abel added, "They really dropped the ball on this. The community is disappointed." On Tuesday, St. Lucie Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Jon Prince addressed the situation during a news conference, apologizing to families for the district’s response. The first flood advisory for the county came in just after 8 a.m. Monday, with the first flash flood warning issued at 10:41 a.m. "I completely understand the frustration families feel," Prince said. "It caused a lot of stress for our families, and for that, I’m profoundly sorry." Despite the apology, some parents remain unsatisfied. "An apology doesn’t fix what is happening," Abel said. Lopez emphasized the need for change: "We need to do better. We need to protect our kids at all costs. Missing a day or two of school is okay if it means keeping our kids safe at all costs." WPBF is working to hear from the school district to address these concerns and questions. entry.title: Martin County flooding leaves cattle farmers struggling, residents demanding solutions - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County flooding leaves cattle farmers struggling, residents demanding solutions    WPBF
entry.article_text: Floodwaters continue to inundate properties in Martin County, leaving cattle farmers struggling to care for their animals and residents concerned about how much longer the water will remain. Residents in the Trailside community say water from neighboring properties is flowing into their drainage system, causing widespread flooding. Flooding threatens cattle, farm operations Hungryland Farms normally operates a 20-acre rotational grazing system for its Florida Cracker cattle. The owner, Melissa, said much of the pasture is now underwater, forcing the animals onto the farm’s elevated driveway. "We're starting to lose big sections of the driveway. We have them concentrated up the house pad, but if we lose too much more, we're just going to have to figure out a way to evacuate them somewhere," she said. Some cattle have struggled to navigate the water, and Melissa said the farm is concerned about losing access to its property as flooding continues. For now, the farm is bringing in hay and hay cubes to keep the cattle on their regular diet while monitoring potential health risks from floodwaters. "We’re more just concerned with the health and safety of our cattle," Melissa said. Melissa said the farm has an emergency contact with the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service if the animals face imminent danger. "We don’t know how long we’re going to be here," she said. HOA says solution is unclear Kyla Shay, president of the Trailside Homeowners Association, said the community’s drainage system is designed to handle water from its 41 lots and designated neighboring properties. However, Shay said water from outside that system is now flowing through county-owned land and other neighboring properties before reaching the community’s southern canal. We can’t handle theirs," Shay said. The flooding has also affected neighboring pastures and reached areas near Bridge Road and an electrical substation, according to Shay. She said some electrical transformers are partially underwater, septic systems are overwhelmed and residents have been warned their well water could be compromised. "The health department issued warnings this morning to me that our water wells could be compromised because of bacteria, because of the standing water," Shay said. Since their septic systems are submerged, Shay said homeowners have been unable to shower or do laundry. County says repairs must wait WPBF 25 News reached out to Martin County about their concerns and learned the county recently acquired approximately 315 acres of land in the area, known as the Elise J. A county spokesperson said establishing access has been their immediate priority so staff can assess conditions and respond. The county said it is working with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District to address a breach affecting drainage into its irrigation canal and that the agencies jointly determined repairs should wait until water levels recede. The county said current conditions make hauling and placing sand unsafe and potentially damaging to the levee. Material could also wash into the canal before crews establish a stable repair. "County staff will continue to monitor water levels and site conditions in close coordination with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District," a county spokesperson said. The county said it will move forward with repairs when conditions allow safe work without compromising the levee. It is also evaluating longer-term options to improve outflow and reduce the risk of flooding happening again. Residents want a long-term solution Shay said the homeowners association has been working with water engineers and other experts to understand how long the flooding could last. "It's probably going to be late January, February before we can see a break, and that's assuming that the south canal wall does not collapse and immediately dump all the water on us," she said. Melissa said the farm’s drainage system normally provides room for water to collect during the rainy season, but the amount coming from outside the property has overwhelmed it. "We have a very extensive drainage system, but it’s just not equipped to handle this amount of water," Melissa said. Both women said they want neighboring properties and the agencies responsible for drainage to address the problem. For now, Martin County said it will continue monitoring conditions and coordinating with the conservancy district before attempting repairs. Meanwhile, Melissa said the farm is focused on keeping its cattle safe as water continues to surround the property.

entry.title: Guns, drugs and lots of money: 40 arrested in major Fort Pierce gang takedown - WPBF
entry.summary: Guns, drugs and lots of money: 40 arrested in major Fort Pierce gang takedown    WPBF
entry.article_text: Law enforcement officials in St. Lucie County announced Thursday that 40 suspected members of a Fort Pierce gang have been arrested following an 18-month investigation. The investigation, known as "Operation Score Board," targeted the 23rd Street Gang, which authorities say has operated in northern St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said the gang has between 70 and 80 members and has been responsible for years of violence in the Fort Pierce community. "This gang has terrorized, basically created a hostage crisis for our community up there," Del Toro said. "There’s a lot of good people that are up there in Fort Pierce that have been just held hostage by this group for the last decade, living in fear." Investigators said the gang even maintained a scoreboard tracking shootings and homicides, a discovery that ultimately gave the operation its name. Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith said detectives reviewed a decade of criminal activity to identify connections between suspected gang members and violent crimes. "Detectives conducted an extensive review of criminal activity spanning ten years, examining incidents and identifying connections between individuals associated with the gang," Smith said. "This intensive analysis revealed a disturbing pattern of organized crime and violence." Authorities said investigators used Florida’s RICO law to connect years of alleged shootings, drug trafficking and other criminal activity to members of the 23rd Street Gang. The investigation involved multiple local and state law enforcement agencies working together over 18 months to build cases against suspected members of the organization. On Wednesday, law enforcement officers executed multiple search warrants throughout the Fort Pierce area, resulting in 11 arrests as part of the larger operation. Authorities said officers also seized multiple firearms, drugs and thousands of dollars in cash. Del Toro said the size of the operation and the cooperation between agencies could have a lasting impact on the community. "I’ve never seen an operation this large with this many agencies at the local and federal level," Del Toro said. "I think this is going to have a significant generational impact in this community." Authorities said similar investigations and operations are expected in the future. entry.title: Viral video of student swimming home raises safety concerns in Port St. Lucie - WPBF
entry.summary: Viral video of student swimming home raises safety concerns in Port St. Lucie    WPBF
entry.article_text: A viral video showing a student swimming home from a school bus in flooded Port St. Lucie streets has raised questions about why schools opened during Monday’s severe weather. The video, filmed in a neighborhood where water has since receded, shows the student navigating deep floodwaters after exiting the bus. "He literally almost went completely underwater," said Lucinda Lopez, a Port St. Another neighbor, Ariel Abel, described the scene: "We watched the school bus get stuck over in that turn area, and then we watched the kid get off, and he sunk straight into the water." The incident has left parents questioning why schools opened on Monday despite the flooding. Concerns include why buses were sent into severely flooded streets and whether students should have sheltered in place at school until conditions improved. "Seeing the danger that all of the kids were put in is not okay," Lopez said. Abel added, "They really dropped the ball on this. The community is disappointed." On Tuesday, St. Lucie Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Jon Prince addressed the situation during a news conference, apologizing to families for the district’s response. The first flood advisory for the county came in just after 8 a.m. Monday, with the first flash flood warning issued at 10:41 a.m. "I completely understand the frustration families feel," Prince said. "It caused a lot of stress for our families, and for that, I’m profoundly sorry." Despite the apology, some parents remain unsatisfied. "An apology doesn’t fix what is happening," Abel said. Lopez emphasized the need for change: "We need to do better. We need to protect our kids at all costs. Missing a day or two of school is okay if it means keeping our kids safe at all costs." WPBF is working to hear from the school district to address these concerns and questions. entry.summary: Flooding shuts down South 25th Street near two St. Lucie County schools    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Flooding continues to plague St. Lucie County roads, with officials closing a stretch of South 25th Street near two schools as the district extends school closures through Thursday. Lucie County announced Wednesday that South 25th Street is closed to through traffic between Fort Pierce Central High School at Cobra Pride Way and the entrance to Forest Grove Middle School at Bulldog Drive. County officials said the closure is due to unsafe road conditions caused by flooding. See also: Evacuations underway as flooding swamps Port St. Lucie neighborhood The road closure comes as St. Lucie Public Schools announced that schools will remain closed Thursday, Nov. 5, for another day as the county continues dealing with widespread flooding. Drivers are urged to use caution in the area and find alternate routes. Officials have not announced when the affected stretch of road will reopen. Anyone with questions about the closure can contact the county's Public Works Engineering Division at 772-462-1707 .

entry.title: Who will lead Congress? Leadership battles take center stage after midterms
entry.summary: With Democrats poised to take control of both chambers of Congress, attention is quickly turning from the 2026 midterm elections to the leadership battles that will determine who guides the new House and Senate majorities. Leadership elections are expected to begin next week, with Democrats facing some internal pressure over their current leaders and House Republicans preparing for a potentially tight contest of their own. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries are expected to remain at the top of their respective caucuses. Jeffries would be in position to become House speaker, while Schumer would become Senate majority leader. Both, however, have faced calls from some progressive activists and incoming lawmakers for a change in leadership. Critics argue Democratic leaders did not push back aggressively enough against President Donald Trump while the party was in the minority. RELATED STORY | Democratic leaders outline agenda after sweeping Congress in midterms Among those calling for change is Maine Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, who said before Election Day that he would not support Schumer for majority leader. 'I've already said that I told Senator Schumer that I'm going to support somebody else, so it's no different now,' Jackson said. Jackson said he plans to push Democratic leaders on priorities including Medicare for All. House Republicans, meanwhile, face their own leadership battle after Speaker Mike Johnson decided not to seek reelection. Rep. entry.title: NTSB recovers part of Learjet engine, asks public to report crash debris
entry.summary: Investigators have recovered a portion of an engine from the Learjet 60 that crashed near Greenacres on Sunday as crews continue excavating the crash site, according to the National Transportation Safety Board. The NTSB said excavation work began late Wednesday and continued Thursday as investigators and local officials worked to recover wreckage from the crash that killed nine people. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Part of jet's engine found, NTSB says NTSB recovers part of Learjet engine after crash Debris from the aircraft has been found away from the main impact site, including on the roofs of nearby homes and buildings, according to the NTSB. All recovered wreckage will be taken to a secure location for further examination. Investigators are also asking residents who find debris believed to be from the Learjet not to keep it or attempt to move, alter or dispose of it. WATCH BELOW: Piece of jet's tail found miles away NTSB: Piece of Learjet's tail found miles away from crash The agency said even small pieces of wreckage could contain evidence that helps investigators determine what happened. Anyone who has found or collected debris from the crash is asked to email witness@ntsb.gov to arrange for its recovery. The NTSB is asking people to include a photograph of the debris in the email, if possible. The NTSB said recovering as much of the aircraft wreckage as possible is critical to its investigation and efforts to determine the cause of the crash.

entry.title: Flooding leaves Creekside community in St. Lucie County without power, most homes evacuated
entry.summary: Floodwaters remain knee-deep in parts of the Creekside community in St. Lucie County, where officials say roughly 75% of the neighborhood's homes have been evacuated, and power remains shut off. St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro provided a Thursday update , saying the community, located off State Road 70 west of Florida's Turnpike, has about 150 homes and remains under a voluntary evacuation. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Flooding leaves Creekside community in St. Lucie County without power, Del Toro said some trucks can now make it into the neighborhood, but water levels remain high. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office also has a high-water vehicle available to assist residents who need help. 'If in fact you need help, please don't hesitate to call 911 or contact one of our deputies,' Del Toro said. Deputies are providing 24-hour security in the community while residents remain displaced and electricity is out, according to the sheriff. WATCH AERIAL VIDEO OF THE FLOODING: Aerial video of flooding in the Creekside community of St. Lucie County Restoring power could take additional time because some of Florida Power Light's equipment remains underwater. 'We continue to monitor the water level just like everybody else,' FPL's Marshall Critchfield said. 'Much of our equipment is presently underwater and our priority number one, as always, is safety.' Critchfield said crews will restore electricity as soon as water recedes enough for them to safely access the equipment. Del Toro said the neighborhood has underground utilities, creating an additional challenge while flooding remains high. Officials did not provide an estimate for when power would be restored or when the water is expected to fully recede. Del Toro urged residents who need assistance to contact deputies or call 911.

entry.title: Father of Meghan Markle arrested on charges related to child sexual abuse material, AP sources say
entry.summary: Meghan Markle's father was arrested Friday morning by federal agents in Florida on charges related to child sexual abuse material, two people familiar with the matter told The Associated Press. Thomas Markle Sr. was arrested outside Tampa, according to the people who were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation and spoke on the condition of anonymity. His arrest follows reports by The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, that Meghan's half brother found a collection of child sexual abuse images while clearing out the home of their father in the Philippines. Meghan Markle, the wife of Prince Harry, recently said she was 'deeply distressed' by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her fathers former home. She also revealed that a letter containing troubling allegations about him had been sent to London police in 2018. 'It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated, Meghan said of the letter. 'I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them . Meghan, an American citizen who starred in the U.S. television drama Suits, married Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. Her father, a retired television lighting and photography director, did not attend the wedding, prompting extensive coverage in the British media of Meghans estrangement from her father. Thomas Markle Sr. was living in the Philippines earlier this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S. The Sun reported that Thomas Markle Jr. recently found hundreds, if not thousands of child sex abuse images in boxes at his fathers former home in Cebu City, in the Philippines, when he was clearing out the property. Markle Jr. told the newspaper that he reported the images to police in the Philippines and contacted the FBI. 'I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years but that stops now,' Markle Jr. told The Sun. 'I won't speak to my father ever again unless Im called to give evidence against him.'

On Tuesday, St. Lucie Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Jon Prince addressed the situation during a news conference, apologizing to families for the district’s response. The first flood advisory for the county came in just after 8 a.m. Monday, with the first flash flood warning issued at 10:41 a.m. "I completely understand the frustration families feel," Prince said. "It caused a lot of stress for our families, and for that, I’m profoundly sorry." Despite the apology, some parents remain unsatisfied. "An apology doesn’t fix what is happening," Abel said. Lopez emphasized the need for change: "We need to do better. We need to protect our kids at all costs. Missing a day or two of school is okay if it means keeping our kids safe at all costs." WPBF is working to hear from the school district to address these concerns and questions. entry.summary: Neighbors hear 'sound of a bomb' in Fort Pierce operation    WPBF
entry.article_text: Residents in a Fort Pierce neighborhood were awakened early Wednesday morning by loud explosions as law enforcement agencies carried out a large-scale operation involving five search warrants across St. Neighbors along Miami Court described the startling events. "When you heard the sound, it sounded like a bomb; I thought, 'That's not a regular handgun, that sounds like a bomb,'" one neighbor said. "There were so many of them they were like a military. There was a military truck out there too," the neighbor added. Law enforcement vehicles were seen investigating at two homes in the area — one at 1708 Miami Court and another nearby at 1904 Georgia Avenue. Lucie County Sheriff's Office confirmed the operation was part of a large-scale criminal investigation, with the Drug Enforcement Administration and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives also present at the scene. That same neighbor shared her experience, saying, "I heard what sounded like bombs going off. Boom, and I said, 'What the heck is going on?' I peeked out the door, and I saw the blue lights from the police." She said the noises woke her up, and she watched as officers blocked off the road and issued commands over a loudspeaker. Authorities have not released details about the investigation or what led to the arrests, but the sheriff's office stated there is no known threat to the community.

entry.title: Martin County flooding leaves cattle farmers struggling, residents demanding solutions - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County flooding leaves cattle farmers struggling, residents demanding solutions    WPBF
entry.article_text: Floodwaters continue to inundate properties in Martin County, leaving cattle farmers struggling to care for their animals and residents concerned about how much longer the water will remain. Residents in the Trailside community say water from neighboring properties is flowing into their drainage system, causing widespread flooding. Flooding threatens cattle, farm operations Hungryland Farms normally operates a 20-acre rotational grazing system for its Florida Cracker cattle. The owner, Melissa, said much of the pasture is now underwater, forcing the animals onto the farm’s elevated driveway. "We're starting to lose big sections of the driveway. We have them concentrated up the house pad, but if we lose too much more, we're just going to have to figure out a way to evacuate them somewhere," she said. Some cattle have struggled to navigate the water, and Melissa said the farm is concerned about losing access to its property as flooding continues. For now, the farm is bringing in hay and hay cubes to keep the cattle on their regular diet while monitoring potential health risks from floodwaters. "We’re more just concerned with the health and safety of our cattle," Melissa said. Melissa said the farm has an emergency contact with the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service if the animals face imminent danger. "We don’t know how long we’re going to be here," she said. HOA says solution is unclear Kyla Shay, president of the Trailside Homeowners Association, said the community’s drainage system is designed to handle water from its 41 lots and designated neighboring properties. However, Shay said water from outside that system is now flowing through county-owned land and other neighboring properties before reaching the community’s southern canal. We can’t handle theirs," Shay said. The flooding has also affected neighboring pastures and reached areas near Bridge Road and an electrical substation, according to Shay. She said some electrical transformers are partially underwater, septic systems are overwhelmed and residents have been warned their well water could be compromised. "The health department issued warnings this morning to me that our water wells could be compromised because of bacteria, because of the standing water," Shay said. Since their septic systems are submerged, Shay said homeowners have been unable to shower or do laundry. County says repairs must wait WPBF 25 News reached out to Martin County about their concerns and learned the county recently acquired approximately 315 acres of land in the area, known as the Elise J. A county spokesperson said establishing access has been their immediate priority so staff can assess conditions and respond. The county said it is working with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District to address a breach affecting drainage into its irrigation canal and that the agencies jointly determined repairs should wait until water levels recede. The county said current conditions make hauling and placing sand unsafe and potentially damaging to the levee. Material could also wash into the canal before crews establish a stable repair. "County staff will continue to monitor water levels and site conditions in close coordination with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District," a county spokesperson said. The county said it will move forward with repairs when conditions allow safe work without compromising the levee. It is also evaluating longer-term options to improve outflow and reduce the risk of flooding happening again. Residents want a long-term solution Shay said the homeowners association has been working with water engineers and other experts to understand how long the flooding could last. "It's probably going to be late January, February before we can see a break, and that's assuming that the south canal wall does not collapse and immediately dump all the water on us," she said. Melissa said the farm’s drainage system normally provides room for water to collect during the rainy season, but the amount coming from outside the property has overwhelmed it. "We have a very extensive drainage system, but it’s just not equipped to handle this amount of water," Melissa said. Both women said they want neighboring properties and the agencies responsible for drainage to address the problem. For now, Martin County said it will continue monitoring conditions and coordinating with the conservancy district before attempting repairs. Meanwhile, Melissa said the farm is focused on keeping its cattle safe as water continues to surround the property.

entry.title: St. Lucie County asks residents, businesses to report flood damage through online survey
entry.summary: St. Lucie County is asking residents, businesses and agricultural property owners affected by recent flooding to report damage through an online survey as officials work to document the extent of the impacts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants across the county, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie, St. Lucie Village and unincorporated St. Lucie County. WATCH: Heavy rains flood Port St. Lucie roads earlier this week Heavy rain floods Port St. Lucie roads, leaving drivers stranded County officials said the information collected will be shared with local, state and federal partners to help assess the extent of the flooding and guide recovery efforts. The survey asks respondents to provide the property's location and building type, along with basic information about flooding and damage. It also includes questions about private wells used for household water and septic systems. People can complete the flood impact survey here through Friday, Nov. 20. County officials stressed that completing the survey is not an application for assistance and does not guarantee that funding will be available. Instead, the information will be used to help officials better understand the scope of the damage. Anyone with multiple affected structures should submit a separate survey for each one. The county is seeking reports about impacts to buildings and their associated systems rather than flooding limited to yards or surrounding property. Residents should only report conditions they have already observed. Officials are warning people not to enter unsafe buildings, walk through floodwater or touch electrical equipment in order to assess damage. Anyone who needs help completing the survey can contact the St. Lucie County Community Services Department at 772-462-1777 or comm_info@stlucieco.gov.

entry.title: Strong El Niño could bring wetter winter, increased flood and severe weather risk to South Florida
entry.summary: With a very strong El Nio event in the Pacific, the U.S. weather pattern is significantly impacted, especially in winter. Historically, El Nio brings stormier weather for the southern United States, including Florida. According to the National Weather Service (NWS) Miami, above-normal rainfall is anticipated for our dry season with a higher risk for flood events and severe weather including tornadoes. This happens as El Nio drives the subtropical jet stream farther south across the U.S. during the winter and dry season and generally steers more storm systems eastward. The NWS says due to the strength of the El Nio, which could match or exceed the historic 19971998 event as the strongest recorded (since 1950), confidence is high for a higher risk of strong storms. The 1997-1998 El Nio is tied to multiple severe weather events and the deadliest tornado outbreak in Florida back in February of '98. AFFECT ON WINTER TEMPERATURES Although more storm systems are in the forecast, it doesn't mean we will necessarily see more cold snaps or days with freezing temperatures. Because the dominant subtropical jet stream drives more southern storm systems, cold air masses from the north rarely penetrate into Florida. This lowers, but does not completely eliminate the overall likelihood of extreme cold events. The NWS forecasts near-average temperatures for South Florida as more frequent storm systems tends to depress daily high temperatures, while streams of milder Pacific air keep overnight lows higher than normal. IMPACT ON DROUGHT AND WILDFIRES Due to these moist conditions, significant wildfire activity is projected to remain below normal through the winter and potentially extending into the spring.

entry.title: Who will lead Congress? Leadership battles take center stage after midterms
entry.summary: With Democrats poised to take control of both chambers of Congress, attention is quickly turning from the 2026 midterm elections to the leadership battles that will determine who guides the new House and Senate majorities. Leadership elections are expected to begin next week, with Democrats facing some internal pressure over their current leaders and House Republicans preparing for a potentially tight contest of their own. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries are expected to remain at the top of their respective caucuses. Jeffries would be in position to become House speaker, while Schumer would become Senate majority leader. Both, however, have faced calls from some progressive activists and incoming lawmakers for a change in leadership. Critics argue Democratic leaders did not push back aggressively enough against President Donald Trump while the party was in the minority. RELATED STORY | Democratic leaders outline agenda after sweeping Congress in midterms Among those calling for change is Maine Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, who said before Election Day that he would not support Schumer for majority leader. 'I've already said that I told Senator Schumer that I'm going to support somebody else, so it's no different now,' Jackson said. Jackson said he plans to push Democratic leaders on priorities including Medicare for All. House Republicans, meanwhile, face their own leadership battle after Speaker Mike Johnson decided not to seek reelection. Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, chairman of the House Judiciary Committee and a prominent conservative, is competing against longtime Republican leader Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana. The winner would become one of the highest-profile Republican voices on Capitol Hill as the party moves into the minority. The leadership races come as vote counting continues in two unexpectedly competitive Senate contests in Mississippi and Alaska. In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom holds a narrow lead over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. entry.title: Thomas Markle, father of Meghan Markle, arrested on charges related to child sexual abuse material in Florida
entry.summary: Thomas Wayne Markle, the father of Meghan Markle, was arrested Friday morning at an assisted living facility in Lakeland, Florida, on a federal charge of possessing child pornography after investigators said they found suspected child sexual abuse material in two Los Angeles-area storage units he had rented for nearly two decades. The 82-year-old Lakeland resident is charged with one count of possession of child pornography, according to federal prosecutors. He was expected to make his initial appearance Friday in federal court in Tampa. The FBI investigation began after authorities learned in October that a person had signed an affidavit describing the discovery of suspected child sexual abuse material among Thomas Markle's belongings in the Philippines, according to an affidavit filed with the criminal complaint. Investigators later learned Thomas Markle rented a storage unit in the Los Angeles area. Information provided by the person who reported the material in the Philippines eventually led authorities to a second storage unit, according to the affidavit. Federal agents obtained search warrants for both units, which investigators said Thomas Markle had rented since 2008. According to prosecutors, his most recent payments for the units were made through automatic payments last month. During searches of the units, FBI agents seized roughly 78 items, including slides, film negatives and books containing suspected child sexual abuse material, according to the news release. Federal authorities allege some of the photographs show an adult man, identified by a witness as Thomas Markle, with prepubescent girls. Investigators said other photographs appeared to depict Markle with children in various stages of undress. 'These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law,' First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said. FBI officials said the case demonstrates the importance of reporting suspected child exploitation to law enforcement. 'This case highlights the importance of the involvement of the public, even if it's a family member or close friend, to be vigilant and speak up if they have information on individuals they suspect may be preying on and exploiting our children,' Patrick Grandy, assistant director in charge of the FBI's Los Angeles Field Office, said. Thomas Markle is the estranged father of Meghan Markle, the Duchess of Sussex and wife of Prince Harry. The FBI is investigating the case. I

She also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about him had been sent to London police in 2018."It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” Meghan said of the letter. "I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them.”Meghan, an American citizen who starred in the U.S. television drama “Suits,” married Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.Her father, a retired television lighting and photography director, did not attend the wedding, prompting extensive coverage in the British media of Meghan's estrangement from her father.Thomas Markle Sr. was living in the Philippines earlier this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated. entry.summary: Floodwaters leave Fort Pierce chimp sanctuary relying on tractors and a drone for care    WPEC
entry.article_text: Five days after heavy rain flooded parts of the region, water still covers much of the Save the Chimp s sanctuary in St. Lucie County, limiting how staff can reach the property and care for more than 200 rescued chimpanzees. The 150-acre sanctuary is accessible to employees only by tractor, trailer or large off-road vehicle, according to the organization. Save the Chimps said an overflowing local canal, Header Canal, has kept floodwaters from receding. The South Florida Water Management District issued an emergency order this week in response to flooding caused by heavy rain across several South Florida counties, including St. See also: 'I wanted to be by her side': Father remembers Nathalia Filgueiras after deadly jet crash The chimpanzees live on islands with care houses at higher elevations and are safe, sanctuary CEO Ana Paula Tavares said. But standing water across the property and surrounding area has made it difficult for staff to get to work and carry out their responsibilities. A crew of caregivers and veterinarians has used a donated swamp buggy to travel around the sanctuary, but it broke down Wednesday, the organization said. Golf carts used to move food and supplies are also out of service after sitting in 1 to 2 feet of water. A staff member’s truck became stuck in a sinkhole near the sanctuary Thursday morning. The sanctuary said food was being delivered to one chimp by drone. The organization did not provide additional details about the animal or how long the drone deliveries might be needed. Save the Chimps Facilities Director Mark Yohannan is scheduled to speak about the emergency at a North St. Lucie River Water District meeting at 10 a.m. The meeting is scheduled at 14666 Orange Ave. Save the Chimps is a sanctuary for chimpanzees rescued from research laboratories, the entertainment industry and the exotic pet trade.

entry.title: St. Lucie County flips blue after 14 years as voters increase turnout despite floods - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County flips blue after 14 years as voters increase turnout despite floods    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County flipped blue in Tuesday's governor's race for the first time in more than a decade, as voter turnout climbed despite historic flooding that forced last-minute polling place changes. Democrat David Jolly carried the county with approximately 51% of the vote , compared with 48% for Republican Byron Donalds. The result marked the first time since 2012 that a Democratic candidate for governor or president won a majority in St. That year, former President Barack Obama carried the county with 53.42% of the vote. According to TCPalm , voter turnout reached 56.5% in the county, up 5.2 percentage points from the 2022 general election , when 51.3% of registered voters cast ballots. Lucie County ranked 51st among Florida's 67 counties, with only 16 counties reporting lower turnout. In 2022, the county had 238,645 registered voters, with 122,361 casting ballots. See also: Neighborhoods in Jensen Beach go underwater as flooding devastates the Treasure Coast Voters turn out despite historic flooding The increase came as widespread flooding forced election officials to relocate several polling places across Port St. Lucie, Tradition and Fort Pierce, per CBS12 reports . Lucie County Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said the changes were necessary to ensure voters had safe and accessible locations to cast their ballots. Voters assigned to Oak Hammock K-8 School, Centennial High School and the Paula A. Lewis Library were among those affected, with some redirected to the Port St. Lucie Community Center, Indian River State College's Veterans Center of Excellence and Tradition Town Hall. The changes followed heavy rainfall that submerged roads, stranded vehicles and prompted evacuations across parts of the county. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency for St. Lucie County and six other Florida counties, while flooding forced local public schools to close Tuesday and Wednesday. Despite the weather-related challenges, St. Lucie County surpassed its 2022 general election turnout rate while delivering a Democratic majority in the governor's race for the first time in 14 years, when Obama won the county. While the flooding complicated Election Day logistics, the higher turnout suggests those challenges did not prevent overall participation from exceeding the previous gubernatorial election.

entry.title: 'Life turned upside down': Family retains attorney after losing home, livelihood in deadly Learjet crash
entry.summary: Nine people lost their lives when a Learjet crashed into Military Trail in Greenacres on Sunday. But the devastation extends beyond those on board, leaving at least one family on the ground without access to their home, their business and the life they knew before the crash. Now, that family has hired an attorney to investigate what went wrong and determine whether anyone could be held legally responsible. Ricardo Martinez-Cid, a partner at Miami law firm Podhurst Orseck, told WPTV his clients were inside the area impacted by the crash when debris struck, injuring family members and sending them to the hospital. Their home was damaged and remains inaccessible. Their food truck, which they relied on for their livelihood, was also lost. 'We want to be really sensitive in talking about how this has impacted their lives because it's been horrific for them,' Martinez-Cid said. 'But they're sensitive to the fact that nine people lost their lives on board that aircraft, and this is a horrible tragedy.' Martinez-Cid said the family is now grappling with the emotional and financial consequences of a disaster they never saw coming. 'Although my clients, you know, lost their home, they lost their livelihood in the food truck that they operated. They were injured and went to the hospital, and they're dealing with the trauma of what they witnessed and experienced,' he said. 'They're lucky, they're blessed because nine folks lost their lives.' Searching for answers and accountability Martinez-Cid, a board-certified aviation attorney with more than two decades of experience, said his firm is conducting its own investigation into the crash. The goal is to determine what caused the Learjet to go down and whether any individual, company or other entity bears legal responsibility. 'You don't want to jump to conclusions,' Martinez-Cid said. 'But in every aviation disaster ... you're really looking at man, the machine and the environment.' That means examining several potential factors, including weather conditions, pilot decisions, air traffic control communications and the aircraft's mechanical performance. 'We're looking at the weather, we're looking at the piloting, we're looking at how the aircraft responds, we're looking at the communications between the tower and with the pilots,' he said. 'We're going to look very closely at how the aircraft responded to what was going on as well.' Martinez-Cid said his firm has previously handled aviation cases involving aircraft manu
entry.article_text: So families need to get their own answers."Martinez-Cid said his firm plans to work with aviation experts to independently analyze available data, including communications, weather information and the aircraft's performance."So we look at it from all angles, and we make sure our experts get all the data that they can," he said.Martinez-Cid confirmed his firm has also been in contact with attorneys connected to families of people killed aboard the Learjet."We've been contacted by, which is often the case, attorneys that either are friends with the family or have been contacted by the family because of our expertise globally on these issues," he said. "And so we've been speaking to some."He said those conversations are not necessarily limited to potential lawsuits."We have experts that can talk to the families and explain the different things that they're hearing and what's going on, and I think that's an important thing for the family to have."Martinez-Cid previously served as lead counsel for death and injury cases stemming from the 2021 Champlain Towers South condominium collapse in Surfside.He said that experience reinforced the importance of recognizing the different kinds of losses families endure after a disaster.For the family Martinez-Cid represents in Greenacres, the immediate future remains uncertain.Their home is inaccessible, their source of income is gone, and they are recovering from injuries and the trauma of witnessing a deadly plane crash.Martinez-Cid declined to identify the family, saying they are still struggling emotionally with the aftermath.But he emphasized that while his clients recognize how fortunate they are to have survived, their lives have been permanently changed."Their life has been turned upside down," he said. "They're going to be living with this trauma forever. They've lost their livelihood."Still, he said the family remains deeply aware of the grief experienced by those who lost loved ones."Their hearts really go out to those who have lost loved ones," Martinez-Cid said.He hopes the investigation will eventually provide answers for everyone affected by the crash, regardless of whether they were aboard the plane or on the ground."They all suffer loss, and you have to respect each individual family member, and you have to respect each individual case and treat them all with the care and the respect that they deserve," he said.The NTSB investigation remains ongoing, and the cause of the crash has not been determined.

She was gifted, and my soulmate," Allan Filgueiras said Friday, fighting back tears as he remembered his daughter, Nathalia Filgueiras.Nathalia was one of nine people killed Sunday when the aircraft crashed into Military Trail near 10th Avenue North in Greenacres, leaving a crater in the roadway and scattering debris across nearby homes and businesses. A driver on the ground was also injured.Five days later, wreckage remained at the scene as investigators continued working to determine what caused the crash.For Nathalia's father, the search for answers is deeply personal. But he wants the world to remember his daughter not for how she died, but for how she lived.Standing alongside his attorneys Friday, Filgueiras spoke publicly about his daughter's life, her love of aviation and the final moments he has replayed in his mind since the crash.His attorney, Stuart Grossman of Grossman, Yaffa & Cohen, said the family has retained legal counsel but has not filed a lawsuit."It is customary among law firms that the moment they file a lawsuit, to call a press conference," Grossman said. "This is not today's topic. We're suing no one yet."Instead, Grossman said the family wanted to express its condolences to the other eight families grieving loved ones and thank the National Transportation Safety Board for its ongoing investigation."We're not making allegations against anybody at this time," Grossman said. "We're going to do the right thing, and we're going to listen to what the government uncovers. Then we'll have our experts look at it and say they agree or not."But Grossman said the family's decision to speak publicly also serves another purpose: protecting Nathalia's reputation."The purpose of this is to preserve not just her memory but her reputation," Grossman said. "Nathalia was beyond an average pilot; she was extraordinary."Despite her young age, Grossman said Nathalia was highly trained and qualified to serve as co-pilot."She was at the top of her class in everything that she did, and she was perfectly qualified to be the co-pilot on this flight, despite her tender years," he said.Grossman also addressed questions about how someone so young could be flying a jet."When you read that someone's 20 years old, and a co-pilot in a jet plane, you say, 'How can this be?'" Grossman said. "Well, wait until you see her hours, and what the government proves about her capabilities and what her instructors had to say."He described her death as a loss not only to her family but to the aviation community."This is a loss to aviation," Grossman said.Long before Nathalia was flying jets, she was a 12-year-old girl discovering her passion for aviation alongside her father.Allan, a pilot himself, introduced his daughter to flying before she was old enough to drive.Grossman said that the early bond between father and daughter made the tragedy even more painful."My client Allan, who is her father, was the reason why she flew," Grossman said. "From the time she was 12 years old, she, who was a pilot, Allan would take her up, and she fell in love with flying."As Nathalia grew older, that childhood passion became her career.Her father recalled how she would marvel at being paid to do something she loved so much."She said, 'Dad, can you believe? Can you believe that I would pay for this, but they're actually paying me,'" Filgueiras recalled. "It was her happiest moment to fly." Eventually, the roles between father and daughter reversed. Allan, who had once taught Nathalia to fly, found himself learning from her."When we were flying together, I used to instruct her, but then she became my instructor," he said. Now, the same father who taught Nathalia to fly is struggling to understand how her life ended.Filgueiras said he has listened repeatedly to air traffic control recordings from the aircraft's final moments, searching for answers. "I did listen to that many times, trying to find a clue in my head how that happened," he said. "And wow, she's tough."He said hearing his daughter's final moments left him proud of her determination."She made me so proud," Filgueiras said. "She showed me what it is to be a hero."The NTSB has not yet determined the cause of the crash. Investigators are examining the circumstances surrounding the aircraft's final flight.Grossman said the family's legal team intends to wait for the federal investigation before reaching its own conclusions."We'll let you know when the report comes out what our point of view is on it," he said.The attorney also acknowledged the families on the ground whose homes and lives were disrupted by the crash, expressing sympathy for those displaced while investigators continue their work.For now, Filgueiras is focused on remembering his daughter and finding a way forward for his wife and surviving children.Speaking partly in Spanish, he described the loss as having his heart ripped from his chest.He said he knows he must find a way to keep going for his family — and for Nathalia. "Nathalia doesn't want to see a father falling apart," he said in Spanish. "So I gotta — I'm gonna find a way. I'm gonna find a way to make her proud."He also recalled their spontaneous flights together, traveling to places like Key West and Naples just to grab a cup of coffee or something to eat.Those simple moments are now memories he will carry for the rest of his life.And while some families grieve privately, Filgueiras chose to share his heartbreak in front of cameras Friday — not to assign blame, but to honor the daughter he wishes he could have protected.When Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey asked what he would say to Nathalia if he could speak to her again, the grieving father broke down."I wanted to be by her side. To be by her teammates," he said through tears. "I had to be next to her."For a father who spent years sharing the skies with his daughter, it is the one flight he wishes he could have taken with her.The NTSB's investigation into the crash remains ongoing. No cause has yet been determined.

entry.title: Flooding leaves Creekside community in St. Lucie County without power, most homes evacuated
entry.summary: Floodwaters remain knee-deep in parts of the Creekside community in St. Lucie County, where officials say roughly 75% of the neighborhood's homes have been evacuated, and power remains shut off. St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro provided a Thursday update , saying the community, located off State Road 70 west of Florida's Turnpike, has about 150 homes and remains under a voluntary evacuation. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Flooding leaves Creekside community in St. Lucie County without power, Del Toro said some trucks can now make it into the neighborhood, but water levels remain high. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office also has a high-water vehicle available to assist residents who need help. 'If in fact you need help, please don't hesitate to call 911 or contact one of our deputies,' Del Toro said. Deputies are providing 24-hour security in the community while residents remain displaced and electricity is out, according to the sheriff. WATCH AERIAL VIDEO OF THE FLOODING: Aerial video of flooding in the Creekside community of St. Lucie County Restoring power could take additional time because some of Florida Power Light's equipment remains underwater. 'We continue to monitor the water level just like everybody else,' FPL's Marshall Critchfield said. 'Much of our equipment is presently underwater and our priority number one, as always, is safety.' Critchfield said crews will restore electricity as soon as water recedes enough for them to safely access the equipment. Del Toro said the neighborhood has underground utilities, creating an additional challenge while flooding remains high. Officials did not provide an estimate for when power would be restored or when the water is expected to fully recede. Del Toro urged residents who need assistance to contact deputies or call 911.

entry.article_text: Lucie will assist income-eligible homeowners to complete critical home repairs due to this week’s flooding event. With the assistance of the State House Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program, the city will provide financial assistance to low and moderate-income homeowners who need help with emergency repairs to their Port St. The pre-application process opens at 8 a.m. Residents may complete the pre-application online at www.cityofpsl.com/housing. Assistance also is available by contacting the City’s Neighborhood Services Department at 772-344-4084, emailing Housing@cityofpsl.com or visiting City Hall at 121 SW Port St. Eligible expenses may include: Tree and debris removal necessary to restore habitability Payment of Homeowner insurance deductibles for eligible rehabilitation work See also: 'We need help': Neighbors remain trapped by Riviera Beach floodwaters The program will also cover temporary repairs to prevent further property damage, such as: Roof repairs Weatherproofing Water extraction Removal of water-damaged materials Emergency plumbing or electrical work Temporary structural stabilization Other reasonable and necessary actions required to protect the home from additional damage.

entry.title: Floodwaters leave Fort Pierce chimp sanctuary relying on tractors and a drone for care - WPEC
entry.summary: Floodwaters leave Fort Pierce chimp sanctuary relying on tractors and a drone for care    WPEC
entry.article_text: Five days after heavy rain flooded parts of the region, water still covers much of the Save the Chimp s sanctuary in St. Lucie County, limiting how staff can reach the property and care for more than 200 rescued chimpanzees. The 150-acre sanctuary is accessible to employees only by tractor, trailer or large off-road vehicle, according to the organization. Save the Chimps said an overflowing local canal, Header Canal, has kept floodwaters from receding. The South Florida Water Management District issued an emergency order this week in response to flooding caused by heavy rain across several South Florida counties, including St. See also: 'I wanted to be by her side': Father remembers Nathalia Filgueiras after deadly jet crash The chimpanzees live on islands with care houses at higher elevations and are safe, sanctuary CEO Ana Paula Tavares said. But standing water across the property and surrounding area has made it difficult for staff to get to work and carry out their responsibilities. A crew of caregivers and veterinarians has used a donated swamp buggy to travel around the sanctuary, but it broke down Wednesday, the organization said. Golf carts used to move food and supplies are also out of service after sitting in 1 to 2 feet of water. A staff member’s truck became stuck in a sinkhole near the sanctuary Thursday morning. The sanctuary said food was being delivered to one chimp by drone. The organization did not provide additional details about the animal or how long the drone deliveries might be needed. Save the Chimps Facilities Director Mark Yohannan is scheduled to speak about the emergency at a North St. Lucie River Water District meeting at 10 a.m. The meeting is scheduled at 14666 Orange Ave. Save the Chimps is a sanctuary for chimpanzees rescued from research laboratories, the entertainment industry and the exotic pet trade.

entry.title: New $48 million Westlake elementary school stays on track despite heavy rain, flooding
entry.summary: A new elementary school in Westlake is quickly taking shape, with project leaders saying construction remains on time and on budget despite recent heavy rain and flooding. WPTV reporter Christy Waite first toured the construction site in August , when much of the school was still a concrete slab. She returned to the site on Friday and found a much different scene, with the building now taking shape. WATCH REPORT BELOW: PROGRESS ON WESTLAKES NEW SCHOOL Site Superintendent Brad Stapleton said recent weather created challenges for crews, with parts of the construction site underwater. 'We joked that we should have brought kayaks and canoes to work to get from our trailer and parking to the building because a lot of this area that we are standing in now was underwater,' Stapleton said. Despite those conditions, Stapleton said construction has stayed on track. 'We are looking great for meeting the August turnover for the next school year,' he said. Principal Darline Winewski has watched the school rise from the ground up and said seeing the individual spaces inside the building is making the project feel more real. 'To actually see the walls come up and really be able to see the individual spaces, I'm just so excited,' Winewski said. As Westlake continues to grow, the $48 million school will have room for 972 students in pre-K through fifth grade. Winewski said the new school will fill a need for families whose children currently attend two different schools. 'We really have a need for this school in our community. Our families deserve that. Our kids deserve that. They are going to two different schools right now,' Winewski said. Waite also connected with parent Krystal Lexima, whose daughter is looking forward to the new school opening. 'She's so excited to walk the halls for the first time,' Lexima said. Another milestone is coming soon. The school's official name, mascot and colors are expected to be revealed next month. 'We submitted our names to the board and we will find out soon enough and start identifying ourselves officially,' Winewski said.

entry.title: Father of 20-year-old pilot killed in Greenacres Learjet crash shares heartbreaking grief
entry.summary: Five days after a Learjet crashed into Military Trail , killing all nine people on board, the father of a 20-year-old co-pilot is breaking his silence, sharing his grief publicly for the first time and vowing to preserve his daughter's legacy. 'She was gifted. She was gifted, and my soulmate,' Allan Filgueiras said Friday, fighting back tears as he remembered his daughter, Nathalia Filgueiras. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Father of pilot killed in Learjet crash shares heartbreaking grief Nathalia was one of nine people killed Sunday when the aircraft crashed into Military Trail near 10th Avenue North in Greenacres, leaving a crater in the roadway and scattering debris across nearby homes and businesses. A driver on the ground was also injured. Five days later, wreckage remained at the scene as investigators continued working to determine what caused the crash. For Nathalia's father, the search for answers is deeply personal. But he wants the world to remember his daughter not for how she died, but for how she lived. 'She was extraordinary' Standing alongside his attorneys Friday, Filgueiras spoke publicly about his daughter's life, her love of aviation and the final moments he has replayed in his mind since the crash. His attorney, Stuart Grossman of Grossman, Yaffa Cohen, said the family has retained legal counsel but has not filed a lawsuit. 'It is customary among law firms that the moment they file a lawsuit, to call a press conference,' Grossman said. 'This is not today's topic. We're suing no one yet.' Instead, Grossman said the family wanted to express its condolences to the other eight families grieving loved ones and thank the National Transportation Safety Board for its ongoing investigation. 'We're not making allegations against anybody at this time,' Grossman said. 'We're going to do the right thing, and we're going to listen to what the government uncovers. Then we'll have our experts look at it and say they agree or not.' But Grossman said the family's decision to speak publicly also serves another purpose: protecting Nathalia's reputation. 'The purpose of this is to preserve not just her memory but her reputation,' Grossman said. 'Nathalia was beyond an average pilot; she was extraordinary.' Despite her young age, Grossman said Nathalia was highly trained and qualified to serve as co-pilot. 'She was at the top of her class in everything that she did, and she was perfectly qualified to be the co-pilot on this flight, despite her tender years,' he said.
entry.article_text: Five days after a Learjet crashed into Military Trail, killing all nine people on board, the father of a 20-year-old co-pilot is breaking his silence, sharing his grief publicly for the first time and vowing to preserve his daughter's legacy."She was gifted. She was gifted, and my soulmate," Allan Filgueiras said Friday, fighting back tears as he remembered his daughter, Nathalia Filgueiras.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Nathalia was one of nine people killed Sunday when the aircraft crashed into Military Trail near 10th Avenue North in Greenacres, leaving a crater in the roadway and scattering debris across nearby homes and businesses. A driver on the ground was also injured.Five days later, wreckage remained at the scene as investigators continued working to determine what caused the crash.For Nathalia's father, the search for answers is deeply personal. But he wants the world to remember his daughter not for how she died, but for how she lived.Standing alongside his attorneys Friday, Filgueiras spoke publicly about his daughter's life, her love of aviation and the final moments he has replayed in his mind since the crash.His attorney, Stuart Grossman of Grossman, Yaffa & Cohen, said the family has retained legal counsel but has not filed a lawsuit."It is customary among law firms that the moment they file a lawsuit, to call a press conference," Grossman said. "This is not today's topic. We're suing no one yet."Instead, Grossman said the family wanted to express its condolences to the other eight families grieving loved ones and thank the National Transportation Safety Board for its ongoing investigation."We're not making allegations against anybody at this time," Grossman said. "We're going to do the right thing, and we're going to listen to what the government uncovers. Then we'll have our experts look at it and say they agree or not."But Grossman said the family's decision to speak publicly also serves another purpose: protecting Nathalia's reputation."The purpose of this is to preserve not just her memory but her reputation," Grossman said. "Nathalia was beyond an average pilot; she was extraordinary."Despite her young age, Grossman said Nathalia was highly trained and qualified to serve as co-pilot."She was at the top of her class in everything that she did, and she was perfectly qualified to be the co-pilot on this flight, despite her tender years," he said.Grossman also addressed questions about how someone so young could be flying a jet."When you read that someone's 20 years old, and a co-pilot in a jet plane, you say, 'How can this be?'" Grossman said. "Well, wait until you see her hours, and what the government proves about her capabilities and what her instructors had to say."He described her death as a loss not only to her family but to the aviation community."This is a loss to aviation," Grossman said.Long before Nathalia was flying jets, she was a 12-year-old girl discovering her passion for aviation alongside her father.Allan, a pilot himself, introduced his daughter to flying before she was old enough to drive.Grossman said that the early bond between father and daughter made the tragedy even more painful."My client Allan, who is her father, was the reason why she flew," Grossman said. "From the time she was 12 years old, she, who was a pilot, Allan would take her up, and she fell in love with flying."As Nathalia grew older, that childhood passion became her career.Her father recalled how she would marvel at being paid to do something she loved so much."She said, 'Dad, can you believe? Can you believe that I would pay for this, but they're actually paying me,'" Filgueiras recalled. "It was her happiest moment to fly." Eventually, the roles between father and daughter reversed. Allan, who had once taught Nathalia to fly, found himself learning from her."When we were flying together, I used to instruct her, but then she became my instructor," he said. Now, the same father who taught Nathalia to fly is struggling to understand how her life ended.Filgueiras said he has listened repeatedly to air traffic control recordings from the aircraft's final moments, searching for answers. "I did listen to that many times, trying to find a clue in my head how that happened," he said. "And wow, she's tough."He said hearing his daughter's final moments left him proud of her determination."She made me so proud," Filgueiras said. "She showed me what it is to be a hero."The NTSB has not yet determined the cause of the crash. Investigators are examining the circumstances surrounding the aircraft's final flight.Grossman said the family's legal team intends to wait for the federal investigation before reaching its own conclusions."We'll let you know when the report comes out what our point of view is on it," he said.The attorney also acknowledged the families on the ground whose homes and lives were disrupted by the crash, expressing sympathy for those displaced while investigators continue their work.For now, Filgueiras is focused on remembering his daughter and finding a way forward for his wife and surviving children.Speaking partly in Spanish, he described the loss as having his heart ripped from his chest.He said he knows he must find a way to keep going for his family — and for Nathalia. "Nathalia doesn't want to see a father falling apart," he said in Spanish. "So I gotta — I'm gonna find a way. I'm gonna find a way to make her proud."He also recalled their spontaneous flights together, traveling to places like Key West and Naples just to grab a cup of coffee or something to eat.Those simple moments are now memories he will carry for the rest of his life.And while some families grieve privately, Filgueiras chose to share his heartbreak in front of cameras Friday — not to assign blame, but to honor the daughter he wishes he could have protected.When Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey asked what he would say to Nathalia if he could speak to her again, the grieving father broke down."I wanted to be by her side. To be by her teammates," he said through tears. "I had to be next to her."For a father who spent years sharing the skies with his daughter, it is the one flight he wishes he could have taken with her.The NTSB's investigation into the crash remains ongoing. No cause has yet been determined.

entry.title: Schools in St. Lucie, Indian River counties to remain closed Friday due to flooding
entry.summary: Public schools in St. Lucie and Indian River counties will remain closed Friday, Nov. 6, as flooding continues to make some roads, bus stops and school campuses difficult or unsafe to access. Both school districts said they expect schools to reopen Monday, Nov. 9. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Schools in St. Lucie, Indian River counties to remain closed Friday While conditions have improved in parts of St. Lucie County, district officials said a significant number of bus stops and roads remain inaccessible because of flooding. Access to some campuses also continues to be affected. The district said some families and employees remain without power or cannot safely leave their neighborhoods. 'Conditions vary greatly across our county,' the St. Lucie Public Schools District said in its announcement. 'Although some neighborhoods have returned to normal, others continue to experience flooding that makes traveling to school, whether on foot, by bus, or by car, unsafe.' Athletics and SAT testing affected All St. Lucie Public Schools athletic activities are canceled through Sunday, Nov. 8. Athletics can resume Monday. The SAT scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 7, has also been postponed. The district said the test is now scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 21. Each location has a capacity of 100 children. Members can attend any of the participating clubs, regardless of which location they normally attend. entry.title: NFL legends from the Dolphins and Lions honor military service members in Broward County
entry.summary: With the Miami Dolphins and Detroit Lions set to play Sunday, retired legends from both teams met up in Broward County for a little competition while honoring America's heroes. NFL legends from the Dolphins and Lions met up Friday to host military veterans for a fun day ahead of Sunday's showdown. The event saluted 50 active-duty service members through the NFL's Salute to Service. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Dolphins and Lions legends honor military members The service members were put to the test running the 40-yard dash, throwing drills and a shuttle drill. It was hard, but Michael Capozzi looked legit. 'You have insight from NFL legends, and it's cool to play with them and get insight on football. I really like playing, so any chance I get, I'll play,' Capozzi said. While Capozzi is still in his physical prime, you can't say the same about the former NFL guys. 'Hey, this is awesome man, and this is what it's all about for guys that have given so much to come back and give like we are,' retired Detroit Lions offensive lineman Lomas Brown said. 'This is two teams coming together to do a great job of entertaining our military and hanging out with them,' Nat Moore said. 'Well, everybody is having a blast, and the guys that can still run are out running.' 'You right, man big fella used to handle those drills; now I just look at them because I done got a little up there in age. I don't want to pull or tear anything,' Brown said. In Indian River County, floodwaters also pushed an alligator out of its usual habitat and into a residential driveway. entry.title: Port St. Lucie grandmother grateful after flood rescue from van swept into canal - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie grandmother grateful after flood rescue from van swept into canal    WPEC
entry.article_text: Maria Andrade-Vasquez of Port St. Lucie has overcome plenty of challenges in her life. The mother of four, grandmother of 10, cancer survivor and dialysis patient never imagined a routine ride home from treatment would turn into a fight for survival. On Monday, Andrade-Vasquez was riding home from dialysis when floodwaters swept the transport van she was in off the road near Lakehurst Drive and into a canal in Port St. Lucie's Swan Park community. Speaking with CBS12 News through her son, Raul Morales, who translated from Spanish, Andrade-Vasquez said she feared she would not survive. "Yes, very, very scared," she said. Morales said as floodwaters rose around the van, his mother thought she might be living her final moments. Also see: Officer, firefighters rescue two from vehicle swept into Port St. Lucie canal "Seeing all the water go up, she was thinking, what's going to happen? Is this it?" Morales said. Police body camera video released this week shows how quickly first responders reacted. Lucie police said Officer Peterson arrived just 100 seconds after being dispatched to reports of a transport van that had gone into a canal off Southwest Hogan Street. Video captured the officer rushing into the water and rescuing the driver first before learning another passenger was still trapped inside. That passenger was Andrade-Vasquez. As water surrounded the vehicle, rescuers say the van tilted into the canal, leaving her trapped in the back. Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said the same wheelchair equipment used to help Andrade-Vasquez after dialysis treatments was now blocking her escape. "She's wheelchair bound, so the equipment that came out of the back of the van was up in place blocking her in," Niemczyk said. "They had to get her out of the wheelchair and pull her up over the equipment to get her out of the van." According to police, firefighters with St. Lucie County Fire District joined the officer at the scene and worked together to free Andrade-Vasquez from the vehicle. Morales said his mother still struggles to understand how rescuers were able to get her out so quickly. "She said, 'I don't know how they did it, but they quickly released her,'" Morales said. "To me it was amazing to see how quick they did what they did." Both Andrade-Vasquez and the driver were rescued safely. Her rescue was one of dozens of flood-related emergencies first responders handled as rainfall inundated roads and neighborhoods across Port St. Now recovering at home with her family, Andrade-Vasquez remains grateful to the first responders who helped save her life. The way I see it, you guys went the extra mile," Morales said. So thank you." Morales said his mother is still processing the trauma of the rescue but plans to continue her dialysis treatments three times a week as she focuses on her recovery.

Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro provided a Thursday update , saying the community, located off State Road 70 west of Florida's Turnpike, has about 150 homes and remains under a voluntary evacuation. "We continue to monitor the water level just like everybody else," FPL's Marshall Critchfield said. "Much of our equipment is presently underwater and our priority number one, as always, is safety."
