entry.article_text: Nearly a week after a Learjet crash killed nine people in Greenacres and forced hundreds from their homes, some residents are still waiting for an answer to the question that has consumed their lives since the crash.For those who haven't been allowed to return, the cost of being displaced is adding up.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "When are they going to let us back home?" Joseph Santana Quiroz asked WPTV.He hasn't been allowed home all week.He told WPTV he has also had to miss work without pay."If you can't work, they can't pay you?" WPTV reporter Joel Lopez asked."Exactly," Santana Quiroz said.But even without a paycheck, the bills don't stop."We can't tell the bank we can't pay because this happened," Santana Quiroz said.He is one of 31 people still sheltering at the Greenacres Community Center as the investigation continues.Now, organizations are stepping in to help with everything from those immediate financial pressures to the challenges residents could face when they are finally allowed back home.The Emergency Assistance Foundation, a West Palm Beach-based nonprofit, launched the People First Fund for Green Acres Mobile Home Community Learjet Crash to provide direct financial assistance to eligible residents impacted by the crash."We actually are ready and prepared to start taking in grant applications at this time," said Josselyn Hodges, director of the People First Fund Initiative at Emergency Assistance Foundation.She told WPTV the organization normally responds to disasters and hardships around the world, but this time the need is close to home."We are a global public charity that does financial assistance to impacted individuals after disasters around the world. However, we're headquartered here in West Palm Beach, so we felt compelled to help our neighbors," Hodges said.The organization plans to provide $1,000 cash grants to eligible individuals, allowing residents to decide where that money is needed most."Our goal is to be able to provide that financial assistance so people can take care of their most urgent self-assessed needs," Hodges said. "We understand that when people get displaced from their homes, they experience financial hardship in seeking temporary housing, in seeking food and other personal hardships."Hodges said the cash assistance is intended to complement the food, shelter and other services being provided by different organizations."While there may be other organizations that support with food or housing, this financial assistance and cash assistance that will be, landing directly into the hands of individuals is meant to be able to help those individuals, take, buy supplies or take care of whatever items are, heaviest in their mind at this time," Hodges said.Through donations from community foundations and individual donors, Hodges said the fund currently has enough money to provide $1,000 grants to 18 people.But the organization wants to go further."We understand that there are about 68 impacted individuals from the mobile home community, the Green Acres mobile home community, so we are calling on to the community to come together and be able to, turn that compassion into tangible support and help us reach every single one of these members," Hodges said.Hodges said the goal is to raise enough money to provide a grant to all 68 individuals the organization has identified.Residents looking for assistance won't simply have to navigate the process on their own. Hodges said EAF is working with members of the Emergency Operations Center to identify people with the greatest needs and provide them with a direct link to apply.For residents who don't know when they'll be able to return home, Hodges said the goal is to provide some immediate relief while other assistance is still coming together."We believe in the power of community. We know that people wanna come together and help community members in the wake of hardships and disasters, so we have a way to be able to provide that immediate impact now while other resources are still mobilizing," Hodges said. "That is our goal, to be able to support people in the very first critical days of their recovery process."Preparing for what happens when residents return homeThe financial fallout may not end when people are finally able to return.State Rep. Debra Tendrich is working through her organization, Eat Better Live Better, to prepare for another expense some families could face: replacing spoiled food."If you look at what's happening with their electricity being cut off and the power grid shut down, you're looking at people returning to their homes and having to throw out their entire refrigerator full of food that they might have just purchased or or that they need to fill now," Tendrich said.For families already dealing with displacement and lost income, Tendrich wants to make replacing those groceries one less thing they have to worry about."I'm really working right now to make sure that we are able to help fill those refrigerators," Tendrich said.Tendrich's nonprofit operates an affordable farmers market-style food pantry with fresh and healthy items.She said her organization was already seeing an increased demand for grocery assistance before the crash."We, we've been seeing an increased need as is. My organization has received between 25 and 100 new applications every week needing grocery assistance," Tendrich said. "So to pile that up with having to now, have your entire refrigerator needs to be thrown out and then also replenish that just doubles down on how hard times are right now for my community."For Tendrich, it's about helping families move toward some sense of normalcy after days of uncertainty."The last thing that you want to worry about is how are you going to feed yourself, your family and your children after a tragedy like this," Tendrich said.Tendrich said displaced families are also dealing with needs that can easily be overlooked during a prolonged evacuation, including getting to doctor's appointments and accessing medications."Families with their children are trying to get to doctor's appointments, get their medications that they need, uh, we're really trying to make sure that people are accessing everything they need at this moment to get through this while they're displaced from their homes," Tendrich said. "We're doing everything we can between the county, the police, the fire and my office. We're working hard to make sure not only while you're, you're displaced, but once you get back home, we're trying to make sure that you're supported as much as possible during this, this tough time."While groups are getting to work countywide, help continues while families wait as other organizations are addressing needs at the shelter itself.Many other organizations like the Red Cross, and community members have dropped off supplies this week.Dare to Care has been providing mobile showers and laundry services at the Greenacres Community Center."They called us on Monday and said, ‘Can you come out?’ We've been here ever since," said Timothy Murphy, with the organization Dare to Care. "My message to residents is that there are people who care. We're here for those in need no matter what," he said. "When crisis happen it just complies, so we're here to relieve some of the loss."It remains unclear how long all of the impacted residents will be displaced.Click here if you'd like to help make monetary donations.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.article_text: Five days after heavy rain flooded parts of the region, water still covers much of the Save the Chimp s sanctuary in St. Lucie County, limiting how staff can reach the property and care for more than 200 rescued chimpanzees. The 150-acre sanctuary is accessible to employees only by tractor, trailer or large off-road vehicle, according to the organization. Save the Chimps said an overflowing local canal, Header Canal, has kept floodwaters from receding. The South Florida Water Management District issued an emergency order this week in response to flooding caused by heavy rain across several South Florida counties, including St. See also: 'I wanted to be by her side': Father remembers Nathalia Filgueiras after deadly jet crash The chimpanzees live on islands with care houses at higher elevations and are safe, sanctuary CEO Ana Paula Tavares said. But standing water across the property and surrounding area has made it difficult for staff to get to work and carry out their responsibilities. A crew of caregivers and veterinarians has used a donated swamp buggy to travel around the sanctuary, but it broke down Wednesday, the organization said. Golf carts used to move food and supplies are also out of service after sitting in 1 to 2 feet of water. A staff member’s truck became stuck in a sinkhole near the sanctuary Thursday morning. The sanctuary said food was being delivered to one chimp by drone. The organization did not provide additional details about the animal or how long the drone deliveries might be needed. Save the Chimps Facilities Director Mark Yohannan is scheduled to speak about the emergency at a North St. Lucie River Water District meeting at 10 a.m. The meeting is scheduled at 14666 Orange Ave. Save the Chimps is a sanctuary for chimpanzees rescued from research laboratories, the entertainment industry and the exotic pet trade.

entry.title: 'Holy smoke': Floodwaters recede in Indian River County as damage assessments continue - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Holy smoke': Floodwaters recede in Indian River County as damage assessments continue    WPBF
entry.article_text: Floodwaters are receding in Indian River County, but some areas remain affected by standing water as crews and officials work to address the aftermath of this week’s severe downpours. Law enforcement officials said County Roads 510 and 512 were reduced to one lane at one point due to flooding. Crews installed an emergency pipe under the roadway Thursday night to help drain the area. Dave Kubacki, a resident of Sebastian, shared cellphone video of the flooding outside his home. "Holy smoke, I can't believe how much water was out there, and I can't believe how fast it disappeared," Kubacki said. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates He said he was surprised by the flooding, noting that the only time it had been this bad was during a hurricane. "The hurricanes were bad, but I've never seen rain come down like this for such a long period of time and so heavy," Kubacki said. Officials shared video of flooded roads taken just after the severe downpours, along with body camera footage showing deputies responding to incidents caused by the high water. Deputies were called to a residential driveway to secure an alligator that had been pushed out of its usual habitat by the flooding. The alligator was safely relocated to another area within the county. County leaders said assessment teams were out Friday surveying the damage, and results are still pending. Schools in Indian River County were closed Friday but are expected to reopen Monday. Kubacki said he shared the news with his granddaughter. "I said, 'Are you mad that schools are closed?' and she said, 'Oh no!' I said, 'What about your friends?' She said, 'That's OK, I'll see them on Monday,'" Kubacki said. Officials are reminding residents to avoid flooded roads as cleanup efforts continue. entry.title: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday
entry.summary: Family, friends and fellow first responders gathered Saturday to say a final goodbye to 34-year-old St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge. Hodge, a nine-year veteran of the St. Lucie County Fire District, was remembered for his service to the community and the impact he had on the people around him. 'He was somebody who was always ready to help someone,' friend Jeff Lewis said on Nov. 6. WATCH: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday For Lewis, Hodge's legacy is personal. 'He leaves this place a better place than he found it. He was that kind of guy. He found you one way but [would] leave you better than he found you.' On Oct. 24, the St. Lucie County Fire District said Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital, where he later died. His unexpected death has been difficult for those closest to him to process. 'It's a shock to literally all of us,' Hodge's sister, Alexis Hodge, said on Oct. 26. She said one of the hardest parts is knowing she can no longer simply call her brother. 'I love him and I just wish I could pick up the phone and talk to him,' Hodge's death comes just over a year after the family suffered another devastating loss. His brother, Jarius Hodge, was also a St. Lucie County firefighter. Jarius died in 2025. 'We've lost two brothers in one year, can't describe to you the pain' Alexis said. On Saturday, an honor guard, a procession and firefighters standing side by side marked a final salute to Hodge and his nine years of service to the St. Lucie County community.

entry.title: Pinewood Elementary's Richard Acosta named Martin County Teacher of Year - WPBF
entry.summary: Pinewood Elementary's Richard Acosta named Martin County Teacher of Year    WPBF
entry.article_text: Richard Acosta of Pinewood Elementary School has been named the 2026-2027 Martin County Teacher of the Year, the Martin County School District and the Education Foundation of Martin County announced. Acosta was selected from 24 educators representing schools throughout the district. He was earlier named the Elementary Teacher of the Year. The announcement was made during the Education Foundation of Martin County’s Teacher of the Year Awards Celebration on Friday at the MIDFLORIDA Credit Union Event Center in Port St. About 800 people attended the event. It was the 42nd year of the Teacher of the Year Award. “The Teacher of the Year celebration is a special tradition that allows us to pause and celebrate the educators who give so much to their students, colleagues and school communities,” Superintendent Michael Maine said. “We are incredibly proud of all of our school-level honorees and especially proud to recognize Richard Acosta as the 2026-27 Martin County Teacher of the Year. Thank you to the Education Foundation of Martin County and our sponsors for helping make this evening such a meaningful celebration of our teachers.” “On behalf of the Education Foundation of Martin County, I am thrilled to congratulate Richard Acosta on being named the 2026-27 Martin County Teacher of the Year,” Kelley Decowski, president of the Education Foundation of Martin County, said. “We are fortunate to have so many exceptional educators who inspire and empower students every day. Selecting just one to represent Martin County's public schools is no easy task. Acosta exemplifies the passion and dedication that make our teachers so extraordinary.” An educator since 1991, Acosta joined the Martin County School District in 2019 and serves at Pinewood Elementary School as the Related Arts-Science teacher. Acosta brings a hands-on approach to learning that connects classroom instruction to real-world discovery, including helping students tackle challenging concepts or encouraging them to explore the world through scientific inquiry. “After I teach a lesson, I’m always thinking of as I teach that lesson, how can I make it better," Acosta said. "And I’m never tired of it because I teach science. And I’m always one-upping the lesson, and I’m always striving to be better than I was the day before.” At Pinewood, Acosta has helped lead schoolwide STEAM initiatives, chaired the STEAM School Improvement Team, and secured two Martin County Education Foundation grants to support innovative science projects. He also developed a Birds of the Everglades curriculum in partnership with Friends of the Everglades and Inwater Research Group, scheduled to be piloted at Pinewood in fall 2026. His efforts have helped strengthen science instruction and contributed to an increase in fifth-grade science proficiency by 12 percentage points. Acosta exemplifies what it means to be a passionate educator. His love for teaching is evident in every learning experience he creates,” former Principal Susanna Deutsch shared. “His ability to make complex concepts accessible, engaging and meaningful has fostered authentic excitement for learning, with students eagerly sharing their discoveries and newfound knowledge throughout the school.” Miriam Hernandez, an intensive reading teacher at Indiantown Middle School, was named Middle School Teacher of the Year. Hernandez’s career with the Martin County School District began in 2006 as a paraprofessional before she became a teacher in 2012. Since joining Indiantown Middle School in 2018, she has served students in a variety of roles, including Spanish and Intensive Reading, building a reputation as a trusted educator who believes deeply in every student’s ability to grow. “In every role, she has approached her work with professionalism, compassion, and an unwavering belief that every student is capable of growth and success,” Assistant Principal Kellie Siters shared. “She meets students where they are, builds meaningful relationships with them, and works tirelessly to ensure they receive the support they need to thrive both academically and personally.” Marc Turull, an International Baccalaureate physics and chemistry teacher at South Fork High School, was named High School Teacher of the Year. An educator since 2007, Mr. Marc Turull has served students at South Fork High School since 2011. He brings science to life through real-world applications, career exploration and hands-on learning. Outside the classroom, he has been involved in the Engineering Club, First Priority Club and Architecture, Construction and Engineering Mentorship Program, as well as annual STEM experiences that connect students with opportunities and careers in their community. “Marc is widely admired for his ability to foster a positive, inclusive, and engaging learning environment,” South Fork High School Principal Jaime Thompson shared. “He believes that every student can achieve at high levels when provided with meaningful, challenging, and supportive instruction – and he brings that belief to life daily in his classroom.” Felix A. Williams Elementary School earned the Spirit Award for the team that displays the most school spirit. The event’s presenting sponsors were Audi Stuart and Infiniti Stuart, along with Cigna Healthcare, Publix Super Markets Charities, and Keiser University. The nominees are listed on the Education Foundation of Martin County website. The A-rated Martin County School District serves approximately 16,000 students with opportunities. entry.article_text: Two South Florida men were arrested Friday after deputies said they stole 34 aluminum light poles from a Fort Pierce property while St. Lucie County was under a state of emergency due to flooding. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said deputies and the South Florida Criminal Apprehension Team investigated suspicious activity Friday night at a property in the 3500 block of Eleven Mile Road. With help from the Fort Pierce Police Department , investigators used a drone to confirm two people were removing property and loading it into a truck, the sheriff’s office said. Deputies tracked the truck as it left the area and stopped it on Okeechobee Road. See also: Woman accused of inventing newborn baby to scam two West Palm Beach adoption agencies The suspects, identified as Pablo Rojas Castro, 33, of Pembroke Pines, and Alberto Guia Hernandez, 35, of Miami, were taken into custody without incident, according to the sheriff’s office. Investigators said about 34 aluminum light poles, valued at $6,800, were stolen. Castro and Hernandez were booked into the St. They face charges of burglary of an unoccupied dwelling during a state of emergency, traveling across county lines to commit burglary, grand theft during a state of emergency and possession of burglary tools. Lucie County remains under a state of emergency following this week’s historic flooding.

entry.title: 23rd Street gang investigation leads to nearly 40 arrests in St. Lucie County - WPEC
entry.summary: 23rd Street gang investigation leads to nearly 40 arrests in St. Lucie County    WPEC
entry.article_text: A nearly two-year investigation into the 23rd Street gang has led to nearly 40 arrests and the seizure of guns, drugs and cash, law enforcement officials said Thursday. The multi-agency investigation, called Operation Score Board, focused on alleged gang activity in northwest Fort Pierce and surrounding areas. Officials said investigators linked 13 people to an alleged criminal conspiracy involving fraud, drug trafficking, shootings and homicides. Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith said investigators reviewed 10 years of criminal activity and connected people associated with the gang to nearly 100 shootings. Investigators also found that gang members allegedly kept a scoreboard tracking shootings and homicides, which inspired the operation’s name. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said local, state and federal agencies took part in the investigation. The sheriff’s office, F ort Pierce Police Department , ATF , FBI , DEA , Florida Department of Law Enforcement , U.S. Marshals Service and Homeland Security Investigations were among the participating agencies. "Hundreds of shootings over the last decade, violent crime terrorizing the north end of this county, and our community deserves better, and they're getting better because of the hard work of the men and women with the special investigation units that the chief mentioned, and our federal partners here," said Sheriff Richard Del Toro. Officials said about 70 to 80 people are documented as members of the gang. The investigation focused on people police described as shot callers who allegedly directed its activities. Authorities said the 23rd Street gang has been a problem in the Fort Pierce area for decades and was the most violent of several gangs in the city. 4, officers served five search warrants four in Fort Pierce and one in Port St. Lucie beginning around 5 a.m. The operation led to 11 arrests on racketeering charges, with two people still wanted on warrants, and four additional probable-cause arrests, officials said. Authorities said some people connected to the investigation had already been arrested during its earlier stages. 4 searches yielded seven firearms, about one pound of marijuana, 15 grams of cocaine, 50 grams of MDMA and $18,474. Across the investigation, police said they seized 18 firearms, 20 pounds of marijuana, 532 grams of cocaine and two grams of MDPV. "We remain committed to identifying, investigating, and holding accountable those responsible for bringing violence and criminal activity into our neighborhoods," Chief Smith said. "Our message is clear: We will not tolerate organized criminal activity that threatens the safety of our residents." Authorities did not identify the people they believe led the gang, but said they believe they have arrested most of the key players. They said some people connected to the investigation have faced murder charges, but declined to discuss active cases. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro called the operation an unusually large collaboration among local, state and federal agencies. He said investigators took significant players off the streets and that more operations are expected. The sheriff said the case took extensive work to connect years of records and evidence, and involved a 2,000-page report and a 150-page affidavit. Officials also credited the State Attorney’s Office with helping build the case. History of problems CBS12 previously reported on gang violence in the region, including a 2022 ride-along with St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office gang intelligence unit Detective Solomon Archie. Archie said Fort Pierce’s 23rd Street and 29th Street gangs operated on opposite sides of the area divided by 25th Street and Martin Luther King Jr. He also described gun violence as a major concern and said law enforcement agencies were working across county lines to identify suspects and respond to crime. In 2017, CBS12 also reported that the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office had launched a six-month crackdown on gangs and drugs in Fort Pierce. At that time, the sheriff said investigators focused on two violent gangs in Fort Pierce, the 10th Street gang and the 23rd Street gang. That operation resulted in more than five dozen arrests and 50 guns seized.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie recovery efforts continue after record breaking floods - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie recovery efforts continue after record breaking floods    WPEC
entry.article_text: Flooding continues in parts of St. Lucie County as recovery efforts move forward. Lucie police department is getting another look at flooding across the city as the sun rises. Water levels have receded in some areas, but significant standing water remains at several locations, including : SW Cashmere Boulevard Lake Forest HOA St. Bernadette Church NW Country Club Drive Tradition Parkway SW Community Boulevard Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continue to check on residents, monitor roadways and assist people affected by the flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations are also working to support recovery efforts and restore normal conditions safely. Officials are reminding residents to drive carefully, watch for flooded roads and never go around barricades or enter closed roadways. They also encourage people to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. The city thanked residents for their patience and support, noting that helping one another can make a difference as the community recovers. Lucie County moves temporary shelters to new locations St. Lucie County Emergency Management is moving its general population and special medical needs shelters to new locations Wednesday morning to help St. Lucie public schools reopen. The general population shelter is moving from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce. The special medical needs shelter, currently at the Fenn Center, is relocating to the Florida Department of Health’s St. Wednesday, 16 people were staying at the general population shelter and five at the special medical needs shelter. The county opened the temporary shelters with St. Lucie Public Schools and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office to help residents displaced by this week’s historic flooding. Lucie removes flood-damaged vehicles from roadways Officials warn that it could take several days for water levels to recede. Although public works and water management agencies have opened water control structures, recent heavy rainfall and King Tides are limiting where the water can drain. For updates on road closures and other services affected by the flooding, visit the St. Lucie County Emergency Readiness Portal.

entry.title: Win or lose, Dolphins fans keep showing up: loyal supporters and new additions to the Dol-fandom
entry.summary: The Miami Dolphins season hasnt given fans much to celebrate so far as in the win column, but at Hard Rock Stadium, the teams most loyal supporters are still showing up. For some, Dolphins fandom is a lifelong commitment. For others, its a brand-new experience. Suzanne Hobbs attended her first Dolphins game last year and quickly found herself hooked. Im going to learn everything I can about football. Im so excited, Hobbs said. WATCH: Win or lose, Dolphins fans keep showing up Win or lose, Dolphins fans keep showing up She said the energy surrounding the game, from the fans in the stands to the tailgating outside the stadium, made her want to become part of the experience. Everybody around us was so fun, and the idea of tailgating and coming to something regularly and really digging into something and being a fan of a team in your area, thats exciting, Hobbs said. Helping guide her through her new Dolphins fandom is longtime fan Ken Ringe. Its been an up-and-down roller coaster ride, but I love the game. I love the Dolphins. Ill never change my allegiances, Ringe said. Ringe has experienced plenty of highs and lows as a Dolphins fan, including some memorable moments in franchise history. I was at Marinos first game, Ringe said. All these names come back. Ive had great times here with great friends. Now, hes passing that passion along to Hobbs. Were going to tailgate now, Ringe said. Were really going to open up a new world to her and have a lot of fun. This year, Hobbs and Ringe became Dolphins season ticket holders, stocked up on new team gear and plan to attend every home game. For them, Dolphins football has become about more than wins and losses. Its about tradition, friendship and being part of a community that keeps showing up.

entry.summary: Flooding leaves Creekside community in St. Lucie County without power, most homes evacuated    WPTV
entry.article_text: Floodwaters remain knee-deep in parts of the Creekside community in St. Lucie County, where officials say roughly 75% of the neighborhood's homes have been evacuated, and power remains shut off.St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro provided a Thursday update, saying the community, located off State Road 70 west of Florida's Turnpike, has about 150 homes and remains under a voluntary evacuation.WATCH REPORT BELOW:Del Toro said some trucks can now make it into the neighborhood, but water levels remain high. Lucie County Sheriff's Office also has a high-water vehicle available to assist residents who need help."If in fact you need help, please don't hesitate to call 911 or contact one of our deputies," Del Toro said.Deputies are providing 24-hour security in the community while residents remain displaced and electricity is out, according to the sheriff.WATCH AERIAL VIDEO OF THE FLOODING: Restoring power could take additional time because some of Florida Power & Light's equipment remains underwater."We continue to monitor the water level just like everybody else," FPL's Marshall Critchfield said. "Much of our equipment is presently underwater and our priority number one, as always, is safety."Critchfield said crews will restore electricity as soon as water recedes enough for them to safely access the equipment.Del Toro said the neighborhood has underground utilities, creating an additional challenge while flooding remains high.Officials did not provide an estimate for when power would be restored or when the water is expected to fully recede.Del Toro urged residents who need assistance to contact deputies or call 911.

entry.title: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday
entry.summary: Family, friends and fellow first responders gathered Saturday to say a final goodbye to 34-year-old St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge. Hodge, a nine-year veteran of the St. Lucie County Fire District, was remembered for his service to the community and the impact he had on the people around him. WATCH: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday 'He was somebody who was always ready to help someone,' friend Jeff Lewis said on Nov. 6. For Lewis, Hodge's legacy is personal. 'He leaves this place a better place than he found it. He was that kind of guy. He found you one way but [would] leave you better than he found you.' On Oct. 24, the St. Lucie County Fire District said Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital, where he later died. His unexpected death has been difficult for those closest to him to process. 'It's a shock to literally all of us,' Hodge's sister, Alexis Hodge, said on Oct. 26. She said one of the hardest parts is knowing she can no longer simply call her brother. 'I love him and I just wish I could pick up the phone and talk to him,' Hodge's death comes just over a year after the family suffered another devastating loss. His brother, Jarius Hodge, was also a St. Lucie County firefighter. Jarius died in 2025. 'We've lost two brothers in one year, can't describe to you the pain' Alexis said. On Saturday, an honor guard, a procession and firefighters standing side by side marked a final salute to Hodge and his nine years of service to the St. Lucie County community.

In Indian River County, floodwaters also pushed an alligator out of its usual habitat and into a residential driveway. On Friday, the Indian River County Sheriff's Office was on the scene, safely removing the animal from the residence and relocated it to a more suitable area within the county. No one was hurt, and the alligator was unharmed. Body camera video shows Indian River County deputies approaching what appears to be a huge gator. As they capture the critter, video shows the gator thrashing and hissing before deputies get it into a caged van. The video continues to show deputies releasing the alligator back into the wild. In Indian River County, the school district cited limited bus driver availability and significant delays along County Roads 510 and 512. School buildings will be accessible to instructional staff preparing for Monday’s return. Activities and extracurriculars are scheduled to resume Thursday, Nov. Lucie County, the district said flooding has left some bus stops and roads inaccessible and affected access to some campuses. entry.title: Jensen Beach residents still trapped by floodwaters days after historic rainfall - WPBF
entry.summary: Jensen Beach residents still trapped by floodwaters days after historic rainfall    WPBF
entry.article_text: Five days after historic rainfall flooded parts of the Treasure Coast, residents along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are still dealing with several feet of standing water inside their homes, with little indication of when it will recede. The street remains accessible only by boat or kayak, with floodwaters reaching mailboxes and entering most homes along the road. For longtime resident Linda Weisbecker, the flooding has left decades of memories and belongings underwater. “Sixty years of your life is gone. We raised our kids, our grandkids, our great-grandkids. It’s all gone,” Weisbecker said. Weisbecker said her home still has several feet of water inside, preventing her from beginning the cleanup process. “Our main goal is to get this water off so we can get in and start getting things done. If we don’t, it’s going to be that much worse,” she said. Just down the road, Lisa French is dealing with similar conditions. French said her home initially avoided flooding during Monday’s heavy rainfall. However, as water continued to accumulate in the neighborhood, it eventually entered her home two days later. Now, she is concerned about mold growth and how much of her home may need to be torn out and replaced. We’re a single-family income. I stay at home with my kids. So it’s, you know, we don’t even know where to start. And we can’t start because the water is still here,” French said. The affected neighborhood sits near the Savannas Preserve, an area where water can naturally flow south when surrounding land becomes oversaturated. Martin County officials told WPBF 25 News that crews will be working to address flooding concerns and evaluate local watersheds to determine whether they have sufficient capacity to handle floodwaters. entry.title: St. Lucie County asks residents, businesses to report flood damage through online survey - WFLX
entry.summary: St. Lucie County asks residents, businesses to report flood damage through online survey    WFLX
entry.article_text: Lucie County is asking residents, businesses and agricultural property owners affected by recent flooding to report damage through an online survey as officials work to document the extent of the impacts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants across the county, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated St. WATCH REPORT BELOW: County officials said the information collected will be shared with local, state and federal partners to help assess the extent of the flooding and guide recovery efforts. The survey asks respondents to provide the property's location and building type, along with basic information about flooding and damage. It also includes questions about private wells used for household water and septic systems. People can complete the flood impact survey here through Friday, Nov. WATCH: Heavy rains flood Port St. Lucie roads earlier this week County officials stressed that completing the survey is not an application for assistance and does not guarantee that funding will be available. Instead, the information will be used to help officials better understand the scope of the damage. Anyone with multiple affected structures should submit a separate survey for each one. The county is seeking reports about impacts to buildings and their associated systems rather than flooding limited to yards or surrounding property. Residents should only report conditions they have already observed. Officials are warning people not to enter unsafe buildings, walk through floodwater or touch electrical equipment in order to assess damage. Anyone who needs help completing the survey can contact the St. Lucie County Community Services Department at 772-462-1777 or comm_info@stlucieco.gov.

entry.title: 'Holy smoke': Floodwaters recede in Indian River County as damage assessments continue - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Holy smoke': Floodwaters recede in Indian River County as damage assessments continue    WPBF
entry.article_text: Floodwaters are receding in Indian River County, but some areas remain affected by standing water as crews and officials work to address the aftermath of this week’s severe downpours. Law enforcement officials said County Roads 510 and 512 were reduced to one lane at one point due to flooding. Crews installed an emergency pipe under the roadway Thursday night to help drain the area. Dave Kubacki, a resident of Sebastian, shared cellphone video of the flooding outside his home. "Holy smoke, I can't believe how much water was out there, and I can't believe how fast it disappeared," Kubacki said. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates He said he was surprised by the flooding, noting that the only time it had been this bad was during a hurricane. "The hurricanes were bad, but I've never seen rain come down like this for such a long period of time and so heavy," Kubacki said. Officials shared video of flooded roads taken just after the severe downpours, along with body camera footage showing deputies responding to incidents caused by the high water. Deputies were called to a residential driveway to secure an alligator that had been pushed out of its usual habitat by the flooding. The alligator was safely relocated to another area within the county. County leaders said assessment teams were out Friday surveying the damage, and results are still pending. Schools in Indian River County were closed Friday but are expected to reopen Monday. Kubacki said he shared the news with his granddaughter. "I said, 'Are you mad that schools are closed?' and she said, 'Oh no!' I said, 'What about your friends?' She said, 'That's OK, I'll see them on Monday,'" Kubacki said. Officials are reminding residents to avoid flooded roads as cleanup efforts continue. entry.title: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County - cw34.com
entry.summary: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Floodwater has covered much of the pasture at a Martin County farm, leaving its Florida Cracker cattle crowded onto a narrow strip of higher ground as flooding continues in the Trailside community. At Hungryland Farms , the cattle’s usual grazing areas are underwater. The herd has been moved onto the farm’s elevated driveway and house pad, owner Melissa Chirico told CBS12 News. The farm is concerned about the animals’ safety and how long they may have to remain there. The flooding has also affected other ranches and properties in the neighborhood, according to residents and Trailside homeowners association leaders. They say water continued rising even after the rain stopped and have raised concerns about a drainage breach near county-owned land. Martin County acquired a 315-acre parcel known as the Elise J. property in March 2026 for conservation purposes. The county has said it is working with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District on a breach affecting drainage into an irrigation canal. The agencies determined repairs should wait until water levels recede, the county said, citing safety concerns and the risk of damaging the levee. The county is also evaluating longer-term options to improve outflow and reduce future flood risk. The county has said its immediate priority is establishing access to assess conditions. It plans to make repairs when crews can work safely without compromising the levee. See also: Water in the gas: Pumps shut off, driver reports costly repairs after South Florida floods The cattle at Hungryland Farms are Florida Cracker cattle , a rare heritage breed recognized by Florida as the state’s official heritage cattle breed. Descended from cattle brought to Florida by the Spanish in the 1500s, the breed is valued for its connection to the state’s agricultural history. The farm’s photographs and those taken by CBS12's Christopher Pollock show cattle standing on dry ground beside broad areas of standing water. Melissa said the flooding has cut off much of the property and left the herd with limited dry space. The drainage system and the source and volume of water flowing into the area remain central questions for residents.

entry.article_text: Five days after heavy rain flooded parts of the region, water still covers much of the Save the Chimp s sanctuary in St. Lucie County, limiting how staff can reach the property and care for more than 200 rescued chimpanzees. The 150-acre sanctuary is accessible to employees only by tractor, trailer or large off-road vehicle, according to the organization. Save the Chimps said an overflowing local canal, Header Canal, has kept floodwaters from receding. The South Florida Water Management District issued an emergency order this week in response to flooding caused by heavy rain across several South Florida counties, including St. See also: 'I wanted to be by her side': Father remembers Nathalia Filgueiras after deadly jet crash The chimpanzees live on islands with care houses at higher elevations and are safe, sanctuary CEO Ana Paula Tavares said. But standing water across the property and surrounding area has made it difficult for staff to get to work and carry out their responsibilities. A crew of caregivers and veterinarians has used a donated swamp buggy to travel around the sanctuary, but it broke down Wednesday, the organization said. Golf carts used to move food and supplies are also out of service after sitting in 1 to 2 feet of water. A staff member’s truck became stuck in a sinkhole near the sanctuary Thursday morning. The sanctuary said food was being delivered to one chimp by drone. The organization did not provide additional details about the animal or how long the drone deliveries might be needed. Save the Chimps Facilities Director Mark Yohannan is scheduled to speak about the emergency at a North St. Lucie River Water District meeting at 10 a.m. The meeting is scheduled at 14666 Orange Ave. Save the Chimps is a sanctuary for chimpanzees rescued from research laboratories, the entertainment industry and the exotic pet trade.

entry.title: Jensen Beach neighborhood submerged as overwhelmed drainage system keeps flooding homes after rain stops
entry.summary: Much of a Jensen Beach neighborhood on Hyline Drive is underwater after this week's heavy rain overwhelmed the local drainage system. As of Wednesday afternoon, water levels inside some homes are still rising long after the rain stopped. For Lisa French and Tiffany Kincaid, a kayak has become the way to get around their flooded community. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Jensen Beach neighborhood submerged as overwhelmed drainage system keeps flooding homes At Kincaid's home, the water level is waist-deep. 'We're currently taking stuff out of our house right now, salvaging what we can,' said Kincaid. At French's home, the damage has just begun, with the water level climbing to 4 inches deep. 'My floorboards are outside, but it's still rising. My husband made a mark inside so it's still coming up and ours isn't nearly as bad as everyone else,' French said. Their homes are among dozens in the neighborhood under water after Monday's heavy rain saturated the ground and inundated the drainage system. 'We were expecting flooding to go down. There hasn't been rain. Clearly drainage is not things are not draining correctly,' Kincaid said. Martin County told us the neighborhood is uniquely located next to the Savannas Preserve, where water is naturally flowing south from other areas that flooded. For now, the county says it's unable to pump water out of the community because the nearby watershed doesn't have capacity, but relief may be on the horizon. 'As the water level drops, that's going to drain the ponds that we need to pump into, and that's going to allow us to do that,' Martin County's Public Works Director Jim Gordon said. 'We're maximizing what we can downstream, and we might see it trending in the right direction.' Residents are hoping relief comes sooner rather than later so they can start the long road to recovery. 'Even after, like, our houses are wrecked,' French said. 'It's just a lot to take in right now for us,' Kincaid said. entry.article_text: Floodwaters remain knee-deep in parts of the Creekside community in St. Lucie County, where officials say roughly 75% of the neighborhood's homes have been evacuated, and power remains shut off. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro provided a Thursday update , saying the community, located off State Road 70 west of Florida's Turnpike, has about 150 homes and remains under a voluntary evacuation. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Del Toro said some trucks can now make it into the neighborhood, but water levels remain high. Lucie County Sheriff's Office also has a high-water vehicle available to assist residents who need help. "If in fact you need help, please don't hesitate to call 911 or contact one of our deputies," Del Toro said. Deputies are providing 24-hour security in the community while residents remain displaced and electricity is out, according to the sheriff. WATCH AERIAL VIDEO OF THE FLOODING: Restoring power could take additional time because some of Florida Power Light's equipment remains underwater. "We continue to monitor the water level just like everybody else," FPL's Marshall Critchfield said. "Much of our equipment is presently underwater and our priority number one, as always, is safety." Critchfield said crews will restore electricity as soon as water recedes enough for them to safely access the equipment. Del Toro said the neighborhood has underground utilities, creating an additional challenge while flooding remains high. Officials did not provide an estimate for when power would be restored or when the water is expected to fully recede. Del Toro urged residents who need assistance to contact deputies or call 911.

entry.title: Guns, drugs and lots of money: 40 arrested in major Fort Pierce gang takedown - WPBF
entry.summary: Guns, drugs and lots of money: 40 arrested in major Fort Pierce gang takedown    WPBF
entry.article_text: Law enforcement officials in St. Lucie County announced Thursday that 40 suspected members of a Fort Pierce gang have been arrested following an 18-month investigation. The investigation, known as "Operation Score Board," targeted the 23rd Street Gang, which authorities say has operated in northern St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said the gang has between 70 and 80 members and has been responsible for years of violence in the Fort Pierce community. "This gang has terrorized, basically created a hostage crisis for our community up there," Del Toro said. "There’s a lot of good people that are up there in Fort Pierce that have been just held hostage by this group for the last decade, living in fear." Investigators said the gang even maintained a scoreboard tracking shootings and homicides, a discovery that ultimately gave the operation its name. Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith said detectives reviewed a decade of criminal activity to identify connections between suspected gang members and violent crimes. "Detectives conducted an extensive review of criminal activity spanning ten years, examining incidents and identifying connections between individuals associated with the gang," Smith said. "This intensive analysis revealed a disturbing pattern of organized crime and violence." Authorities said investigators used Florida’s RICO law to connect years of alleged shootings, drug trafficking and other criminal activity to members of the 23rd Street Gang. The investigation involved multiple local and state law enforcement agencies working together over 18 months to build cases against suspected members of the organization. On Wednesday, law enforcement officers executed multiple search warrants throughout the Fort Pierce area, resulting in 11 arrests as part of the larger operation. Authorities said officers also seized multiple firearms, drugs and thousands of dollars in cash. Del Toro said the size of the operation and the cooperation between agencies could have a lasting impact on the community. "I’ve never seen an operation this large with this many agencies at the local and federal level," Del Toro said. "I think this is going to have a significant generational impact in this community." Authorities said similar investigations and operations are expected in the future. entry.title: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County - cw34.com
entry.summary: Trailside flooding threatens cattle and renews calls for drainage fix in Martin County    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Floodwater has covered much of the pasture at a Martin County farm, leaving its Florida Cracker cattle crowded onto a narrow strip of higher ground as flooding continues in the Trailside community. At Hungryland Farms , the cattle’s usual grazing areas are underwater. The herd has been moved onto the farm’s elevated driveway and house pad, owner Melissa Chirico told CBS12 News. The farm is concerned about the animals’ safety and how long they may have to remain there. The flooding has also affected other ranches and properties in the neighborhood, according to residents and Trailside homeowners association leaders. They say water continued rising even after the rain stopped and have raised concerns about a drainage breach near county-owned land. Martin County acquired a 315-acre parcel known as the Elise J. property in March 2026 for conservation purposes. The county has said it is working with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District on a breach affecting drainage into an irrigation canal. The agencies determined repairs should wait until water levels recede, the county said, citing safety concerns and the risk of damaging the levee. The county is also evaluating longer-term options to improve outflow and reduce future flood risk. The county has said its immediate priority is establishing access to assess conditions. It plans to make repairs when crews can work safely without compromising the levee. See also: Water in the gas: Pumps shut off, driver reports costly repairs after South Florida floods The cattle at Hungryland Farms are Florida Cracker cattle , a rare heritage breed recognized by Florida as the state’s official heritage cattle breed. Descended from cattle brought to Florida by the Spanish in the 1500s, the breed is valued for its connection to the state’s agricultural history. The farm’s photographs and those taken by CBS12's Christopher Pollock show cattle standing on dry ground beside broad areas of standing water. Melissa said the flooding has cut off much of the property and left the herd with limited dry space. The drainage system and the source and volume of water flowing into the area remain central questions for residents.

entry.title: Okeechobee family forced to rebuild after historic flooding destroys home
entry.summary: A family in Okeechobee is facing a long road to recovery after historic flooding sent more than two feet of water into their home, destroying much of what they spent years building. Jennifer McArthur says her family never expected to experience flooding like this, especially because their home is not in a designated flood zone. Ring camera video captured the frightening moments when the family rushed out of their home with backpacks on their shoulders as floodwaters quickly overtook the property. 'We really didn't have a warning, we knew it was going to rain but that was it. Within an hour everything was under water,' McArthur said. One week later, McArthur took WPTV reporter Brooke Chau inside the home, showing the damage left behind. 'For six years I worked so hard to give my family a beautiful home,' she said. Now, the family is left trying to figure out how to rebuild. 'We never thought we'd have to go through something like this and watch everything that we built and worked for be literally washed away,' McArthur said. The home is currently unlivable, and the family does not know when they will be able to return. McArthur's husband, Richard Maraj, also hopes the flooding will bring attention to drainage concerns in the area. 'This area especially we'd really like to improve the drainage; it's something that as taxpayers we'd really like to see an improvement,' Maraj said. For now, the family is focused on picking up the pieces and rebuilding their lives after losing the home they worked so hard to create. A friend of the family has also set up a GoFundMe to help Jennifer and her family cover home repairs and other essential needs as they navigate the difficult road ahead. Those who wish to help can find the fundraiser here .

entry.article_text: Video above: News and weather for Sunday, November 8, 2026 A southwest Florida resident is in jail on allegations of making threats. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office announced on Sunday, Nov. 8, that 51-year-old Michael G. Davis, from Cape Coral, was arrested on Saturday night in Cape Coral. According to the Lee County Sheriff’s Office, Davis is facing a charge of resisting officers without violence along with an out-of-county warrant from Martin County. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said it was contacted by a concerned citizen on Friday, Nov. 6, about a video that a man, later identified as Davis, posted on the social media platform TikTok threatening the lives of a local student, members of the community and Martin County law enforcement. Investigators reviewed the threats that targeted a school and were able to identify Davis, who posted the video. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said its criminal investigations division and warrants unit worked with the U.S. Marshals Service and the Cape Coral Police Department to arrest Davis. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office added that at first, Davis refused to surrender to law enforcement outside his home but was eventually taken into law enforcement custody. “If you threaten any of our students, our schools, anyone in our community or any of our law enforcement officers, we will use every investigative resource available to identify you, find you and lock you up,” Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said in a statement on Sunday morning. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office noted it is undetermined why Davis targeted Martin County or the specific people he threatened. The following statement by Felix A. Williams Elementary School Principal Sarah Tuthill was posted to the school’s Facebook page on Sunday morning: FAWE Families, This is Principal Tuthill writing to make you aware of a law enforcement investigation involving threatening statements posted on social media that included a reference to our school. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office has been investigating an individual who made multiple threats on social media, including one that referenced a specific student, as well as vague threats against the school. Law enforcement has confirmed that the individual was arrested last night in Cape Coral and is currently in custody. We understand that information of this nature can be concerning for families, particularly when it involves the safety of our students. We also recognize the importance of providing you with accurate information directly rather than leaving families to rely on social media speculation or secondhand accounts. Here is what we want our families to know: -The threatening statements were brought to the attention of law enforcement, which has been actively investigating the matter. -The individual responsible for the statements has been arrested and is currently in custody. -School and District officials are coordinating with the Martin County Sheriff’s Office and will continue to follow law enforcement’s guidance regarding any necessary safety measures. -To protect the privacy of the student referenced in the statements, we will not be sharing identifying information or discussing the student’s circumstances. We anticipate that the Sheriff’s Office will release additional information about this investigation. Because this remains a law enforcement matter, we encourage families to rely on official communications from MCSO for details rather than information circulating on social media. Please know that we remain committed to maintaining a safe, secure, and supportive learning environment for every child and adult on our campus. We appreciate the work of our law enforcement partners and thank you for your continued trust and support. Williams Elementary is located in Stuart. entry.title: St. Lucie County asks residents, businesses to report flood damage through online survey
entry.summary: St. Lucie County is asking residents, businesses and agricultural property owners affected by recent flooding to report damage through an online survey as officials work to document the extent of the impacts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants across the county, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie, St. Lucie Village and unincorporated St. Lucie County. WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County asks residents to report flood damage County officials said the information collected will be shared with local, state and federal partners to help assess the extent of the flooding and guide recovery efforts. The survey asks respondents to provide the property's location and building type, along with basic information about flooding and damage. It also includes questions about private wells used for household water and septic systems. People can complete the flood impact survey here through Friday, Nov. 20. WATCH: Heavy rains flood Port St. Lucie roads earlier this week Heavy rain floods Port St. Lucie roads, leaving drivers stranded County officials stressed that completing the survey is not an application for assistance and does not guarantee that funding will be available. Instead, the information will be used to help officials better understand the scope of the damage. Anyone with multiple affected structures should submit a separate survey for each one. The county is seeking reports about impacts to buildings and their associated systems rather than flooding limited to yards or surrounding property. Residents should only report conditions they have already observed. Officials are warning people not to enter unsafe buildings, walk through floodwater or touch electrical equipment in order to assess damage. Anyone who needs help completing the survey can contact the St. Lucie County Community Services Department at 772-462-1777 or comm_info@stlucieco.gov.

entry.article_text: Five days after heavy rain flooded parts of the region, water still covers much of the Save the Chimp s sanctuary in St. Lucie County, limiting how staff can reach the property and care for more than 200 rescued chimpanzees. The 150-acre sanctuary is accessible to employees only by tractor, trailer or large off-road vehicle, according to the organization. Save the Chimps said an overflowing local canal, Header Canal, has kept floodwaters from receding. The South Florida Water Management District issued an emergency order this week in response to flooding caused by heavy rain across several South Florida counties, including St. See also: 'I wanted to be by her side': Father remembers Nathalia Filgueiras after deadly jet crash The chimpanzees live on islands with care houses at higher elevations and are safe, sanctuary CEO Ana Paula Tavares said. But standing water across the property and surrounding area has made it difficult for staff to get to work and carry out their responsibilities. A crew of caregivers and veterinarians has used a donated swamp buggy to travel around the sanctuary, but it broke down Wednesday, the organization said. Golf carts used to move food and supplies are also out of service after sitting in 1 to 2 feet of water. A staff member’s truck became stuck in a sinkhole near the sanctuary Thursday morning. The sanctuary said food was being delivered to one chimp by drone. The organization did not provide additional details about the animal or how long the drone deliveries might be needed. Save the Chimps Facilities Director Mark Yohannan is scheduled to speak about the emergency at a North St. Lucie River Water District meeting at 10 a.m. The meeting is scheduled at 14666 Orange Ave. Save the Chimps is a sanctuary for chimpanzees rescued from research laboratories, the entertainment industry and the exotic pet trade.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie launches disaster relief program for flood-damaged homes - WPBF
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie launches disaster relief program for flood-damaged homes    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie is providing financial assistance to income-eligible homeowners for critical home repairs caused by this week’s flooding through its Disaster Relief Program, funded by the Florida Housing Finance Corporation. The program, part of the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP), offers support to low- and moderate-income homeowners for emergency repairs to their primary residences in Port St. Eligible expenses include tree and debris removal necessary to restore habitability, payment of homeowner insurance deductibles for eligible rehabilitation work, and temporary repairs to prevent further property damage. These repairs may include roof repairs, weatherproofing, water extraction, removal of water-damaged materials, emergency plumbing or electrical work, temporary structural stabilization, and other actions necessary to protect the home from additional damage. Eligible homeowners may receive up to $25,000 through 0% interest deferred payment loans, with no monthly payments required. Loans are forgiven over a five-year period in accordance with program guidelines. All work must be directly related to the declared disaster, deemed necessary to preserve the safety and integrity of the property, and approved by the city before assistance is provided. Funding is not available for mold or mildew inspection, testing, removal, or remediation. Homeowners must complete any necessary mold remediation before approved repairs can proceed. Eligible repairs may be funded after remediation is complete. Manufactured homes, pools, hot tubs, and illegal or non-permitted work are not eligible for assistance. The city has allocated $1 million for the program, which will run until the funds are exhausted. The program’s pre-application will open at 8 a.m. To qualify, applicants must meet income guidelines, have owned and occupied their home within city limits for at least one year, have an assessed home value of $560,154 or less, and be current on mortgage and property tax payments. 5, residents may complete the pre-application online. Assistance is also available by contacting the city’s Neighborhood Services Department at 772-344-4084, emailing Housing@cityofpsl.com, or visiting City Hall at 121 SW Port St. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

entry.summary: St. Lucie County asks residents, businesses to report flood damage through online survey    WFLX
entry.article_text: Lucie County is asking residents, businesses and agricultural property owners affected by recent flooding to report damage through an online survey as officials work to document the extent of the impacts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants across the county, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated St. WATCH REPORT BELOW: County officials said the information collected will be shared with local, state and federal partners to help assess the extent of the flooding and guide recovery efforts. The survey asks respondents to provide the property's location and building type, along with basic information about flooding and damage. It also includes questions about private wells used for household water and septic systems. People can complete the flood impact survey here through Friday, Nov. WATCH: Heavy rains flood Port St. Lucie roads earlier this week County officials stressed that completing the survey is not an application for assistance and does not guarantee that funding will be available. Instead, the information will be used to help officials better understand the scope of the damage. Anyone with multiple affected structures should submit a separate survey for each one. The county is seeking reports about impacts to buildings and their associated systems rather than flooding limited to yards or surrounding property. Residents should only report conditions they have already observed. Officials are warning people not to enter unsafe buildings, walk through floodwater or touch electrical equipment in order to assess damage. Anyone who needs help completing the survey can contact the St. Lucie County Community Services Department at 772-462-1777 or comm_info@stlucieco.gov.

entry.title: Two men accused of stealing light poles during St. Lucie County flooding emergency - WPEC
entry.summary: Two men accused of stealing light poles during St. Lucie County flooding emergency    WPEC
entry.article_text: Two South Florida men were arrested Friday after deputies said they stole 34 aluminum light poles from a Fort Pierce property while St. Lucie County was under a state of emergency due to flooding. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said deputies and the South Florida Criminal Apprehension Team investigated suspicious activity Friday night at a property in the 3500 block of Eleven Mile Road. With help from the Fort Pierce Police Department , investigators used a drone to confirm two people were removing property and loading it into a truck, the sheriff’s office said. Deputies tracked the truck as it left the area and stopped it on Okeechobee Road. See also: Woman accused of inventing newborn baby to scam two West Palm Beach adoption agencies The suspects, identified as Pablo Rojas Castro, 33, of Pembroke Pines, and Alberto Guia Hernandez, 35, of Miami, were taken into custody without incident, according to the sheriff’s office. Investigators said about 34 aluminum light poles, valued at $6,800, were stolen. Castro and Hernandez were booked into the St. They face charges of burglary of an unoccupied dwelling during a state of emergency, traveling across county lines to commit burglary, grand theft during a state of emergency and possession of burglary tools. Lucie County remains under a state of emergency following this week’s historic flooding.

entry.title: Jensen Beach families still surrounded by floodwater a week after historic rainfall - WPEC
entry.summary: Jensen Beach families still surrounded by floodwater a week after historic rainfall    WPEC
entry.article_text: Eight days after historic rainfall flooded communities across the Treasure Coast, some Jensen Beach families remain trapped by standing water that is several feet deep in parts of their neighborhood. Many homeowners along Hyline Drive say the flooding is unlike anything they've seen before. They estimate water levels remain as high as five feet in some areas, and they say the floodwater is mixed with sewage because many homes in the neighborhood rely on septic systems. "It's just a shame that this happened," said homeowner Todd Doss who's lived in the neighborhood for more than two decades. For Doss and his partner, Susan Boeve, getting to their front door has become more like a game of leapfrog as they carefully step across concrete cinder blocks to avoid the water. See also: After a week of flooding and evacuations, Vitalia response comes to an end "The smell is bad," Doss said. "It has been very uncomfortable, but we're managing. It's kind of like camping." The couple, like many of their neighbors , say they cannot move their cars, take showers or flush their toilets. Despite those challenges, Doss says they consider themselves lucky compared to some of their neighbors. "Some of these people, our neighbors, have lost everything in their house, everything," Doss said. "The flooding in some my neighbors' homes are up to three, four feet high." So far, Doss has managed to keep floodwater out of his home. However, water has entered his Florida room and spilled into his pool. "It's dirty water," Doss said. Leaving is not an option for the family, which includes two dogs, a cat and a pet tortoise named Walter. "We were hopeful that it would drain," Doss said. "After the rain stopped, it started to drain and then the next morning it rose higher. That's when we got scared." See also: After a week of flooding and evacuations, Vitalia response comes to an end Neighbors gathered Sunday for a flood relief meeting with county leaders, hoping for answers about when conditions might improve. But officials told neighbors they do not know when the water will recede. With nowhere to put the water, some homeowners fear it could take months before the flooding fully subsides. "It's extremely frustrating," said homeowner Mike Bresette. Bresette said the neighborhood has experienced flooding before and believes infrastructure improvements should have been made years ago. "They've had since 2011 to make changes to the infrastructure for drainage and no one's done anything," Bresette said. "I went to that meeting this morning and I didn't get one iota of information about what they're going to do after this is over to fix the problem for long term." For many homeowners, the concern now is what happens if more rain falls before the standing water disappears. "If we have one more bad rain, we will definitely be flooded," Doss said. The neighborhood is not located in a designated flood zone, meaning many homeowners do not carry flood insurance. While Florida has declared a state of emergency that includes Martin County, homeowners say they are hoping the governor requests a federal disaster declaration that could allow FEMA to provide assistance.

entry.article_text: Five days after historic rainfall flooded parts of the Treasure Coast, residents along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are still dealing with several feet of standing water inside their homes, with little indication of when it will recede. The street remains accessible only by boat or kayak, with floodwaters reaching mailboxes and entering most homes along the road. For longtime resident Linda Weisbecker, the flooding has left decades of memories and belongings underwater. “Sixty years of your life is gone. We raised our kids, our grandkids, our great-grandkids. It’s all gone,” Weisbecker said. CLICK HERE FOR INFORMATION ON HOW TO DONATE TO THE WEISBECKER FAMILY Weisbecker said her home still has several feet of water inside, preventing her from beginning the cleanup process. “Our main goal is to get this water off so we can get in and start getting things done. If we don’t, it’s going to be that much worse,” she said. Just down the road, Lisa French is dealing with similar conditions. French said her home initially avoided flooding during Monday’s heavy rainfall. However, as water continued to accumulate in the neighborhood, it eventually entered her home two days later. CLICK HERE FOR INFORMATION ON HOW TO DONATE TO THE FRENCH FAMILY Now, she is concerned about mold growth and how much of her home may need to be torn out and replaced. We’re a single-family income. I stay at home with my kids. So it’s, you know, we don’t even know where to start. And we can’t start because the water is still here,” French said. The affected neighborhood sits near the Savannas Preserve, an area where water can naturally flow south when surrounding land becomes oversaturated. entry.title: Brightline train strikes, kills pedestrian in St. Lucie County - WPBF
entry.summary: Brightline train strikes, kills pedestrian in St. Lucie County    WPBF
entry.article_text: A pedestrian was struck and killed by a Brightline train on Sunday afternoon in Port St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office said. At approximately 1:10 p.m., deputies responded to a report of a pedestrian struck by a train on the railroad tracks about a mile north of Walton Road and near Savannas Preserve State Park. The tracks, which run east of U.S. 1, are operated by Florida East Coast Railway. Freight trains also use the route. Preliminary information indicates that a northbound train struck a person who entered the path of the approaching train, a sheriff's office spokesman told WPBF. The circumstances surrounding this incident remain under investigation. "Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the victim's family and friends during this difficult time," the agency said. Some other northbound trains were affected. Brightline trains go between Miami and Orlando. 22, 2023, the private company extended service from West Palm Beach to a new station at Orlando International Airport. Brightline trains reach maximum operating speeds of 110 mph from West Palm Beach to Cocoa, and up to 125 mph on the dedicated track between Cocoa and Orlando International Airport. They go at a maximum operating speed of 79 mph on the track segment between Miami and West Palm Beach. There are no train stations between West Palm Beach and Orlando. There are plans for a a Brightline station in downtown Stuart, though the project faces significant funding and operational hurdles.

entry.article_text: Five days after heavy rain flooded parts of the region, water still covers much of the Save the Chimp s sanctuary in St. Lucie County, limiting how staff can reach the property and care for more than 200 rescued chimpanzees. The 150-acre sanctuary is accessible to employees only by tractor, trailer or large off-road vehicle, according to the organization. Save the Chimps said an overflowing local canal, Header Canal, has kept floodwaters from receding. The South Florida Water Management District issued an emergency order this week in response to flooding caused by heavy rain across several South Florida counties, including St. See also: 'I wanted to be by her side': Father remembers Nathalia Filgueiras after deadly jet crash The chimpanzees live on islands with care houses at higher elevations and are safe, sanctuary CEO Ana Paula Tavares said. But standing water across the property and surrounding area has made it difficult for staff to get to work and carry out their responsibilities. A crew of caregivers and veterinarians has used a donated swamp buggy to travel around the sanctuary, but it broke down Wednesday, the organization said. Golf carts used to move food and supplies are also out of service after sitting in 1 to 2 feet of water. A staff member’s truck became stuck in a sinkhole near the sanctuary Thursday morning. The sanctuary said food was being delivered to one chimp by drone. The organization did not provide additional details about the animal or how long the drone deliveries might be needed. Save the Chimps Facilities Director Mark Yohannan is scheduled to speak about the emergency at a North St. Lucie River Water District meeting at 10 a.m. The meeting is scheduled at 14666 Orange Ave. Save the Chimps is a sanctuary for chimpanzees rescued from research laboratories, the entertainment industry and the exotic pet trade.
