entry.title: Palm Beach County school district employee accused of soliciting person he believed was 14-year-old boy
entry.summary: A Palm Beach County School District employee was arrested after police said he had sexually explicit conversations with an undercover detective posing as a 14-year-old boy. Boynton Beach police said Donald Rush, 65, of Lake Worth was arrested following an investigation by the department's Human Exploitation Task Force. According to police, detectives posed as a 14-year-old boy advertising lawn mowing services on Craigslist's Community messaging board. Investigators said they were contacted by someone using the screen name 'Palm Guy,' who was later identified by police as Rush. Police said Rush asked the person his age, whether adult men had approached him about sexual activity and whether he had told his parents about those interactions. The conversation later moved to text messages, according to police. Detectives said they again made clear that the person Rush was communicating with was supposedly 14 years old. Despite the stated age, police allege Rush continued the conversation, asking sexually explicit questions and making statements about his own sexual activity. With assistance from the Palm Beach County School Board Police Department, detectives located and interviewed Rush. Boynton Beach police said Rush admitted his involvement during that interview. Police said Rush also claimed during the investigation that he was a youth pastor. The department did not identify a church or organization with which he was allegedly affiliated. Rush faces charges of solicitation of a minor to engage in sexual conduct and unlawful use of a two-way communications device, according to police. He was being held at the Palm Beach County Jail. Police identified Rush as an employee of the Palm Beach County School District. However, the department did not specify his position with the district. Investigators said they believe there could be additional victims. Anyone who believes they may have been victimized by Rush or has information about similar incidents involving him is asked to contact Boynton Beach police Detective Joseph at 561-742-6158.

It has now been closed for more than a week following the crash.The closure has been particularly difficult for a business with 15 employees and bills that did not stop when customers could no longer get through."Financially wise, it's been a pretty economical impact, considering we've got 15 employees and we've got a lot of businesses in the area," Rivera said.Add on the lost sales, customers, food waste, rent and payroll continuing to add up."Anything helps at this point, especially if it comes to payroll because we've got 15 employees trying to survive as well and help out as much as we can personally, but if we can have the county do some sort of grant program or maybe talk to the state or maybe talk to some at federal level that they can have some sort of help with us, that'll be great," Rivera said.Now, Palm Beach County is preparing to offer some of that help.The county's proposed Military Trail Business Interruption Grant Program would set aside $250,000 in Ad Valorem funds for eligible businesses affected by the incident and the associated Military Trail closure. Businesses could receive up to $5,000, depending on eligibility, available funding and the county's calculation of each award.Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said the program was created after businesses began reaching out about the financial strain caused by the closure."We've been receiving hundreds of calls about when are we gonna reopen. You know, we have employees, we have people that need to get paid that are not getting paid," Flores said. "We need to be able to cover our own rent, and a lot of these are small businesses. These are mom-and-pop shops, and we wanna make sure that we take care of them."For businesses like Rivera's, even that amount could make a meaningful difference."Absolutely. That at least helps out for half of the payroll so we can get, you know, at least help them go on because I've got employees that got bills to pay as well," Rivera said.Businesses will have to apply through the County's Housing and Economic Development Department.The money can be used for expenses including rent or mortgage payments, employee payroll, utilities, essential inventory and supplies and other approved operating costs. It cannot be used for personal expenses, expansion, owner distributions or expenses already covered by insurance or other assistance.The grants are capped at $5,000. Only one award is allowed per legal business as they take steps to return to normalcy.The county’s proposed $250,000 business grant program is not the only financial assistance being brought into the recovery effort. Flores said more than $50,000 has also been raised through United Way from the private sector, with funding going to Catholic Charities to help provide temporary housing, rental cars and Uber and Lyft vouchers for people affected by the crash.Separate from the county’s proposed assistance for businesses, the Emergency Assistance Foundation, a West Palm Beach-based nonprofit, is offering $1,000 cash grants to eligible residents impacted by the crash through its People First Fund. He said the county's goal was to get residents back within the coming days, or by the end of the week at the latest, as long as officials determine the area is safe.Businesses could also begin reopening within days, according to Flores, although work remains underway around the crash site and there is not yet a firm date for Military Trail to completely reopen.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Flood-damaged Florida homeowners may qualify for property tax break. Here's what to know
entry.summary: In some areas of South Florida and the Treasure Coast, the flooding from last week's heavy rains persists. 'It's been a definite challenge,' says Jesse Cabral in the Grand Isles condos, located off Haverhill Road in West Palm Beach. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Flood damage could qualify homeowners for tax break The water around his condo is still over ankle - deep and laps up to his garage. 'It didnt come into the unit itself, but it did flood my garage and did do a lot of damage in there,' Cabral said. For some homeowners, flood damage can lead to a break on property taxes. 'Under Florida law, homeowners whose residences are uninhabitable for at least 30 consecutive days due to a catastrophic event may qualify for a partial property tax refund,' according to an email from Palm Beach County Appraiser Dorothy Jacks. Homeowners seeking a refund for damage must submit an Application for Catastrophic Event Tax Refund (Form DR-465) and supporting documentation by March 1, 2027. Damage sustained during this flooding will not change a property's 2026 assessment but may affect its 2027 assessment if repairs remain incomplete as of Jan. 1, 2027. Having flood insurance is still the best protection from sudden flooding events, even in areas not known for flooding in the past. 'This isn't a designated flood zone, and I didn't get flood insurance, so it might be a problem,' Cabral said.

entry.title: West Palm Beach neighbors say they've been flooded in for a week with no answers on who will help them recover
entry.summary: Eight days after the rain stopped, neighbors in a West Palm Beach community remain flooded, and they say they are not getting the answers they need to get their lives back on track. In communities like Hamilton Bay, located off of Jog Road, people know they need help a week after record rainfall moved out. But they say their requests are falling on deaf ears. So I set out to answer one of their biggest questions: Who is accountable for providing that help? WATCH REPORT BELOW: West Palm Beach residents still flooded 8 days after rain 'I don't know if who's responsible, the HOA, the city,' Juliet Bradford said as she drove a rented Jeep through floodwaters. She told me her car had been totaled in those same floodwaters. 'It's unacceptable,' Bradford said. Jackie Copan, standing on the dry upper portion of her driveway, said she hadn't left her home since last Tuesday, when she waded through floodwaters to vote. 'We brought a stick in case we saw a gator,' Copan noted. By Monday, the water had somewhat subsided in Hamilton Bay since last week. But the frustration among neighbors has not. Sal Pahzoor said at one point, water had gotten into his garage, where he now stores the inflatable canoe and life vests he bought last week. 'The water has been mixed with the sewage. We've not had bulk pick up all week long,' Williams said. 'We are very disappointed about this. I know I am.' 'I've been living in West Palm Beach for 30 years. With significant standing water remaining in these communities, the City is focused on residents’ safety and is continuing to coordinate with the agencies responsible for drainage while providing direct assistance where possible.The Hamal Community Development District (CDD) is responsible for maintaining the community’s surface water management system. Its existing system has two pumps that currently cannot operate simultaneously. The Northern Palm Beach County Improvement District (NPBCID) has provided two additional pumps, and Hamal CDD informed the City this morning that an electrician is being brought in to enable its two pumps to operate concurrently.Since the beginning of this event, the City has maintained ongoing communication with the NPBCID and has also made direct outreach to Hamal CDD, offering personnel, equipment, and technical assistance. Both districts have informed us that there is nothing further the City can do at this time to assist with drainage operations. The City is not withholding permits, delaying improvements on the current pumping and drainage efforts. We will continue monitoring conditions, coordinating with the responsible agencies and offering assistance as needs change.While the drainage system is outside our jurisdiction, our commitment to these residents is not. The City partially activated its Emergency Operations Center on November 2. Since then, City crews have been working around the clock to respond to flooding throughout West Palm Beach, while continuing to provide direct assistance to residents in these communities. This includes offering transportation to shelters for residents unable to leave their neighborhoods and helping hospice nurses reach patients when they were flooded in. entry.title: Martin County school increases security after TikTok threat suspect is released on bond - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County school increases security after TikTok threat suspect is released on bond    WPEC
entry.article_text: Less than 12 hours after he was booked into jail, a Cape Coral man accused of making TikTok threats involving a Stuart elementary school was out on a $100,000 bond. By Monday morning, deputies were watching the school entrance, and Jessica and John Greisen had decided to keep their third grader home. Wanted to vomit, Jessica Greisen said. She recalled thinking, My child is not going to school. Their daughter, Teigan, attends Felix A. Williams Elementary School. Classes went on as planned Monday. CBS12 News saw several sheriff’s office vehicles near the entrance. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said it would also add deputies at several other schools as a precaution. Principal Sarah Tuthill told families Sunday evening that deputies were monitoring the situation and the school would stay open. In response, some parents asked whether absences would be excused and whether their children could complete assignments at home. Tuthill’s message did not address those questions. How detectives found the threats A tip late Friday led detectives to TikTok videos in which Michael George Davis, 51, threatened to kill law enforcement officers, the sheriff’s office said. Sheriff John Budensiek said the videos were repeatedly posted and taken down. In one video reviewed by CBS12 News, Davis said he was going to shoot people. As many as I can, dawg, as soon as I get there, he said. Budensiek said the threat in that video was directed at law enforcement officers. As detectives looked through the account, they found a separate post naming Felix A. So it went from threatening law enforcement to threatening Jews to threatening one of our students here in Martin County, Budensiek said. See also: HOA tries to block billionaire Larry Ellison’s home purchases for staff The sheriff said the post also threatened a local family. Tuthill described the threats against the school as vague and said the posts referenced a specific student. Budensiek said the student hasn’t attended Felix A. Williams in years, but Davis appeared to believe the student was still there. An alleged dispute dating back to 2006 2014 Davis lives in Cape Coral, but Budensiek said he surfed in Martin County years ago. The sheriff said Davis appeared to link the family he named online to a dispute he claims happened sometime between 2006 and 2014. Budensiek also described a later incident Davis claims happened at a gym. According to that account, people Davis associated with a surf group were supposed to spot him while he lifted weights. Davis claims they failed to do so and a significant amount of weight fell on his chest. Budensiek said investigators found no direct connection between the alleged dispute and the family. They have no idea what he’s talking about, he said. Arrested Saturday night, released Sunday afternoon Martin County investigators worked with Cape Coral police and a U.S. Marshals fugitive task force to arrest Davis at his Cape Coral home Saturday night on a felony warrant for written threats to kill. The sheriff’s office said Davis initially refused to come outside. Budensiek said deputies found no weapons when they arrested Davis. He said investigators were unaware of any prior arrests or any instances in which Davis was taken for an involuntary mental health evaluation under Florida’s Baker Act. Lee County jail records show Davis was booked at 2:53 a.m. Sunday and released at 2:12 p.m. on a $100,000 bond on the Martin County warrant. The records list a separate $1,000 bond on a charge of resisting an officer without violence, with a hearing set for Nov. I was hoping that $100,000 bond he would still be sitting in jail, and our parents, especially our school parents, wouldn’t have to worry, Budensiek said. The Greisens said they want to know whether Davis is being monitored and what restrictions he faces while out on bond. Is he wearing an ankle monitor? Why was he even released first off? Budensiek said Davis rides an e-bike, his driver’s license was suspended and deputies don’t know of a car he uses. The sheriff said that makes it harder to track his movements. But just the mere fact that he’s out of jail does create an opportunity for a threat, Budensiek said. What happens next Budensiek urged parents to stay vigilant and asked anyone who sees Davis in Martin County to call the sheriff’s office. He said deputies would maintain extra security at Felix A. Williams and that his office would support parents as they decide what’s best for their children. Jessica Greisen said she was grateful deputies made the arrest. The couple said they’ll keep Teigan home until they get answers about the precautions in place. Their education is important to us, but their safety is more important, she said. Detectives are still working with Cape Coral police. Budensiek said investigators recovered a device and are seeking a warrant to search it. His office also sent preservation requests to TikTok. We are working diligently to come up with other cases and other charges that may change that, but we are not there yet, Budensiek said. He said he expects more charges in Martin County and that other jurisdictions could also bring charges.

entry.article_text: A southwest Florida resident is accused of making threats on TikTok against Felix A. Williams Elementary School in Stuart, law enforcement officers and members of the Martin County community. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said Sunday that 51-year-old Michael G. Davis, from Cape Coral, was arrested on Saturday night in Cape Coral on a Martin County warrant directly related to those threats. He was released from the Lee County Jail on Sunday after posting a $100,000 bond. "We know parents are concerned about his release," the sheriff's office posted on Facebook. "As a precaution, you’ll see more deputies at and around Felix A. Williams Elementary School and at several other Martin County schools. Davis uses a bicycle as his primary form of transportation, MCSO said. "If you think you see Davis in Martin County or notice anything suspicious, please call the Martin County Sheriff’s Office," the agency said. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said it was contacted by a concerned citizen on Friday, Nov. 6, about a video that a man, later identified as Davis, posted on the social media platform TikTok threatening the lives of a local student, members of the community and Martin County law enforcement. Investigators reviewed the threats that targeted a school and were able to identify Davis, who posted the video. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said its criminal investigations division and warrants unit worked with the U.S. Marshals Service and the Cape Coral Police Department to arrest Davis. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office added that at first, Davis refused to surrender to law enforcement outside his home but was eventually taken into law enforcement custody. “If you threaten any of our students, our schools, anyone in our community or any of our law enforcement officers, we will use every investigative resource available to identify you, find you and lock you up,” Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said in a statement on Sunday morning. Please pardon our interruption this evening. We want to provide an update regarding the individual recently arrested in connection with social media threats that included references to our school community. The individual has since been released on bond. We understand that this news may raise concerns among our families and employees, and we want to reassure you that the Martin County Sheriff’s Office is fully aware of the individual’s release and continues to monitor the situation closely. Out of an abundance of caution, the Sheriff’s Office will have an increased law enforcement presence on our campus. This is a proactive precaution being taken in coordination with our law enforcement partners, who remain actively engaged in monitoring the situation and protecting our school community. We appreciate our families and employees for remaining alert and taking matters involving school safety seriously. At the same time, we want to emphasize that our law enforcement partners are closely monitoring this matter and taking appropriate precautions to safeguard our campus. School will remain open, and teaching and learning will continue as planned. Our priority is to ensure that students and staff feel safe, supported, and able to focus on the important work taking place in our classrooms each day. Thank you for your continued trust, understanding, and partnership. We are grateful to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office for its vigilance and ongoing commitment to the safety of our students, employees, and families.

entry.title: Fort Pierce chimp sanctuary recovers after historic flooding - WPBF
entry.summary: Fort Pierce chimp sanctuary recovers after historic flooding    WPBF
entry.article_text: Save the Chimps, a 150-acre chimpanzee sanctuary in Fort Pierce, is recovering after 19 inches of rain caused historic flooding, disrupting operations and making it difficult for staff to care for more than 200 rescued chimpanzees. Mark Yohannan, facilities director at Save the Chimps, said water levels have dropped significantly, allowing staff to regain access to most of the sanctuary’s roads. "We've probably lost at least 7 or 8 inches of water. Now we have 1.2 miles of road here on property, 90% of that we can actually see and drive on. We expect the last little bit to dry up overnight," Yohannan said. Before the water began receding, staff faced challenges, including delivering food to a chimpanzee via drone. The sanctuary has 12 islands that house 11-21 chimpanzees in a family group. In total, there are 211 chimpanzees on the property. "We saw that we had a situation. Caleb was the one that stayed out; he loves his island as many others do," said Ana Paula Tavares, CEO of Save the Chimps. "He decided he was going to stay out until he realized that he was not going to be able to go indoors anymore because of the land bridge that connects the island to his indoor house got flooded as well. Not on all the islands, but on that island. That's when we had to get creative and think, how can we drop fluid and food?" The sanctuary’s chimps live on islands with care houses situated on higher ground, but staff struggled to navigate the flooded property. "We have a lot of golf carts that care staff use to move themselves, staff, 3,000 pounds of food a day, and so, those were rendered inoperable because you couldn't see the road; they're battery carts... Not to mention some were damaged," Yohannan said. Employees have been relying on tractors, trailers, and large off-road vehicles to access the sanctuary. An overflowing header canal has slowed the water’s recession. On Monday, Yohannan met with the St. Lucie Water River District to discuss the flooding. "We left with the understanding that everyone already knows. This rain event was a 200-year event, and I think that the county's working as hard as they can to get stuff moving," Yohannan said. Despite the historic flood, rescue leaders felt they were mostly prepared but acknowledged areas for improvement. "The one thing that came to mind is we have insurance...very good insurance but not flood insurance because we didn't have floods in Florida. So now we do, or now we will look into that...that was one lesson learned," Tavares said. Yohannan added, "We would have needed some very large pumps, watched the forecast a little better maybe...but other than that I think we're in the same boat as all the other neighbors. It's the first thing that's rained this hard in 200 years; I don't know what we could've done to be more prepared." Aubrey Greene shared with CBS12 News that they had a great citrus season last year, and we’re anticipating another good year this year, that was until the flooding put their crops, trees, and livestock in jeopardy. Greene Sugars boasts 800 acres of lemon trees, 50 acres of sugar belle trees, and 1000’s of cattle. They put out roughly 60,000-80,000 boxes of citrus per year and have a contract with Coca-Cola. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium Greene shared that the farm was hit with over 10 inches of rain in one single night, and that the citrus groves have been flooded trunk to trunk in water for over a week, despite heavy pumping every morning and night. entry.title: Keiser football faces must-win season finale with playoff streak on the line
entry.summary: Since 2019, the Keiser University football team has made the NAIA football playoffs each season, including making it to the title game the last four years, but that streak could be in jeopardy. 'We always talk about process over results, and I know the results have shown us going to countless amount of national championships but we continue to focus on the process of what got us there,' said head coach Myles Russ. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Keiser's playoff streak comes down to season finale Keiser's push to national prominence is thanks to an all-in approach by every man on the team, and for the last few years the leader of that attack was Shea Spencer, the former quarterback who led Keiser to two straight national title appearances. These days, however, a new signal caller, JT Tabora, has taken over. 'It's been awesome being the quarterback here at Keiser. I've been backup for the past two years, and it's been great learning behind him, and giving me the opportunity to start this year has been great,' said Tabora. In seven games this season, the sophomore has passed for 1,300 yards and 13 touchdowns. While his numbers are strong, the Seahawks find themselves in uncharted waters. They're 6-3 and ranked 15th overall in the country, and after suffering a loss Saturday, the fellas could fall out of the top 15. Sounds like no problem, right? Well, only the top 15 teams are guaranteed a spot in the NAIA Playoffs, making Saturday's season finale against Warner a must-win. 'I think we can clean up some things, that's our mindset: just clean up some things, and once we get those things (fixed), were a tough team to beat,' Tabora said.

entry.summary: Port St. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie City Council approved the site plan Monday for a proposed 6,000-seat soccer stadium at Walton & One , clearing another step for the project planned near U.S. 1, SE Village Green Drive and Walton Road. The council held a brief discussion before approving the plan, which calls for seven buildings totaling 133,412 square feet on city-owned land. The development would include the stadium, a cabana, concession and restroom facilities, and three retail buildings. The stadium is proposed to stand 61 feet tall. Its LED scoreboard could reach 85 feet, while field-light poles could rise to 135 feet. The project is planned in four phases, beginning with the approximately 97,296-square-foot, two-story stadium, followed by the retail buildings. The site-plan approval comes as the city advances related zoning and sign-program changes to allow the stadium and its taller lights and scoreboard. The city’s agenda listed those measures for second reading Monday. Staff recommended approval of the site plan subject to recording a replat; the project also has outstanding requirements involving water and sewer service, drainage plans and public art. RELATED: PSL has spent decades searching for a downtown. Could a new vision finally create one? The stadium is planned as the home of Port St. Lucie SC , a United Soccer League League One team. The club is expected to begin play in 2027, with matches at the new stadium planned to begin in 2028. The venue is also intended to host concerts, festivals and other events. The stadium is part of the broader Walton & One redevelopment, envisioned as a mix of residential, retail, office, hotel and entertainment uses. The city says it acquired 22 parcels in the district in 2022 and that the stadium is intended to help spur development there. Parking for stadium events would use other city-owned parcels under a parking license in the operating arrangement. The site-plan review also included a traffic analysis and a special-event traffic plan reviewed by police and Public Works. Residents have previously raised concerns about traffic near the proposed site . The city says the project will not use money from its general fund. Under the city’s published project terms, the developer could be reimbursed for up to 50% of eligible stadium and infrastructure costs through community redevelopment agency tax-increment revenue, capped at $27.5 million.

entry.title: Residents wait for FEMA assistance after Florida puts in request after widespread flooding
entry.summary: Historic flooding has damaged 66 homes in Martin County, including 25 that were destroyed, according to new county numbers, as displaced residents wait to learn whether federal assistance will be made available. The flooding has left damage across WPTV's five-county viewing area, stretching from Indian River County through Palm Beach County. But in Martin County's Jensen Beach community, the latest numbers show just how destructive the flooding has been. Jensen Beach residents describe unlivable conditions. West Palm Beach residents still flooded 8 days after rain Michael Drawdy is among the Jensen Beach residents dealing with severe flooding inside his home. 'Right now I've got 6 to 8 inches of water depending on the level of the house inside the house, and you can see the fecal matter that's coming through the house,' Drawdy told WPTV. Drawdy and his neighbors now face conditions they say have made their homes unlivable. Residents also told WPTV much of their immediate help has come from one another, along with churches and community donations. 'All these neighbors have all pulled together. They've brought us donations here every day. People have fed us from the churches. Everybody's really been really good that way,' resident Suzie Keith said. 'No one else has really helped us. I mean, we've all been helping ourselves.' Florida has formally requested federal disaster assistance to help communities recover from recent flooding across Central and South Florida. At the request of Gov. Ron DeSantis, the Florida Division of Emergency Management announced Monday that the state submitted a Major Disaster Declaration request seeking federal assistance for communities impacted by the flooding. The request comes after heavy rainfall caused significant flooding in portions of the state, leaving communities dealing with lingering water and damage more than a week later. 'We remain committed to working with our federal partners to ensure impacted Floridians receive the assistance they need to recover,' the Florida Division of Emergency Management said in a post on X. A Major Disaster Declaration must receive federal approval before the requested assistance becomes available. The state's announcement did not specify which counties are included in the request or detail what types of federal assistance Florida is seeking. entry.article_text: Less than 12 hours after he was booked into jail, a Cape Coral man accused of making TikTok threats involving a Stuart elementary school was out on a $100,000 bond. By Monday morning, deputies were watching the school entrance, and Jessica and John Greisen had decided to keep their third grader home. Wanted to vomit, Jessica Greisen said. She recalled thinking, My child is not going to school. Their daughter, Teigan, attends Felix A. Williams Elementary School. Classes went on as planned Monday. CBS12 News saw several sheriff’s office vehicles near the entrance. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said it would also add deputies at several other schools as a precaution. Principal Sarah Tuthill told families Sunday evening that deputies were monitoring the situation and the school would stay open. In response, some parents asked whether absences would be excused and whether their children could complete assignments at home. Tuthill’s message did not address those questions. How detectives found the threats A tip late Friday led detectives to TikTok videos in which Michael George Davis, 51, threatened to kill law enforcement officers, the sheriff’s office said. Sheriff John Budensiek said the videos were repeatedly posted and taken down. In one video reviewed by CBS12 News, Davis said he was going to shoot people. As many as I can, dawg, as soon as I get there, he said. Budensiek said the threat in that video was directed at law enforcement officers. As detectives looked through the account, they found a separate post naming Felix A. So it went from threatening law enforcement to threatening Jews to threatening one of our students here in Martin County, Budensiek said. See also: HOA tries to block billionaire Larry Ellison’s home purchases for staff The sheriff said the post also threatened a local family. Tuthill described the threats against the school as vague and said the posts referenced a specific student. Budensiek said the student hasn’t attended Felix A. Williams in years, but Davis appeared to believe the student was still there. An alleged dispute dating back to 2006 2014 Davis lives in Cape Coral, but Budensiek said he surfed in Martin County years ago. The sheriff said Davis appeared to link the family he named online to a dispute he claims happened sometime between 2006 and 2014. Budensiek also described a later incident Davis claims happened at a gym. According to that account, people Davis associated with a surf group were supposed to spot him while he lifted weights. Davis claims they failed to do so and a significant amount of weight fell on his chest. Budensiek said investigators found no direct connection between the alleged dispute and the family. They have no idea what he’s talking about, he said. Arrested Saturday night, released Sunday afternoon Martin County investigators worked with Cape Coral police and a U.S. Marshals fugitive task force to arrest Davis at his Cape Coral home Saturday night on a felony warrant for written threats to kill. The sheriff’s office said Davis initially refused to come outside. Budensiek said deputies found no weapons when they arrested Davis. He said investigators were unaware of any prior arrests or any instances in which Davis was taken for an involuntary mental health evaluation under Florida’s Baker Act. Lee County jail records show Davis was booked at 2:53 a.m. Sunday and released at 2:12 p.m. on a $100,000 bond on the Martin County warrant. The records list a separate $1,000 bond on a charge of resisting an officer without violence, with a hearing set for Nov. I was hoping that $100,000 bond he would still be sitting in jail, and our parents, especially our school parents, wouldn’t have to worry, Budensiek said. The Greisens said they want to know whether Davis is being monitored and what restrictions he faces while out on bond. Is he wearing an ankle monitor? Why was he even released first off? Budensiek said Davis rides an e-bike, his driver’s license was suspended and deputies don’t know of a car he uses. The sheriff said that makes it harder to track his movements. But just the mere fact that he’s out of jail does create an opportunity for a threat, Budensiek said. What happens next Budensiek urged parents to stay vigilant and asked anyone who sees Davis in Martin County to call the sheriff’s office. He said deputies would maintain extra security at Felix A. Williams and that his office would support parents as they decide what’s best for their children. Jessica Greisen said she was grateful deputies made the arrest. The couple said they’ll keep Teigan home until they get answers about the precautions in place. Their education is important to us, but their safety is more important, she said. Detectives are still working with Cape Coral police. Budensiek said investigators recovered a device and are seeking a warrant to search it. His office also sent preservation requests to TikTok. We are working diligently to come up with other cases and other charges that may change that, but we are not there yet, Budensiek said. He said he expects more charges in Martin County and that other jurisdictions could also bring charges.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie cooking class helps adults with disabilities build skills, independence
entry.summary: A recent cooking class in Port St. Lucie is helping adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities learn valuable life skills and gain more independence. The participants are part of the Legal Aid Society of Palm Beach Countys Guardian Advocacy Program, which provides guardianship support to people with developmental disabilities. WATCH: Cooking class helps adults with disabilities build skills for independent living Cooking up confidence: Port St. Lucie program helps adults with disabilities gain independence Some of the participants are young adults who have aged out of foster care and don't have family members to rely on for support. Through a partnership with GL Homes that has lasted nearly a decade, participants are given hands-on experiences and opportunities to develop skills that can help them in everyday life. During the latest class in October, participants learned how to prepare a healthier meal, with Mediterranean chicken on the menu. From chopping vegetables and preparing ingredients to following a recipe and practicing kitchen safety, the lesson was about more than just cooking. Organizers say the goal is to give participants experiences and opportunities that are often not readily available to them while helping them become more self-sufficient. 'We wanted to give them these experiences that they just don't have and the rest of us take for granted,' said Sarah Alsofrom, Vice President of Community Relations at GL Homes. Jessica Kelson with the Legal Aid Society of Palm Beach County says watching participants learn new skills and take part in activities can make a meaningful difference. 'Being able to watch them learn a new skill or participate in something that's not typically offered to them is just really heartwarming and nice to see them be able to grow,' Kelson said. By the end of the class, participants had prepared their meal and sat down to enjoy what they made. For one participant, the accomplishment was something to be proud of. 'I'm proud of it,' she said. 'I am going to try this at home.' Organizers hope these experiences will give participants the confidence and practical skills to take greater control of their daily lives one meal at a time.

entry.title: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday
entry.summary: Family, friends and fellow first responders gathered Saturday to say a final goodbye to 34-year-old St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge. Hodge, a nine-year veteran of the St. Lucie County Fire District, was remembered for his service to the community and the impact he had on the people around him. WATCH: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday 'He was somebody who was always ready to help someone,' friend Jeff Lewis said on Nov. 6. For Lewis, Hodge's legacy is personal. 'He leaves this place a better place than he found it. He was that kind of guy. He found you one way but [would] leave you better than he found you.' On Oct. 24, the St. Lucie County Fire District said Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital, where he later died. His unexpected death has been difficult for those closest to him to process. 'It's a shock to literally all of us,' Hodge's sister, Alexis Hodge, said on Oct. 26. She said one of the hardest parts is knowing she can no longer simply call her brother. 'I love him, and I just wish I could pick up the phone and talk to him,' Alexis Hodge said. Hodge's death comes just over a year after the family suffered another devastating loss. His brother, Jarius Hodge, was also a St. Lucie County firefighter. Jarius died in 2025. 'We've lost two brothers in one year, can't describe to you the pain,' Alexis said. On Saturday, an honor guard, a procession and firefighters standing side by side marked a final salute to Hodge and his nine years of service to the St. Lucie County community.

The site-plan review also included a traffic analysis and a special-event traffic plan reviewed by police and Public Works. Residents have previously raised concerns about traffic near the proposed site . The city says the project will not use money from its general fund. Under the city’s published project terms, the developer could be reimbursed for up to 50% of eligible stadium and infrastructure costs through community redevelopment agency tax-increment revenue, capped at $27.5 million.

entry.title: Martin County commissioners revisit proposed train quiet zones
entry.summary: The debate over train horns in Martin County is back before county commissioners Tuesday morning as residents continue pushing for quiet zones along the Florida East Coast Railway. Commissioners are scheduled to hear an update from Public Works staff at 10:30 a.m. on the Railroad Safety Capital Improvement Program and the county's evaluation of establishing one or more quiet zones along the railroad. Quiet zones would eliminate the requirement for trains to routinely sound their horns at designated crossings, provided those crossings meet federal safety requirements. Train engineers would still be able to sound their horns when necessary for safety. For neighbors living near the tracks, the issue comes down to finding a balance between safety and quality of life. 'Safety considerations may not be as important, but they need to have the ability to sound that horn,' said Glenn Malone of Hobe Sound, 'If they can regulate it down just a bit so the option for safety is still viable.' Brightline began commercial operations along the Florida East Coast Railway through the Treasure Coast in September 2023, adding approximately 32 daily train trips through the corridor. The increased rail traffic prompted residents to call on county leaders to explore quiet zones. 'We dont have a problem with that. We just dont want the inherent noise all day and night long,' said Jeffry Aderman of Hobe Sound, 'All these big counties around us have quiet zones and here we are in this beautiful quiet, quaint little area and weve got train bars blowing 24/7.' At a March 11, 2025, meeting, commissioners decided not to pursue quiet zones after reviewing options presented by county staff. However, following continued concerns from residents, commissioners revisited the issue in May 2026 and directed staff to continue evaluating the possibility. Tuesday's presentation will outline the potential risks and benefits of quiet zones, along with the safety requirements and improvements that would be necessary to establish them in Martin County. Commissioners are expected to discuss the findings and provide direction to staff on how to move forward. WPTV will continue following the discussion and any decisions made by county leaders.

entry.title: Palm Beach County shelter dog with endless energy lands new career in police K-9 work
entry.summary: A dog that arrived at Palm Beach County Animal Care and Control spinning in circles in his kennel is now headed toward a future in police work. The dog, named Bayblade, caught attention for the very energy that made him stand out at the shelter. 'He had a tendency to spin, which is typically something that dogs will do when they are really backed up with energy and they need something to do,' Arielle Weinberger said. Weinberger is a PR specialist with Palm Beach County Animal Care Control. That energy caught the attention of animal rescue advocate Jim Bradley. 'I work with all sorts of rescues. Malinois, Dutch Shepherd Rescue, so a lot of local rescues. Oftentimes they might have a more challenging dog,' Bradley said. He put Bayblade to the test, looking at his energy, focus and drive to work. 'A working dog they are genetically just a complete different dog. Their energy, their drive, their tenacity, their desire to bite and grip into whole things,' Bradley said. He recognized those traits could make Bayblade ideal for police work. So Bradley contacted a canine organization in Ohio, and Bayblade was accepted. 'They'll be doing some bite work because he'll be a dual purpose canine that he can do apprehensions and also find find drugs or weapons,' Bradley said. Now, Bayblade is getting a chance to put all that energy to work. 'That cute little puppy with the pointy ears that in 6 months you've got a working dog who needs to work, who needs to move, who needs to do his what he was bred to do. And so I'm happy that Bayblade is going to get that chance,' Bradley said. From providing video of the dog in the kennel to the flight to Ohio, several people were instrumental in getting Bayblade who is now called Blade to his destination. Those involved included Fabienne with the Canine Enrichment Team, Alpha Pack K9 training, plane owners Harrison Gevirtz and Adam Young, and Wendy Cristantiello.

entry.title: Western St. Lucie County residents seek answers after historic flooding
entry.summary: Residents and farmers in western St. Lucie County are seeking answers and long-term drainage solutions after historic flooding left homes, farms and roads underwater last week. The North St. Lucie River Water Control District held an emergency meeting Monday to hear concerns from people in the area, including farmers, residents and representatives from Save the Chimps. District members said the drainage system can handle only so much water during an extreme rainfall event and discussed engineering as part of a possible long-term plan. Some of the hardest-hit areas are now seeing significant improvement, including Save the Chimps in western St. Lucie County. But residents and farmers say they want to know what can be done to reduce the risk of similar flooding during the next extreme rainfall event. For one resident, the flooding has already changed how they view their future in the area. I will be selling my house cause I am not going to risk my investment, the resident said during Mondays meeting. entry.title: 'Devastating': Flood assessments underway in Palm Beach and Okeechobee counties and Treasure Coast - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Devastating': Flood assessments underway in Palm Beach and Okeechobee counties and Treasure Coast    WPBF
entry.article_text: Emergency management officials are working to assess damage and assist residents in Palm Beach and Okeechobee counties and the Treasure Coast following last week’s severe flooding caused by heavy rain. In Palm Beach County, much of the water has receded, but some neighborhoods are still dealing with the aftermath. In Palm Beach County, a state of local emergency has been extended for another week. In Riviera Beach’s Long Pines Estates, piles of debris from damaged homes are stacked along the streets. Jeffrey Simms, a 14-year resident, described the impact. "The rain came, we thought it was going to stop, but it didn't. I mean, it didn't stop until it demolished our home, as you can see; this is our junk pile, which used to be our home on the inside," Simms said. Simms and his neighbor Denise Smith said they do not believe their homes were in a FEMA-designated flood zone. "It's been a devastating experience, and now my neighbors and I are left with the task of replacing everything, restoring everything, and most of us, although we have homeowners' insurance, we don't have flood insurance. Because this is not a flood zone? This is not a flood zone; it's not a flood zone," Smith said. Lucie County, officials reported receiving 273 submissions to their damage assessment survey as of Monday morning. At the height of the flooding, more than 100 roads were closed, and as of Sunday afternoon, two roads remained closed. FLOODING UPDATE: Martin County crews begin process of pumping water from flooded Hyline Drive In Okeechobee County, damage assessment teams have surveyed about half the area, with preliminary damage estimates already exceeding $10 million. Officials reported two homes destroyed and 59 others sustaining major damage. Residential losses are estimated at more than $6 million, while damage to county infrastructure is estimated at $4.3 million. The county noted that infrastructure damage alone exceeds the threshold for FEMA assistance consideration, though officials emphasized that these estimates are preliminary and could increase as assessments continue. In Martin County, officials say 30 homes have been classified as destroyed, and another 40 sustained moderate damage. A damage assessment also found an estimated $750,000 in damage to unpaved roads across the county. Martin County’s Flood Recovery Assistance webpage has been updated with additional information and resources, including details about a Multi-Agency Resource Center (MARC) opening Tuesday, Nov. 10, as well as opportunities for community members to support neighbors in need through United Way of Martin County’s Disaster Donor Program. Some residents impacted by the flooding are still looking for relief. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "I will say Riviera Beach has been out here helping us. But the biggest resource now is really funding so that we can try to get our lives back to some sense of normalcy," Smith said. "And also, for the school district, that they would reinstate my personal days that I have had to use." To assist residents, a Multi-Agency Resource Center (MARC) will open on Tuesday, November 10, at the Wells Recreation Center in Riviera Beach. The center will operate from 7 a.m. and will be staffed by personnel from state and local agencies, as well as nonprofit organizations, to provide resources to those affected by the flooding. It's expected to run for 14 days. entry.title: Martin County school increases security after TikTok threat suspect is released on bond - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County school increases security after TikTok threat suspect is released on bond    WPEC
entry.article_text: Less than 12 hours after he was booked into jail, a Cape Coral man accused of making TikTok threats involving a Stuart elementary school was out on a $100,000 bond. By Monday morning, deputies were watching the school entrance, and Jessica and John Greisen had decided to keep their third grader home. Wanted to vomit, Jessica Greisen said. She recalled thinking, My child is not going to school. Their daughter, Teigan, attends Felix A. Williams Elementary School. Classes went on as planned Monday. CBS12 News saw several sheriff’s office vehicles near the entrance. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said it would also add deputies at several other schools as a precaution. Principal Sarah Tuthill told families Sunday evening that deputies were monitoring the situation and the school would stay open. In response, some parents asked whether absences would be excused and whether their children could complete assignments at home. Tuthill’s message did not address those questions. How detectives found the threats A tip late Friday led detectives to TikTok videos in which Michael George Davis, 51, threatened to kill law enforcement officers, the sheriff’s office said. Sheriff John Budensiek said the videos were repeatedly posted and taken down. In one video reviewed by CBS12 News, Davis said he was going to shoot people. As many as I can, dawg, as soon as I get there, he said. Budensiek said the threat in that video was directed at law enforcement officers. As detectives looked through the account, they found a separate post naming Felix A. So it went from threatening law enforcement to threatening Jews to threatening one of our students here in Martin County, Budensiek said. See also: HOA tries to block billionaire Larry Ellison’s home purchases for staff The sheriff said the post also threatened a local family. Tuthill described the threats against the school as vague and said the posts referenced a specific student. Budensiek said the student hasn’t attended Felix A. Williams in years, but Davis appeared to believe the student was still there. An alleged dispute dating back to 2006 2014 Davis lives in Cape Coral, but Budensiek said he surfed in Martin County years ago. The sheriff said Davis appeared to link the family he named online to a dispute he claims happened sometime between 2006 and 2014. Budensiek also described a later incident Davis claims happened at a gym. According to that account, people Davis associated with a surf group were supposed to spot him while he lifted weights. Davis claims they failed to do so and a significant amount of weight fell on his chest. Budensiek said investigators found no direct connection between the alleged dispute and the family. They have no idea what he’s talking about, he said. Arrested Saturday night, released Sunday afternoon Martin County investigators worked with Cape Coral police and a U.S. Marshals fugitive task force to arrest Davis at his Cape Coral home Saturday night on a felony warrant for written threats to kill. The sheriff’s office said Davis initially refused to come outside. Budensiek said deputies found no weapons when they arrested Davis. He said investigators were unaware of any prior arrests or any instances in which Davis was taken for an involuntary mental health evaluation under Florida’s Baker Act. Lee County jail records show Davis was booked at 2:53 a.m. Sunday and released at 2:12 p.m. on a $100,000 bond on the Martin County warrant. The records list a separate $1,000 bond on a charge of resisting an officer without violence, with a hearing set for Nov. I was hoping that $100,000 bond he would still be sitting in jail, and our parents, especially our school parents, wouldn’t have to worry, Budensiek said. The Greisens said they want to know whether Davis is being monitored and what restrictions he faces while out on bond. Is he wearing an ankle monitor? Why was he even released first off? Budensiek said Davis rides an e-bike, his driver’s license was suspended and deputies don’t know of a car he uses. The sheriff said that makes it harder to track his movements. But just the mere fact that he’s out of jail does create an opportunity for a threat, Budensiek said. What happens next Budensiek urged parents to stay vigilant and asked anyone who sees Davis in Martin County to call the sheriff’s office. He said deputies would maintain extra security at Felix A. Williams and that his office would support parents as they decide what’s best for their children. Jessica Greisen said she was grateful deputies made the arrest. The couple said they’ll keep Teigan home until they get answers about the precautions in place. Their education is important to us, but their safety is more important, she said. Detectives are still working with Cape Coral police. Budensiek said investigators recovered a device and are seeking a warrant to search it. His office also sent preservation requests to TikTok. We are working diligently to come up with other cases and other charges that may change that, but we are not there yet, Budensiek said. He said he expects more charges in Martin County and that other jurisdictions could also bring charges.

entry.article_text: Many businesses are reeling in the effects of last week’s historic flooding event across South Florida, including a local Vero Beach citrus grove farm. CBS12 News Photojournalist Chris Pollock visited Greene Sugars Farm in Vero Beach, a family-owned farm business that spans multiple generations. The farm has been amongst the hardest hit from the historic flooding. Aubrey Greene shared with CBS12 News that they had a great citrus season last year, and were anticipating another good year this year, that was until the flooding put their crops, trees, and livestock in jeopardy. Greene Sugars boasts 800 acres of lemon trees, 50 acres of sugar belle trees, and 1000’s of cattle. They put out roughly 60,000-80,000 boxes of citrus per year and have a contract with Coca-Cola. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium Greene shared that the farm was hit with over 10 inches of rain in one single night, and that the citrus groves have been flooded trunk to trunk in water for over a week, despite heavy pumping every morning and night. That amount of rain over all of this land, it’s crazy, Greene said.

entry.title: Residents wait for FEMA assistance after Florida puts in request after widespread flooding
entry.summary: Historic flooding has damaged 66 homes in Martin County, including 25 that were destroyed, according to new county numbers, as displaced residents wait to learn whether federal assistance will be made available. Florida requests federal disaster assistance after widespread flooding The flooding has left damage across WPTV's five-county viewing area, stretching from Indian River County through Palm Beach County. But in Martin County's Jensen Beach community, the latest numbers show just how destructive the flooding has been. Jensen Beach residents describe unlivable conditions. West Palm Beach residents still flooded 8 days after rain Michael Drawdy is among the Jensen Beach residents dealing with severe flooding inside his home. 'Right now I've got 6 to 8 inches of water depending on the level of the house inside the house, and you can see the fecal matter that's coming through the house,' Drawdy told WPTV. Drawdy and his neighbors now face conditions they say have made their homes unlivable. Residents also told WPTV much of their immediate help has come from one another, along with churches and community donations. 'All these neighbors have all pulled together. They've brought us donations here every day. People have fed us from the churches. Everybody's really been really good that way,' resident Suzie Keith said. 'No one else has really helped us. I mean, we've all been helping ourselves.' Florida has formally requested federal disaster assistance to help communities recover from recent flooding across Central and South Florida. At the request of Gov. Ron DeSantis, the Florida Division of Emergency Management announced Monday that the state submitted a Major Disaster Declaration request seeking federal assistance for communities impacted by the flooding. The request comes after heavy rainfall caused significant flooding in portions of the state, leaving communities dealing with lingering water and damage more than a week later. 'We remain committed to working with our federal partners to ensure impacted Floridians receive the assistance they need to recover,' the Florida Division of Emergency Management said in a post on X. A Major Disaster Declaration must receive federal approval before the requested assistance becomes available. The request is the latest step in the recovery process as residents, businesse
entry.article_text: Historic flooding has damaged 66 homes in Martin County, including 25 that were destroyed, according to new county numbers, as displaced residents wait to learn whether federal assistance will be made available.The flooding has left damage across WPTV's five-county viewing area, stretching from Indian River County through Palm Beach County.But in Martin County's Jensen Beach community, the latest numbers show just how destructive the flooding has been.Jensen Beach residents describe unlivable conditions.Michael Drawdy is among the Jensen Beach residents dealing with severe flooding inside his home."Right now I've got 6 to 8 inches of water depending on the level of the house inside the house, and you can see the fecal matter that's coming through the house," Drawdy told WPTV.Drawdy and his neighbors now face conditions they say have made their homes unlivable.Residents also told WPTV much of their immediate help has come from one another, along with churches and community donations."All these neighbors have all pulled together. They've brought us donations here every day. People have fed us from the churches. Everybody's really been really good that way," resident Suzie Keith said. "No one else has really helped us. I mean, we've all been helping ourselves."Florida has formally requested federal disaster assistance to help communities recover from recent flooding across Central and South Florida.At the request of Gov. Ron DeSantis, the Florida Division of Emergency Management announced Monday that the state submitted a Major Disaster Declaration request seeking federal assistance for communities impacted by the flooding.The request comes after heavy rainfall caused significant flooding in portions of the state, leaving communities dealing with lingering water and damage more than a week later."We remain committed to working with our federal partners to ensure impacted Floridians receive the assistance they need to recover," the Florida Division of Emergency Management said in a post on X.A Major Disaster Declaration must receive federal approval before the requested assistance becomes available.The state's announcement did not specify which counties are included in the request or detail what types of federal assistance Florida is seeking.The request is the latest step in the recovery process as residents, businesses and local governments continue assessing damage from the flooding.Residents say they can't afford to waitThat process comes as some Jensen Beach residents say they are already out of their homes and struggling to figure out what comes next.Keith said residents understand the process takes time but need assistance now."They know it's moving slowly and we're all out of our homes and we have nowhere to live, but they said they're doing everything they can to expedite it to FEMA," Keith told WPTV.For residents facing destroyed homes and potentially lengthy recoveries, the question is now how quickly additional assistance can reach the people who need it.Until then, Keith said neighbors are continuing to rely heavily on one another.

entry.summary: Martin County school increases security after TikTok threat suspect is released on bond    WPEC
entry.article_text: Less than 12 hours after he was booked into jail, a Cape Coral man accused of making TikTok threats involving a Stuart elementary school was out on a $100,000 bond. By Monday morning, deputies were watching the school entrance, and Jessica and John Greisen had decided to keep their third grader home. Wanted to vomit, Jessica Greisen said. She recalled thinking, My child is not going to school. Their daughter, Teigan, attends Felix A. Williams Elementary School. Classes went on as planned Monday. CBS12 News saw several sheriff’s office vehicles near the entrance. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said it would also add deputies at several other schools as a precaution. Principal Sarah Tuthill told families Sunday evening that deputies were monitoring the situation and the school would stay open. In response, some parents asked whether absences would be excused and whether their children could complete assignments at home. Tuthill’s message did not address those questions. How detectives found the threats A tip late Friday led detectives to TikTok videos in which Michael George Davis, 51, threatened to kill law enforcement officers, the sheriff’s office said. Sheriff John Budensiek said the videos were repeatedly posted and taken down. In one video reviewed by CBS12 News, Davis said he was going to shoot people. As many as I can, dawg, as soon as I get there, he said. Budensiek said the threat in that video was directed at law enforcement officers. As detectives looked through the account, they found a separate post naming Felix A. So it went from threatening law enforcement to threatening Jews to threatening one of our students here in Martin County, Budensiek said. See also: HOA tries to block billionaire Larry Ellison’s home purchases for staff The sheriff said the post also threatened a local family. Tuthill described the threats against the school as vague and said the posts referenced a specific student. Budensiek said the student hasn’t attended Felix A. Williams in years, but Davis appeared to believe the student was still there. An alleged dispute dating back to 2006 2014 Davis lives in Cape Coral, but Budensiek said he surfed in Martin County years ago. The sheriff said Davis appeared to link the family he named online to a dispute he claims happened sometime between 2006 and 2014. Budensiek also described a later incident Davis claims happened at a gym. According to that account, people Davis associated with a surf group were supposed to spot him while he lifted weights. Davis claims they failed to do so and a significant amount of weight fell on his chest. Budensiek said investigators found no direct connection between the alleged dispute and the family. They have no idea what he’s talking about, he said. Arrested Saturday night, released Sunday afternoon Martin County investigators worked with Cape Coral police and a U.S. Marshals fugitive task force to arrest Davis at his Cape Coral home Saturday night on a felony warrant for written threats to kill. The sheriff’s office said Davis initially refused to come outside. Budensiek said deputies found no weapons when they arrested Davis. He said investigators were unaware of any prior arrests or any instances in which Davis was taken for an involuntary mental health evaluation under Florida’s Baker Act. Lee County jail records show Davis was booked at 2:53 a.m. Sunday and released at 2:12 p.m. on a $100,000 bond on the Martin County warrant. The records list a separate $1,000 bond on a charge of resisting an officer without violence, with a hearing set for Nov. I was hoping that $100,000 bond he would still be sitting in jail, and our parents, especially our school parents, wouldn’t have to worry, Budensiek said. The Greisens said they want to know whether Davis is being monitored and what restrictions he faces while out on bond. Is he wearing an ankle monitor? Why was he even released first off? Budensiek said Davis rides an e-bike, his driver’s license was suspended and deputies don’t know of a car he uses. The sheriff said that makes it harder to track his movements. But just the mere fact that he’s out of jail does create an opportunity for a threat, Budensiek said. What happens next Budensiek urged parents to stay vigilant and asked anyone who sees Davis in Martin County to call the sheriff’s office. He said deputies would maintain extra security at Felix A. Williams and that his office would support parents as they decide what’s best for their children. Jessica Greisen said she was grateful deputies made the arrest. The couple said they’ll keep Teigan home until they get answers about the precautions in place. Their education is important to us, but their safety is more important, she said. Detectives are still working with Cape Coral police. Budensiek said investigators recovered a device and are seeking a warrant to search it. His office also sent preservation requests to TikTok. We are working diligently to come up with other cases and other charges that may change that, but we are not there yet, Budensiek said. He said he expects more charges in Martin County and that other jurisdictions could also bring charges.

CBS12 News Photojournalist Chris Pollock visited Greene Sugars Farm in Vero Beach, a family-owned farm business that spans multiple generations. The farm has been amongst the hardest hit from the historic flooding. Aubrey Greene shared with CBS12 News that they had a great citrus season last year, and were anticipating another good year this year, that was until the flooding put their crops, trees, and livestock in jeopardy. Greene Sugars boasts 800 acres of lemon trees, 50 acres of sugar belle trees, and 1000’s of cattle. They put out roughly 60,000-80,000 boxes of citrus per year and have a contract with Coca-Cola. Lucie approves site plan for 6,000-seat soccer stadium Greene shared that the farm was hit with over 10 inches of rain in one single night, and that the citrus groves have been flooded trunk to trunk in water for over a week, despite heavy pumping every morning and night. That amount of rain over all of this land, it’s crazy, Greene said.

entry.title: Western St. Lucie County residents seek answers after historic flooding - WFLX
entry.summary: Western St. Lucie County residents seek answers after historic flooding    WFLX
entry.article_text: Residents and farmers in western St. Lucie County are seeking answers and long-term drainage solutions after historic flooding left homes, farms and roads underwater last week. Lucie River Water Control District held an emergency meeting Monday to hear concerns from people in the area, including farmers, residents and representatives from Save the Chimps. District members said the drainage system can handle only so much water during an extreme rainfall event and discussed engineering as part of a possible long-term plan. Some of the hardest-hit areas are now seeing significant improvement, including Save the Chimps in western St. But residents and farmers say they want to know what can be done to reduce the risk of similar flooding during the next extreme rainfall event. For one resident, the flooding has already changed how they view their future in the area. “I will be selling my house cause I am not going to risk my investment,” the resident said during Monday’s meeting. Water control district hears concerns from western St. Lucie County The North St. Lucie River Water Control District held an emergency meeting Monday to hear from people affected by the flooding. Farmers, residents and representatives of Save the Chimps attended as district members discussed the drainage system and the scale of last week’s flooding. President Steve Cassens said there are limits to what the existing system can handle when extraordinary amounts of rain fall in a short period. “If we have a rainfall event like that, my personal feeling is you can have gates open, shut, it doesn’t matter,” said Cassens. “We can manage water maybe 3, 4, 5, 6 inches. We can’t manage water in the quantities that we got.” District officials also discussed maintenance of waterways and ditches, including concerns surrounding a creek in Western Fort Pierce that serves as a primary drainage route. The district said it systematically cleans ditches within its boundaries. The district said engineering could be examined as part of developing a long-range plan. Conditions improve at Save the Chimps Save the Chimps, a sanctuary in western St. Lucie County, was among the places hit hard by the flooding. WPTV previously reported that staff members had to use drones to deliver food to chimpanzees because several roads through the sanctuary were underwater. When WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache returned days later, staff said conditions had significantly improved. “A short 40 hours after that, we’re almost completely dry on our roads,” said Mark Yohannan. The improvement came after days of challenges caused by standing water at the sanctuary. West Fort Pierce farmer raises concerns The concerns extended beyond residential neighborhoods. Justin Akerley, who helps operate Saint Lucie Farm Preserve in west Fort Pierce, spoke later Monday at a Port St. Lucie City Council meeting after attending the water control district meeting. Akerley told council members he believes continued development is adding pressure to the area's drainage infrastructure. “I just spent my morning in a meeting with the North St. Lucie River Water Control District trying to figure out what we can do to alleviate the water issues, and there’s really no right answer except for stop building,” Akerley said. Akerley shared a video with WPTV showing flooding at Saint Lucie Farm Preserve, a working agritourism farm operated by Akerley and Michael Hale. The farm produces hay, cut flowers, beef and assorted vegetables and hosts community agricultural events. Akerley told council members the consequences extend to other farms and families. “I’ve got friends that have calves dying that are flooded, they can’t get out,” he said. “It’s a terrible, terrible situation for everybody. There’s people that have lost their homes.” He urged city leaders to reconsider the effect future development could have on flooding and drainage. “Just please reconsider because it’s not a good situation for everybody, and it’s only gonna get worse,” Akerley said. Officials consider what comes next During Monday’s Port St. Lucie City Council meeting, Councilman David Pickett also called for greater scrutiny of flooding and the city’s stormwater infrastructure. Pickett said he sent two memos to the city manager earlier in the week addressing floodwaters and wants the city to expedite a planned stormwater study rather than wait until 2029. He also raised concerns about flooding in Tradition and called for the city to examine stormwater systems before distributing certain stormwater fees to community development districts. Lucie River Water Control District has said engineering options can be assessed as officials consider a long-term plan. For residents and farmers still recovering from last week’s flooding, those discussions are now turning toward a larger question: what can be done before the next extreme rainfall event? The Associated Press determined Monday that ‘no’ had received enough votes to win.The “no” side raised roughly 10 times as much as the “yes” side. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone dumped more than $100 million into a political action committee working to defeat the measure.The measure would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. Most of the money would have been used to backfill federal funding cuts to healthcare, and 10% would have gone toward education and food-assistance programs. Bernie Sanders, who rallied in cities across California in the race’s closing weeks to urge voters to pass it.The “Yes on 40” campaign said the measure sought to protect healthcare for Californians and that they will put a tax back on the ballot in 2028 if patients are not protected.“Buying an election is not the same as winning the debate,” the measure's proponents said in a statement on Monday. “The billionaires may have bought themselves a temporary victory at the ballot box, but they have not bought themselves an end to this debate, and this is only round one.”Billionaires donated millions of dollars to a political action committee, Building a Better California, working to defeat the measure. The committee, which backed other measures on the ballot designed to nullify the tax, raised more than $333 million, nearly a third of which came from Brin.The AP Voter Poll indicates that the majority of young voters in California — those younger than 30 — voted “yes” on Proposition 40. Older voters were far less supportive, with roughly 7 in 10 voters who were 65 and older saying they voted “no” on the ballot measure.About half of voters with a household income under $100,000 annually said they were in support of the initiative. Closer to 6 in 10 California voters with an income of $100,000 or higher said they were opposed.Brin, along with his fellow Google co-founder Larry Page, was among the billionaires who started cutting ties with the state in anticipation of the possible tax. Another tech mogul, Mark Zuckerberg, said he would remain in the state for eight years and made a deal with Meta to help him pay the tax without losing his ownership stake in the company.Some feared the measure could drive wealthy taxpayers out of stateSome traditional Democratic allies, including Planned Parenthood and the California Medical Association, were part of a coalition opposing it. They were concerned about how the tax revenue would be divvied up and about the potential impact on the state’s budget if there was a mass exodus of wealthy taxpayers. California’s budget relies heavily on the income tax of the state’s richest residents.“Proposition 40 was a reckless experiment conducted on our state’s economy with little regard for the harms it would cause,” the coalition said in a statement.Robert Swonger, an auto glass technician living near Sacramento who’s politically independent, said before voting concluded Nov. 3 that he planned to vote against it.RELATED STORY | Zuckerberg strikes deal with Meta’s board to stay in California as billionaire tax vote looms“Obviously, I would like billionaires not to have as much money as they do,” he said. “But I don’t believe taxing them out of existence is going to work.”Progressive politicians, including Sanders and Massachusetts Sen.
