entry.title: Martin County commissioners revisit proposed train quiet zones - WPTV
entry.summary: Martin County commissioners revisit proposed train quiet zones    WPTV
entry.article_text: The debate over train horns in Martin County is back before county commissioners Tuesday morning as residents continue pushing for quiet zones along the Florida East Coast Railway.Commissioners are scheduled to hear an update from Public Works staff at 10:30 a.m. on the Railroad Safety Capital Improvement Program and the county's evaluation of establishing one or more quiet zones along the railroad.Quiet zones would eliminate the requirement for trains to routinely sound their horns at designated crossings, provided those crossings meet federal safety requirements. Train engineers would still be able to sound their horns when necessary for safety.For neighbors living near the tracks, the issue comes down to finding a balance between safety and quality of life."Safety considerations may not be as important, but they need to have the ability to sound that horn," said Glenn Malone of Hobe Sound, "If they can regulate it down just a bit so the option for safety is still viable."Brightline began commercial operations along the Florida East Coast Railway through the Treasure Coast in September 2023, adding approximately 32 daily train trips through the corridor.The increased rail traffic prompted residents to call on county leaders to explore quiet zones."We don’t have a problem with that. We just don’t want the inherent noise all day and night long," said Jeffry Aderman of Hobe Sound, "All these big counties around us have quiet zones and here we are in this beautiful quiet, quaint little area and we’ve got train bars blowing 24/7."At a March 11, 2025, meeting, commissioners decided not to pursue quiet zones after reviewing options presented by county staff.However, following continued concerns from residents, commissioners revisited the issue in May 2026 and directed staff to continue evaluating the possibility.Tuesday's presentation will outline the potential risks and benefits of quiet zones, along with the safety requirements and improvements that would be necessary to establish them in Martin County.Commissioners are expected to discuss the findings and provide direction to staff on how to move forward.WPTV will continue following the discussion and any decisions made by county leaders.

entry.title: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change for a roughly 34-acre property near South 25th Street and West Midway Road that could allow nearly 500 homes. The vote came as residents sought answers about recent flooding and commissioners questioned how the property handles drainage. An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The property sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties. If designated for residential use, the site could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request. See also: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems, and explain how to prevent future flooding. I love my community, but it’s not fair that we’re suffering because nobody has taken the initiative to do what’s right for us, one resident said. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of the neighborhood and surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also asked for a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. It covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.

Martin County Emergency Management Director Sally Waite told commissioners the flooding affected 77 homes and that assessment teams planned to visit each one to document the damage. Where to get help The Multi-Agency Resource Center is at Hoke Library, 1150 NW Jack Williams Way in Jensen Beach . The county lists those hours for Wednesday through Saturday until further notice. The center is closed Sundays. Martin County is also accepting applications for state disaster housing assistance. Households must meet income requirements. Residents can call 772-320-3169 for details. They can also report flood damage and fill out a needs survey on the county’s flood recovery page. Read more: 'We're not getting any answers': Hamilton Bay residents frustrated as flooding continues Where FEMA aid stands Florida announced Monday that it had requested a presidential major disaster declaration for the flooding. As of Wednesday morning, federal approval had yet to be announced. The state’s announcement did not specify whether the request included FEMA Individual Assistance for Martin County. If that aid is authorized for Martin County, eligible households could apply for help with expenses such as temporary housing and essential home repairs.

entry.title: Martin County commissioners revisit proposed train quiet zones - WPTV
entry.summary: Martin County commissioners revisit proposed train quiet zones    WPTV
entry.article_text: The debate over train horns in Martin County is back before county commissioners Tuesday morning as residents continue pushing for quiet zones along the Florida East Coast Railway.Commissioners are scheduled to hear an update from Public Works staff at 10:30 a.m. on the Railroad Safety Capital Improvement Program and the county's evaluation of establishing one or more quiet zones along the railroad.Quiet zones would eliminate the requirement for trains to routinely sound their horns at designated crossings, provided those crossings meet federal safety requirements. Train engineers would still be able to sound their horns when necessary for safety.For neighbors living near the tracks, the issue comes down to finding a balance between safety and quality of life."Safety considerations may not be as important, but they need to have the ability to sound that horn," said Glenn Malone of Hobe Sound, "If they can regulate it down just a bit so the option for safety is still viable."Brightline began commercial operations along the Florida East Coast Railway through the Treasure Coast in September 2023, adding approximately 32 daily train trips through the corridor.The increased rail traffic prompted residents to call on county leaders to explore quiet zones."We don’t have a problem with that. We just don’t want the inherent noise all day and night long," said Jeffry Aderman of Hobe Sound, "All these big counties around us have quiet zones and here we are in this beautiful quiet, quaint little area and we’ve got train bars blowing 24/7."At a March 11, 2025, meeting, commissioners decided not to pursue quiet zones after reviewing options presented by county staff.However, following continued concerns from residents, commissioners revisited the issue in May 2026 and directed staff to continue evaluating the possibility.Tuesday's presentation will outline the potential risks and benefits of quiet zones, along with the safety requirements and improvements that would be necessary to establish them in Martin County.Commissioners are expected to discuss the findings and provide direction to staff on how to move forward.WPTV will continue following the discussion and any decisions made by county leaders.

entry.summary: 'We’re homeless': Martin County residents voice frustrations over flooding at commission meeting    WPBF
entry.article_text: Martin County residents gathered at the commission chambers Tuesday morning to express their concerns about ongoing flooding in their neighborhoods and demand action from county leaders. "For 40 years, I’ve raised my family here, built my life here, and in the hours, watched everything we worked for become submerged in flood water and sewage," Jensen Beach resident Mary Berner said. Resident Lisa French described the impact of the flooding, saying, "Today, we’re homeless. We have nowhere to have Christmas. We don’t have much to come home to." Some residents questioned whether drainage infrastructure and development contributed to the flooding, while Yamila Rollan Escalona, who's with the Yaya por Vida Foundation, raised concerns about response efforts. MARTIN COUNTY FLOODING: Jensen Beach residents struggle with flooding and damaged homes after historic rainfall "Take Rich, a historic Black American in a Bahamian neighborhood inhabited and preserved for generations by a majority Black Americans. With a capital 'B.' They still have not been properly mitigated. Standing water, no pumps, no headlines, not a peep on social media, and just one article in the news today! Katrina much?" Rollan Escalona said. County leaders said crews are pumping water around the clock and assured residents that once the immediate flooding is addressed, they will explore ways to reduce future risks. Some proposed solutions include having one agency, such as the South Florida Water Management District, manage the nearby Savannas as a single watershed and exploring additional drainage options. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "I do expect you to make additional funding available to your staff today to mitigate this emergency as efficiently as possible. Thank you for your time and expect to continue to hear from us," resident Kyle Pond said. Commissioner Sarah Heard responded, saying, "Jensen Beach residents, we’ve heard you loud and clear. You are our top priority." County leaders also said they plan to review the county’s warning system and will address the flooding issue again at their next meeting, where they will provide updates and discuss a potential grant program. entry.title: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site - cw34.com
entry.summary: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change for a roughly 34-acre property near South 25th Street and West Midway Road that could allow nearly 500 homes. The vote came as residents sought answers about recent flooding and commissioners questioned how the property handles drainage. An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The property sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties. If designated for residential use, the site could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request. See also: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems, and explain how to prevent future flooding. I love my community, but it’s not fair that we’re suffering because nobody has taken the initiative to do what’s right for us, one resident said. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of the neighborhood and surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also asked for a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. It covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.

"So the passion behind that is, hey, stay out of the system, stay out of the judicial system, stay out of the cemetery. I want you to be free, and I want them to succeed in life."The nonprofit's website says Bates and fellow founder Yolanda Bates both grew up in underserved communities. Their experiences helped create a desire to help other families address childhood trauma and generational challenges. Family, unity, education, empowerment and accountability are among the values the organization lists as central to its work.That work extends well beyond the holidays.Love, Hope & Healing Inc. has partnered with Palm Beach State College on summer programming that exposes high school students to skilled trades, careers and personal development. It has also offered entrepreneurship programming for young men ages 14 to 18.But Bates says helping children also means supporting the families they go home to."We mainly deal with the young, young men and women, but we can't deal with the young men and women and send them back into a toxic environment," Bates said. "So we actually tackle the parents as well."He describes that work as an effort to rebuild a support network around those families."Our kids definitely need it. Families need it as a whole. We're trying to recreate, no, not recreate, reestablish the village," Bates said. "They all, everybody says it takes a village. We want to reestablish and put a stronghold on that village."That village now includes volunteers like Christopher Hepburn, CEO and co-founder of a West Palm Beach branding and marketing agency.Hepburn said he has only been volunteering with the nonprofit for a few months, but its focus on bringing families together connected with his own childhood."Wow, it's really the families," Hepburn said. "When I grew up, I didn't really spend some time with my mom and my dad, so to see them putting that together for the families and the kids and seeing everyone come together, that's amazing to me. So yeah, it means everything."Hepburn has volunteered at events including a father-son grill challenge. Seeing fathers and sons spending time together was especially meaningful to him."Oh man, it was amazing," Hepburn said. "Yeah, I didn't really, like I said, I didn't spend that much time with my dad growing up, so to see fathers and sons get together and really just connect and, you know, just love each other, is, it's dope."For him, the idea behind a Season of Hope can be as simple as making time for one another."That just means to me just getting together as a family, talking with each other and really just connecting," Hepburn said.And he hopes the nonprofit's reach continues growing."I hope that it keeps going. I hope that the events get even bigger, get even better," Hepburn said. "I hope that more families get impacted and that it just spreads as fast as it can."Love, Hope & Healing Inc. is collaborating with United Way of Palm Beach Countysomething Bates believes can broaden the impact organizations have when they work together."That's been wonderful with the help we've been getting from United Way and actually coming up under their umbrella now. We're looking for volunteers. We're looking for mentors," Bates said. entry.title: Democrat Scott Colom projected to flip Mississippi Senate seat in major upset
entry.summary: Democrat Scott Colom is projected to defeat Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's U.S. Senate race, according to the Associated Press, pulling off a major upset in a state that has long favored Republicans. Colom's victory makes him the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since 1982. The state has not had a Democratic senator since John Stennis left office in 1989. WATCH: A new generation on Capitol Hill could challenge Chuck Schumer's Senate leadership New generation on Capitol Hill could challenge Schumer's leadership The race was not initially considered competitive, but polling tightened in the closing weeks of the campaign as voters expressed growing frustration with the economy. Hyde-Smith faced criticism after suggesting during an interview that consumers could choose other sources of protein when asked about rising beef prices. Colom seized on the remark, launching a campaign ad featuring voters who said they would rather choose another senator than another protein. The race also drew attention from national political figures. President Donald Trump visited Mississippi a week before Election Day to rally support for Hyde-Smith, while former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned for Colom in the closing weeks of the race. Colom's victory delivers Democrats an unexpected pickup in the U.S. Senate.

entry.title: Delray Beach mayor looks to private sponsors to save 2027 St. Patrick’s Day Parade
entry.summary: Delray Beach Mayor Tom Carney says he's exploring a private-sector solution to keep the city's 2027 St. Patrick's Day Parade alive after a new Florida law prompted the city to announce it would cancel the event. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: Delray Beach mayor looks to private sponsors to save St. Patrick's Day Parade The city's annual Pride Festival is also affected by the decision, which Carney says stems from Senate Bill 1134. The legislation restricts local governments from funding, promoting or taking official actions related to certain diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) activities. Carney said the potential impact on the two events has been top of mind since the bill passed. 'We learned very quickly that, within the scope of the definition of DEI, it could (impact both) the St. Patrick's Day parade and the Pride festival,' Carney said. After the city announced the cancellation, Carney said residents quickly voiced their concerns. 'I would say by Saturday I had a good 50 emails in my box saying, 'What are you doing?'' he said. Now, the mayor is looking at another option: allowing private organizers and sponsors to take the lead. Carney said the St. Patrick's Day parade used to be a private event and his family also participated in underwriting it in the past. He said he's already reached out to potential supporters, and others have contacted him offering to help fund the parade. 'I decided, well, let's just make it a private event again, so I reached out to a half dozen people. More than that reached out to me saying, 'We'll help underwrite the parade,' and we've already got people submitting applications to try and do the parade for us,' Carney said. The mayor said a similar arrangement could be considered for the Pride Festival. 'If the private sector wants to support that, I would as well,' Carney said. 'You don't want to cancel things people have grown accustomed to.' Residents said losing either event would have an impact beyond the festivities themselves, including on the local business community and residents who look forward to celebrating their traditions. Carney says discussions are still in the early stages, but he's confident the St. Patrick's Day Parade will go on as scheduled in 2027. The city has not yet announced a finalized plan for either event. Senate Bill 1143 takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.

entry.summary: If the 2026 midterms were an opportunity for voters to express their feelings about President Donald Trumps administration, the election in two years will be their first opportunity to cast a vote for president without his name on the ballot. Trump is constitutionally barred from running again, which means, as the lame duck portion of his presidency comes into view, its not too early to start thinking about who might replace him. Potential candidates certainly are. While they might bat away speculation, many are starting to think seriously about their potential path or wrestling with the ultimate question is it worth the investment of time and energy and the guarantee of being vilified by your political rivals in the off chance that you could be the most powerful person in the world? entry.title: Port St. Lucie Veterans Day ceremony honors generations of veterans and their service
entry.summary: Veterans of all eras and residents of all ages packed Veterans Memorial Park in Port St. Lucie on Wednesday for the annual Veterans Day ceremony. WPTV anchor and Navy veteran Mike Trim connected with fellow veterans about the significance of the day. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Veterans honored at Port St. Lucie event Vietnam veteran Michael Greene wore a newly decorated vest commemorating his Army service 'It's all like my whole history. I started in transportation. I think it's very important. I enlisted and was not supposed to go but ended up over there,' Greene told Trim. Wayne Thomas, another Vietnam War veteran in attendance, told Trim he felt this day now properly honors their service, which was not previously recognized. 'It's good to get the recognition that we didn't get,' Thomas said. The Port St. Lucie High School Junior ROTC attended the ceremony in full force while crowds of all ages looked on. That included a member of the greatest generation: 98-year-old World War II veteran Robert Vogel. 'I'm one of the few left. I just thank God. I would really encourage anyone to come to these events because they're really important to support the veterans,' Vogel told Trim. Those veterans heard keynote speaker, Retired Air Force Master Sgt. Vincent Lavelle Jr. A special touch from the Port St. Lucie community band featured songs from each branch of service. That prompted service members in attendance to stand for their respective branch song. There was also a special flyover by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office helicopter.

entry.title: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change for a roughly 34-acre property near South 25th Street and West Midway Road that could allow nearly 500 homes. The vote came as residents sought answers about recent flooding and commissioners questioned how the property handles drainage. An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The property sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties. If designated for residential use, the site could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request. See also: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems, and explain how to prevent future flooding. I love my community, but it’s not fair that we’re suffering because nobody has taken the initiative to do what’s right for us, one resident said. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of the neighborhood and surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also asked for a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. It covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.

entry.summary: FHP probes fatal SUV-motorcycle crash on 37th Street in Indian River County    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Florida Highway Patrol is investigating a fatal crash that occurred in Indian River County Monday afternoon. FHP says that at around 3:43 p.m. on Monday, a 2018 Toyota Rav 4 SUV and a 2017 Harley Davidson Electra Guide Motorcycle collided near 1850 37th Street within unincorporated Indian River County. According to FHP , the driver of the Rav 4 SUV an 82-year-old female was traveling east on 37th Street before coming to a stop in the roadway and waiting to turn left into Indian River MRI. At the same time, the driver of the Harley Davidson a 58-year-old male was traveling west before colliding with the SUV, who turned into the path of the motorcycle as it approached. See also: Vero Beach family citrus grove reels after historic South Florida flooding damages crops The 82-year-old woman came away with minor injuries, while the 58-year-old male on the motorcycle was pronounced dead after being transported HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. As a result, Westbound 37th Street between U.S. Highway 1 and 17th Avenue is currently closed. This remains an active investigation.

entry.title: 'Today we are homeless': Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home
entry.summary: A Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding is searching for more permanent housing and money to rebuild after water destroyed much of the inside of their home. Lisa and Jeremy French, who have two young boys, told WPTV's Michael Hoffman they ultimately have one goal: to get their family back home. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Jensen Beach family displaced by historic flooding pleads for help rebuilding home WPTV first met the French family shortly after historic rainfall hit South Florida and the Treasure Coast. Floodwater had surrounded their neighborhood, forcing residents to use kayaks to get around and check on neighbors. Days later, much of the water has receded. The damage has not. 'My floorboards are outside,' Lisa French said. Family says nearly everything inside is gone Hoffman returned to the French family's Jensen Beach home for an update, but the family said it was not safe to go inside. French said the flooding wiped out much of what her family had accumulated over the years. 'Our appliances are gone, our cabinets are gone, every piece of furniture,' French said. The family is now trying to determine how to pay for repairs while securing a more permanent place to live. entry.title: Treasure Coast woman loses second home in 2 years after devastating Fort Pierce flooding
entry.summary: A Treasure Coast woman who lost her home two years ago to a tornado from Hurricane Milton has lost another home to devastating flooding in Fort Pierce. 'I'm starting to feel like I'm invincible at this point,' says Terry Polk as she watched the debris pile of drywall and ruined furniture in front of her home get bigger. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Treasure Coast woman loses a second home in 2 years The water in her home was measured in feet, not inches, as the heavy rain in the first weekend of November flooded her block. 'We were actually in the house,' Polk said. 'When we were wading around, like around knee-deep water, I started getting scared.' She said they were rescued by kayaks and returned when the water receded, leaving so much damage. 'You know, to keep your focus, you just have to realize there are people out there that have it way worse. There are people out there that are so much worse, you know, and I have to be thankful that we got out with our lives,' she said. Two years ago she was living in the Spanish Lakes community of St. Lucie County when Hurricane Milton's winds created widespread tornadoes. One of the twisters, an EF3, struck the community, killing six people and destroying homes, including Terry's. 'Terry is one of the most amazing people I've met,' said friend Cindy McGee. 'She's very strong, does a lot for the community, a lot for the neighborhood.' Polk said she has flood insurance, but the damage is so extensive, she's not sure if there is enough coverage to fix everything. 'I already explained to the cats, who are looking at me like, we didn't exactly sign up for your survivor world,' she said.

entry.title: Dolphins turn to Kyle McCord against Colts after injuries sideline Malik Willis, Zach Sieler
entry.summary: The Miami Dolphins will attempt to get their second win of the season in Indianapolis on Sunday, but they will have to do it without two of their best players. On Tuesday, it was reported that defensive tackle Zach Sieler will miss the rest of the season with a ruptured bicep. WATCH REPORT BELOW: QB Kyle McCord takes the reins with Malik Willis on IR 'I give him a ton of credit not only for pushing through that game and playing at a high level but just for everything he's done,' said Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley said Wednesday. The second injury is quarterback Malik Willis, who's been battling a groin injury that has landed him on the injured reserve, meaning he will miss at least the next four games. 'The injury had progressed enough that the medical team believed that he needed the rest,' Hafley said. Quarterback Kyle McCord, in his second NFL season, will get the start against Indianapolis. Hafley said he has a live arm and has faith in his new signal caller. 'I'm excited, but at the same time the production on the field matters most so I'm doing everything I can to do everything I can to play,' said McCord. Arguably the best news of the day was linebacker Josh Uche being named team captain. Players cheered for the South Florida native, but for Uche, he says it's business as usual. 'I've been dreaming about this since I was a kid, and for the guys to trust me and to be a part of the leadership is everything,' said Uche. Kickoff against the Colts is scheduled for 1 p.m. at Lucas Oil Stadium.

entry.title: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes - WPBF
entry.summary: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes    WPBF
entry.article_text: After more than a week of standing floodwater, some residents near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are finally beginning to clean up their homes as water slowly recedes. Martin County began pumping water out of the neighborhood Monday, allowing some homeowners to begin assessing the damage. For Lisa French, the receding water means she can finally begin the difficult work of cleaning out her home. “I mean, we’ve been underwater for a week,” French said. When WPBF 25 News visited French’s home several days ago, water was still standing inside, reaching more than a foot deep in some rooms. CLICK HERE FOR INFORMATION ON HOW TO DONATE TO THE FRENCH FAMILY Now, the water is gone, but much of what she owns has been destroyed. Since early Wednesday morning, French, her husband and several neighbors have been removing damaged drywall, tearing out the kitchen and carrying ruined furniture and belongings into the front yard. “You know, you’re sitting there with your house full of water, sitting in the fact that you lost your entire home. But now we can actually move and work instead of think,” French said. While French has begun cleaning up, other residents are still waiting for floodwaters to recede. Susan Destafney, who has lived in the neighborhood for four decades, said she has never experienced anything like it. “We’ve lived in our home for 40 years. We’ve never seen the likes of this,” Destafney said. Community volunteers have also stepped in to help, including Alaura Macpherson, who runs the local group Quit Messen With Jensen. Macpherson said volunteers have been collecting cleaning supplies and other necessities for affected families. She is also organizing a community fundraiser and meal on November 25 to raise money for flood victims. Local restaurants are expected to donate food, while the event will also serve as a resource center connecting residents with contractors, cleanup services and other recovery assistance. “The community is what helps each other. We are a family,” Macpherson said. Martin County officials have opened a Multi-Agency Resource Center at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach to connect flood victims with recovery assistance. entry.title: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now - WPEC
entry.summary: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now    WPEC
entry.article_text: A day after Jensen Beach residents told Martin County commissioners that flooding forced them from their homes, families can go to Hoke Library for recovery help while they wait for word on federal aid. The flood recovery center is open Wednesday even though regular library services are closed for Veterans Day. State agencies and local nonprofits are there to connect residents with recovery resources, and the county says more agencies and services will be added throughout the week. At Tuesday’s commission meeting, residents pressed county leaders about drainage and how they were warned. Martin County Emergency Management Director Sally Waite told commissioners the flooding affected 77 homes and that assessment teams planned to visit each one to document the damage. Cleanup begins in Skyline Heights On Wednesday, CBS12 News returned to Jensen Beach’s Skyline Heights neighborhood, where part of Hyline Drive remained underwater. At Lisa French’s home, the cleanup had finally started. French said hers was the first home in the neighborhood being cleared out and gutted. Cabinets, furniture and pieces of drywall covered the front yard as workers carried out nearly everything floodwater touched. After a week, this is like celebration, French said. But that progress came with tears as she watched her family’s belongings get thrown away. The crib was a rough one to watch go, French said. It’s just my kids, you know. One week earlier, streets throughout the neighborhood were underwater and residents used kayaks to check on their homes and neighbors. Waite told CBS12 News that some homes took on three to five feet of water. She estimated about 24 of the 77 affected homes were destroyed. French and her family are staying with her parents and waiting to hear about longer-term housing. She said they do not have flood insurance. Alaura Macpherson, co-founder of Quit Messing With Jensen, went to the Hoke Library resource center Wednesday to collect cleanup supplies for affected families. CBS12 News later met up with her at French’s home, where she was helping the family clear out the damage. Absolutely not, Macpherson said. I will do this any day for my community. For French, getting everything out is only the beginning. This is bittersweet because we’re moving forward, French said. But, you know, how do we rebuild? Where to get help The Multi-Agency Resource Center is at Hoke Library, 1150 NW Jack Williams Way in Jensen Beach . The county lists those hours for Wednesday through Saturday until further notice. The center is closed Sundays. Martin County is also accepting applications for state disaster housing assistance. Households must meet income requirements. Residents can call 772-320-3169 for details. They can also report flood damage and fill out a needs survey on the county’s flood recovery page. Read more: 'We're not getting any answers': Hamilton Bay residents frustrated as flooding continues Where FEMA aid stands Florida announced Monday that it had requested a presidential major disaster declaration for the flooding. As of Wednesday morning, federal approval had yet to be announced. The state’s announcement did not specify whether the request included FEMA Individual Assistance for Martin County. If that aid is authorized for Martin County, eligible households could apply for help with expenses such as temporary housing and essential home repairs.

entry.title: Doctors warn of infection risks from contaminated floodwater in Palm Beach and Treasure Coast - WPBF
entry.summary: Doctors warn of infection risks from contaminated floodwater in Palm Beach and Treasure Coast    WPBF
entry.article_text: As flooding persists across Palm Beach and the Treasure Coast, doctors are urging residents to take precautions against infections caused by walking through contaminated floodwater. Moti Ramgopal, an infectious disease specialist at Florida Coast Medical Center, expressed concern for individuals with underlying health conditions. "What we tend to be very concerned about are our patients who are individuals who have underlying medical problems, diabetes, for an example. Receiving chemotherapy, patients who have their immune system compromised for many reasons," Ramgopal said. He warned that anyone could be at risk of infection if they are not careful or lack proper protective attire. "You definitely have to wear protective shoes. You definitely have to wear protection around it, and as soon as you get out of that water area, check your feet," Ramgopal said. Ramgopal also highlighted the dangers of ingesting harmful bacteria from contaminated water. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 "A healthy person can ingest E. coli, you can ingest salmonella, you can ingest contaminated water," Ramgopal said. Over the past week, news crews have observed flooding conditions that forced some residents to evacuate due to high levels of contaminated water in their homes. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. Ramgopal advised against allowing children to play in floodwater and warned of potential fungal and mold issues as water seeps into homes. "Do not let kids play in contaminated water, and even in the household, as the water seeps into your house, you can have, as the water recedes, fungal problems, and you can have mold building up," Ramgopal said. He explained that historic flooding events like this raise concerns about multiple levels of infections. "If you're diabetic, look for open wounds because many patients may have something called neuropathy. And with neuropathy, you may not have the feeling of your feet, and you walk in this water. If you're barefoot, it could become macerated, you can get fungal infections. The concern is regular strep infections, streptococcal infections, and bacterial infections," Ramgopal said. Ramgopal shared that he has been treating one to two patients per day for floodwater-related infections. "I saw a patient today who had a gash in their leg from the floodwater, and because of that infection, she needs different, aggressive care of these wounds. We're seeing one to two people with lower extremity infections and cellulitis. These are older patients who had difficulty moving around and had to get into the water for sustainability purposes," Ramgopal said. Standing water is also a breeding ground for mosquitoes, and doctors are concerned that dengue cases may increase in the coming weeks. They are monitoring the situation closely.

entry.title: 'We’re homeless': Martin County residents voice frustrations over flooding at commission meeting - WPBF
entry.summary: 'We’re homeless': Martin County residents voice frustrations over flooding at commission meeting    WPBF
entry.article_text: Martin County residents gathered at the commission chambers Tuesday morning to express their concerns about ongoing flooding in their neighborhoods and demand action from county leaders. "For 40 years, I’ve raised my family here, built my life here, and in the hours, watched everything we worked for become submerged in flood water and sewage," Jensen Beach resident Mary Berner said. Resident Lisa French described the impact of the flooding, saying, "Today, we’re homeless. We have nowhere to have Christmas. We don’t have much to come home to." Some residents questioned whether drainage infrastructure and development contributed to the flooding, while Yamila Rollan Escalona, who's with the Yaya por Vida Foundation, raised concerns about response efforts. MARTIN COUNTY FLOODING: Jensen Beach residents struggle with flooding and damaged homes after historic rainfall "Take Rich, a historic Black American in a Bahamian neighborhood inhabited and preserved for generations by a majority Black Americans. With a capital 'B.' They still have not been properly mitigated. Standing water, no pumps, no headlines, not a peep on social media, and just one article in the news today! Katrina much?" Rollan Escalona said. County leaders said crews are pumping water around the clock and assured residents that once the immediate flooding is addressed, they will explore ways to reduce future risks. Some proposed solutions include having one agency, such as the South Florida Water Management District, manage the nearby Savannas as a single watershed and exploring additional drainage options. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "I do expect you to make additional funding available to your staff today to mitigate this emergency as efficiently as possible. Thank you for your time and expect to continue to hear from us," resident Kyle Pond said. Commissioner Sarah Heard responded, saying, "Jensen Beach residents, we’ve heard you loud and clear. You are our top priority." County leaders also said they plan to review the county’s warning system and will address the flooding issue again at their next meeting, where they will provide updates and discuss a potential grant program. entry.title: 'It's heartwarming': Fort Pierce community gathers to honor veterans and military families - WPBF
entry.summary: 'It's heartwarming': Fort Pierce community gathers to honor veterans and military families    WPBF
entry.article_text: Community members in Fort Pierce gathered Wednesday to honor veterans, military families, and those who continue to serve the country in a heartfelt ceremony. The event recognized the brave men and women who have worn the uniform and represented the United States Armed Forces. Dennis Mallon, who served in the U.S. Army from 1966 to 1968, shared his personal loss. "I lost my best friend," Mallon said. "He ended up going into the Marines, I ended up going in the Army, and he did the ultimate sacrifice. To this day, I miss him." The ceremony also expressed gratitude to military families for their support. I come from a military family," one attendee said. "Everything was pretty nice. I'm out here to support the veterans, and everything turned out pretty nice. I'm glad to be a part of it," Retired U.S. Army veteran Zachary Pressley said. Cynthia Shelton, representing the American Legion Post 171. Army veteran, who served from 1987 to 2021, highlighted the importance of supporting service members. "One of our members is deployed at this time, so we are also keeping her in our prayers because the wars are always going to be there, so we have to always show up and do our part," Shelton said. Vietnam veteran Dave Kauffman, who served in 1968, reflected on the progress made in honoring veterans. "When we came home from Vietnam, none of this existed. We were not welcomed home, and I think we learned from that, and we won't make that mistake again. It's heartwarming to see people coming out," Kauffman said. Members of Fort Pierce Central High School's JROTC attended the event, along with recent graduate Private First-Class Jason Salinas, now a U.S. "It's great that they're still doing things like this because it not only shows appreciation and love that we show due to the loss of veterans that we have, I'm so thankful that I'm here and able to follow in their footsteps so that I can still continue in their legacy and hold on to that no matter what," Salinas said. "I'm so thankful for the opportunity I was given and blessed with by not only my friends and family and the people that support me but also to God that gave me the opportunity to raise my right hand and take it further on," Salinas said. This year’s guest speaker, Sergeant Major Brian Huston, U.S. Army (Retired), shared a message of gratitude for veterans and those still serving, thanking them for answering the call. entry.title: St. Lucie County shelter waives adoption fees after taking in 114 cats from alleged hoarding case
entry.summary: A St. Lucie County animal shelter is making an urgent push to find homes for cats and kittens after taking in more than 100 animals from a home last month. The Humane Society of St. Lucie County is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for an emergency 'Empty the Shelters' adoption event on Nov. 13 and 14. Adoption fees will be waived for all cats and kittens during the two-day event. The shelter says it's facing a capacity crunch after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. Lucie home in October. The cats were rescued from a home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case that led to a woman's arrest on 29 felony animal cruelty charges. Now, the Humane Society is hoping the adoption event will free up much-needed space so it can continue caring for the animals. All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. The event runs from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Friday, Nov. 13, and Saturday, Nov. 14, at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, located at 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road in Port St. Lucie. Anyone interested in adopting can view available pets at hsslc.org .

entry.title: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site - cw34.com
entry.summary: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change for a roughly 34-acre property near South 25th Street and West Midway Road that could allow nearly 500 homes. The vote came as residents sought answers about recent flooding and commissioners questioned how the property handles drainage. An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The property sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties. If designated for residential use, the site could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request. See also: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems, and explain how to prevent future flooding. I love my community, but it’s not fair that we’re suffering because nobody has taken the initiative to do what’s right for us, one resident said. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of the neighborhood and surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also asked for a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. It covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie Veterans Day ceremony honors generations of veterans and their service - WFLX
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie Veterans Day ceremony honors generations of veterans and their service    WFLX
entry.article_text: Veterans of all eras and residents of all ages packed Veterans Memorial Park in Port St. Lucie on Wednesday for the annual Veterans Day ceremony. WFLX anchor and Navy veteran Mike Trim connected with fellow veterans about the significance of the day. Vietnam veteran Michael Greene wore a newly decorated vest commemorating his Army service “It’s all like my whole history. I started in transportation. I think it’s very important. I enlisted and was not supposed to go but ended up over there,” Greene told Trim. Wayne Thomas, another Vietnam War veteran in attendance, told Trim he felt this day now properly honors their service, which was not previously recognized. “It’s good to get the recognition that we didn’t get,” Thomas said. Lucie High School Junior ROTC attended the ceremony in full force while crowds of all ages looked on. That included a member of the greatest generation: 98-year-old World War II veteran Robert Vogel. I would really encourage anyone to come to these events because they’re really important to support the veterans,” Vogel told Trim. Those veterans heard keynote speaker, Retired Air Force Master Sgt. A special touch from the Port St. Lucie community band featured songs from each branch of service. That prompted service members in attendance to stand for their respective branch song. There was also a special flyover by the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office helicopter.

entry.title: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes - WPBF
entry.summary: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes    WPBF
entry.article_text: After more than a week of standing floodwater, some residents near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are finally beginning to clean up their homes as water slowly recedes. Martin County began pumping water out of the neighborhood Monday, allowing some homeowners to begin assessing the damage. For Lisa French, the receding water means she can finally begin the difficult work of cleaning out her home. “I mean, we’ve been underwater for a week,” French said. When WPBF 25 News visited French’s home several days ago, water was still standing inside, reaching more than a foot deep in some rooms. CLICK HERE FOR INFORMATION ON HOW TO DONATE TO THE FRENCH FAMILY Now, the water is gone, but much of what she owns has been destroyed. Since early Wednesday morning, French, her husband and several neighbors have been removing damaged drywall, tearing out the kitchen and carrying ruined furniture and belongings into the front yard. “You know, you’re sitting there with your house full of water, sitting in the fact that you lost your entire home. But now we can actually move and work instead of think,” French said. While French has begun cleaning up, other residents are still waiting for floodwaters to recede. Susan Destafney, who has lived in the neighborhood for four decades, said she has never experienced anything like it. “We’ve lived in our home for 40 years. We’ve never seen the likes of this,” Destafney said. Community volunteers have also stepped in to help, including Alaura Macpherson, who runs the local group Quit Messen With Jensen. Macpherson said volunteers have been collecting cleaning supplies and other necessities for affected families. She is also organizing a community fundraiser and meal on Nov. 25 to raise money for flood victims. Local restaurants are expected to donate food, while the event will also serve as a resource center connecting residents with contractors, cleanup services and other recovery assistance. “The community is what helps each other. We are a family,” Macpherson said. Martin County officials have opened a Multi-Agency Resource Center at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach to connect flood victims with recovery assistance. entry.title: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now - WPEC
entry.summary: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now    WPEC
entry.article_text: A day after Jensen Beach residents told Martin County commissioners that flooding forced them from their homes, families can go to Hoke Library for recovery help while they wait for word on federal aid. The flood recovery center is open Wednesday even though regular library services are closed for Veterans Day. State agencies and local nonprofits are there to connect residents with recovery resources, and the county says more agencies and services will be added throughout the week. At Tuesday’s commission meeting, residents pressed county leaders about drainage and how they were warned. Martin County Emergency Management Director Sally Waite told commissioners the flooding affected 77 homes and that assessment teams planned to visit each one to document the damage. Cleanup begins in Skyline Heights On Wednesday, CBS12 News returned to Jensen Beach’s Skyline Heights neighborhood, where part of Hyline Drive remained underwater. At Lisa French’s home, the cleanup had finally started. French said hers was the first home in the neighborhood being cleared out and gutted. Cabinets, furniture and pieces of drywall covered the front yard as workers carried out nearly everything floodwater touched. After a week, this is like celebration, French said. But that progress came with tears as she watched her family’s belongings get thrown away. The crib was a rough one to watch go, French said. It’s just my kids, you know. One week earlier, streets throughout the neighborhood were underwater and residents used kayaks to check on their homes and neighbors. Waite told CBS12 News that some homes took on three to five feet of water. She estimated about 24 of the 77 affected homes were destroyed. French and her family are staying with her parents and waiting to hear about longer-term housing. She said they do not have flood insurance. Alaura Macpherson, co-founder of Quit Messing With Jensen, went to the Hoke Library resource center Wednesday to collect cleanup supplies for affected families. CBS12 News later met up with her at French’s home, where she was helping the family clear out the damage. Absolutely not, Macpherson said. I will do this any day for my community. For French, getting everything out is only the beginning. This is bittersweet because we’re moving forward, French said. But, you know, how do we rebuild? Where to get help The Multi-Agency Resource Center is at Hoke Library, 1150 NW Jack Williams Way in Jensen Beach . The county lists those hours for Wednesday through Saturday until further notice. The center is closed Sundays. Martin County is also accepting applications for state disaster housing assistance. Households must meet income requirements. Residents can call 772-320-3169 for details. They can also report flood damage and fill out a needs survey on the county’s flood recovery page. Read more: 'We're not getting any answers': Hamilton Bay residents frustrated as flooding continues Where FEMA aid stands Florida announced Monday that it had requested a presidential major disaster declaration for the flooding. As of Wednesday morning, federal approval had yet to be announced. The state’s announcement did not specify whether the request included FEMA Individual Assistance for Martin County. If that aid is authorized for Martin County, eligible households could apply for help with expenses such as temporary housing and essential home repairs.

entry.title: 'We’re homeless': Martin County residents voice frustrations over flooding at commission meeting - WPBF
entry.summary: 'We’re homeless': Martin County residents voice frustrations over flooding at commission meeting    WPBF
entry.article_text: Martin County residents gathered at the commission chambers Tuesday morning to express their concerns about ongoing flooding in their neighborhoods and demand action from county leaders. "For 40 years, I’ve raised my family here, built my life here, and in the hours, watched everything we worked for become submerged in flood water and sewage," Jensen Beach resident Mary Berner said. Resident Lisa French described the impact of the flooding, saying, "Today, we’re homeless. We have nowhere to have Christmas. We don’t have much to come home to." Some residents questioned whether drainage infrastructure and development contributed to the flooding, while Yamila Rollan Escalona, who's with the Yaya por Vida Foundation, raised concerns about response efforts. MARTIN COUNTY FLOODING: Jensen Beach residents struggle with flooding and damaged homes after historic rainfall "Take Rich, a historic Black American in a Bahamian neighborhood inhabited and preserved for generations by a majority Black Americans. With a capital 'B.' They still have not been properly mitigated. Standing water, no pumps, no headlines, not a peep on social media, and just one article in the news today! Katrina much?" Rollan Escalona said. County leaders said crews are pumping water around the clock and assured residents that once the immediate flooding is addressed, they will explore ways to reduce future risks. Some proposed solutions include having one agency, such as the South Florida Water Management District, manage the nearby Savannas as a single watershed and exploring additional drainage options. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates "I do expect you to make additional funding available to your staff today to mitigate this emergency as efficiently as possible. Thank you for your time and expect to continue to hear from us," resident Kyle Pond said. Commissioner Sarah Heard responded, saying, "Jensen Beach residents, we’ve heard you loud and clear. You are our top priority." County leaders also said they plan to review the county’s warning system and will address the flooding issue again at their next meeting, where they will provide updates and discuss a potential grant program. entry.summary: St. Lucie County shelter waives adoption fees after taking in 114 cats from alleged hoarding case    WFLX
entry.article_text: Lucie County animal shelter is making an urgent push to find homes for cats and kittens after taking in more than 100 animals from a home last month. Lucie County is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for an emergency "Empty the Shelters" adoption event on Nov. Adoption fees will be waived for all cats and kittens during the two-day event. The shelter says it's facing a capacity crunch after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. The cats were rescued from a home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case that led to a woman's arrest on 29 felony animal cruelty charges. Now, the Humane Society is hoping the adoption event will free up much-needed space so it can continue caring for the animals. All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. The event runs from 11 a.m. 14, at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, located at 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road in Port St. Anyone interested in adopting can view available pets at hsslc.org .

entry.title: Martin County looks for flood fixes after Port St. Lucie pumping into Savannas Preserve
entry.summary: More than a week after historic rainfall hit the Treasure Coast, Martin County leaders are looking at how to prevent another flooding disaster after officials said Port St. Lucie pumped floodwater into the Savannas Preserve before water flowed south toward neighborhoods in Jensen Beach. WPTV's Michael Hoffman has been following those questions as families continue recovering from homes that were damaged or destroyed. Residents question what happened after the rain Residents have told WPTV they believe pumping floodwater from areas to the north contributed to the natural flow of water moving south and overflowing into their Jensen Beach neighborhoods. Tiffany Kincaid was among the residents whose homes were devastated. I've never seen anything like this, not this level of devastation that has been sort of sitting in water for now eight days, Kincaid said. Kincaid said her family believed protections were in place until rising water forced them out. 'We trusted that a plan was in place to protect us, until midnight when water became entering our home, and then we quickly realized that we needed to get out,' Kincaid said. Martin County official: 'The severity of that rainfall caught us unprepared' At a Martin County Commission meeting, Public Works Director James Gorton acknowledged the challenge presented by the historic rainfall. 'The severity of that rainfall caught us unprepared,' Gorton said. 'It caught St. Lucie County unprepared. It caught Indian River unprepared.' Gorton also addressed pumping from Port St. Lucie into the Savannas Preserve. 'They pumped Monday and they pumped Tuesday morning. They stopped Tuesday morning,' Gorton said. Gorton said one concern is that individual jurisdictions may be looking primarily at conditions within their own watersheds rather than what happens farther downstream. entry.article_text: More than a week after historic rainfall hit the Treasure Coast, Martin County leaders are looking at how to prevent another flooding disaster after officials said Port St. Lucie pumped floodwater into the Savannas Preserve before water flowed south toward neighborhoods in Jensen Beach.WATCH REPORT BELOW:The flooding and damage came days after the historic rainfall stopped, leaving residents questioning what happened, who was pumping water into the preserve and what can be changed before another major storm.WPTV's Michael Hoffman has been following those questions as families continue recovering from homes that were damaged or destroyed.Residents have told WPTV they believe pumping floodwater from areas to the north contributed to the natural flow of water moving south and overflowing into their Jensen Beach neighborhoods.Tiffany Kincaid was among the residents whose homes were devastated.“I've never seen anything like this, not this level of devastation that has been sort of sitting in water for now eight days,” Kincaid said.Kincaid said her family believed protections were in place until rising water forced them out."We trusted that a plan was in place to protect us, until midnight when water became entering our home, and then we quickly realized that we needed to get out," Kincaid said.At a Martin County Commission meeting, Public Works Director James Gorton acknowledged the challenge presented by the historic rainfall."The severity of that rainfall caught us unprepared," Gorton said. It caught Indian River unprepared."Gorton also addressed pumping from Port St. Lucie into the Savannas Preserve."They pumped Monday and they pumped Tuesday morning. They stopped Tuesday morning," Gorton said.Gorton said one concern is that individual jurisdictions may be looking primarily at conditions within their own watersheds rather than what happens farther downstream."They're just looking at the water levels that are in their watershed," Gorton said. "They're not looking at their impacts to the downstream."The pumping itself is not an illegal practice. Lucie has a permit allowing it to pump into the preserve, and Martin County leaders said there are not concrete regulation schedules governing the Savannas as a whole.That has raised a bigger question for local leaders: Who should be responsible for considering the consequences across the entire watershed?“I don't know that we can modify their permit, but I would hope that we'd be able to look at that and say, you know, do no harm, which is really what kind of — or shared adversity, I think, is a better way to say it,” Gorton said.One potential solution discussed by Martin County officials would put management of the Savannas watershed under one overarching organization rather than relying on decisions made by individual jurisdictions.“Once we get that water out, there's a larger discussion that we need to have, which is: What are we going to do to mitigate this in the future?” Gorton said.He suggested the water management district could potentially play a role."One such idea might be looking at treating the Savannas as a watershed that needs to be managed by one party," Gorton said. "Maybe it would be the water management district."Martin County Commissioner Edward Ciampi agreed that the current situation warrants another look."I agree with what your suggestion was, is that it just can't be whoever pumps fastest and first wins," Ciampi said.For people still dealing with the consequences in Jensen Beach, those discussions come as they search for answers, assistance and, in some cases, a dry place to call home.WPTV will continue following whether Martin County and other agencies develop a new plan for managing water in the Savannas and what changes could be made before another major rainfall event.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. French and her family are staying with her parents and waiting to hear about longer-term housing. She said they do not have flood insurance. Alaura Macpherson, co-founder of Quit Messing With Jensen, went to the Hoke Library resource center Wednesday to collect cleanup supplies for affected families. CBS12 News later met up with her at French’s home, where she was helping the family clear out the damage. Absolutely not, Macpherson said. I will do this any day for my community. For French, getting everything out is only the beginning. This is bittersweet because we’re moving forward, French said. But, you know, how do we rebuild? Where to get help The Multi-Agency Resource Center is at Hoke Library, 1150 NW Jack Williams Way in Jensen Beach . The county lists those hours for Wednesday through Saturday until further notice. The center is closed Sundays. Martin County is also accepting applications for state disaster housing assistance. Households must meet income requirements. Residents can call 772-320-3169 for details. They can also report flood damage and fill out a needs survey on the county’s flood recovery page. Read more: 'We're not getting any answers': Hamilton Bay residents frustrated as flooding continues Where FEMA aid stands Florida announced Monday that it had requested a presidential major disaster declaration for the flooding. As of Wednesday morning, federal approval had yet to be announced. The state’s announcement did not specify whether the request included FEMA Individual Assistance for Martin County. If that aid is authorized for Martin County, eligible households could apply for help with expenses such as temporary housing and essential home repairs.

entry.title: 'Quit is not an option': Fort Pierce woman loses house for a second time to a storm - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Quit is not an option': Fort Pierce woman loses house for a second time to a storm    WPBF
entry.article_text: A Fort Pierce woman is recovering from devastating flooding that destroyed her childhood home, marking the second time in two years she has lost everything. Terri Polk, who previously lost her home in the Spanish Lakes community to a tornado during Hurricane Milton, moved back into her childhood home to care for her mother, who has Alzheimer’s. Now, that home has been severely damaged by floodwaters. “The heart throb of our whole family is here,” Polk said. Polk shared that the house, built by her parents, has always been a central place for her family. “My mother’s door has always been open to everyone in the family,” she said. “This breaks your heart because I grew up in this house, I actually grew up here.” Last Monday, floodwaters rushed into the home, leaving behind destruction. “In the morning, the water was up to the tops of the beds,” Polk said. By the time the water receded, the damage was done. Polk’s belongings, including her bed and bookcases, now lie in a pile on the front lawn. Polk said she hasn’t slept in days as she tries to process the loss. The home is now filled with dehumidifiers, and Polk’s flood insurance won’t cover all the damages. Despite the challenges, she remains determined to rebuild. “No is not the answer; quit is not an option,” she said. “I’m not going to give up." It caught Indian River unprepared."Gorton also addressed pumping from Port St. Lucie into the Savannas Preserve."They pumped Monday and they pumped Tuesday morning. They stopped Tuesday morning," Gorton said.Gorton said one concern is that individual jurisdictions may be looking primarily at conditions within their own watersheds rather than what happens farther downstream."They're just looking at the water levels that are in their watershed," Gorton said. "They're not looking at their impacts to the downstream."The pumping itself is not an illegal practice. Lucie has a permit allowing it to pump into the preserve, and Martin County leaders said there are not concrete regulation schedules governing the Savannas as a whole.That has raised a bigger question for local leaders: Who should be responsible for considering the consequences across the entire watershed?“I don't know that we can modify their permit, but I would hope that we'd be able to look at that and say, you know, do no harm, which is really what kind of — or shared adversity, I think, is a better way to say it,” Gorton said.One potential solution discussed by Martin County officials would put management of the Savannas watershed under one overarching organization rather than relying on decisions made by individual jurisdictions.“Once we get that water out, there's a larger discussion that we need to have, which is: What are we going to do to mitigate this in the future?” Gorton said.He suggested the water management district could potentially play a role."One such idea might be looking at treating the Savannas as a watershed that needs to be managed by one party," Gorton said. "Maybe it would be the water management district."Martin County Commissioner Edward Ciampi agreed that the current situation warrants another look."I agree with what your suggestion was, is that it just can't be whoever pumps fastest and first wins," Ciampi said.For people still dealing with the consequences in Jensen Beach, those discussions come as they search for answers, assistance and, in some cases, a dry place to call home.WPTV will continue following whether Martin County and other agencies develop a new plan for managing water in the Savannas and what changes could be made before another major rainfall event.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.article_text: Lucie County animal shelter is making an urgent push to find homes for cats and kittens after taking in more than 100 animals from a home last month. Lucie County is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for an emergency "Empty the Shelters" adoption event on Nov. Adoption fees will be waived for all cats and kittens during the two-day event. The shelter says it's facing a capacity crunch after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. The cats were rescued from a home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case that led to a woman's arrest on 29 felony animal cruelty charges. Now, the Humane Society is hoping the adoption event will free up much-needed space so it can continue caring for the animals. All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. The event runs from 11 a.m. 14, at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, located at 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road in Port St. Anyone interested in adopting can view available pets at hsslc.org .

entry.title: Port St. Lucie Veterans Day ceremony honors generations of veterans and their service - WFLX
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie Veterans Day ceremony honors generations of veterans and their service    WFLX
entry.article_text: Veterans of all eras and residents of all ages packed Veterans Memorial Park in Port St. Lucie on Wednesday for the annual Veterans Day ceremony. WFLX anchor and Navy veteran Mike Trim connected with fellow veterans about the significance of the day. Vietnam veteran Michael Greene wore a newly decorated vest commemorating his Army service “It’s all like my whole history. I started in transportation. I think it’s very important. I enlisted and was not supposed to go but ended up over there,” Greene told Trim. Wayne Thomas, another Vietnam War veteran in attendance, told Trim he felt this day now properly honors their service, which was not previously recognized. “It’s good to get the recognition that we didn’t get,” Thomas said. Lucie High School Junior ROTC attended the ceremony in full force while crowds of all ages looked on. That included a member of the greatest generation: 98-year-old World War II veteran Robert Vogel. I would really encourage anyone to come to these events because they’re really important to support the veterans,” Vogel told Trim. Those veterans heard keynote speaker, Retired Air Force Master Sgt. A special touch from the Port St. Lucie community band featured songs from each branch of service. That prompted service members in attendance to stand for their respective branch song. There was also a special flyover by the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office helicopter.

entry.title: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site - cw34.com
entry.summary: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change for a roughly 34-acre property near South 25th Street and West Midway Road that could allow nearly 500 homes. The vote came as residents sought answers about recent flooding and commissioners questioned how the property handles drainage. An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The property sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties. If designated for residential use, the site could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request. See also: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems, and explain how to prevent future flooding. I love my community, but it’s not fair that we’re suffering because nobody has taken the initiative to do what’s right for us, one resident said. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of the neighborhood and surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also asked for a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. It covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.

entry.title: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes - WPBF
entry.summary: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes    WPBF
entry.article_text: After more than a week of standing floodwater, some residents near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are finally beginning to clean up their homes as water slowly recedes. Martin County began pumping water out of the neighborhood Monday, allowing some homeowners to begin assessing the damage. For Lisa French, the receding water means she can finally begin the difficult work of cleaning out her home. “I mean, we’ve been underwater for a week,” French said. When WPBF 25 News visited French’s home several days ago, water was still standing inside, reaching more than a foot deep in some rooms. CLICK HERE FOR INFORMATION ON HOW TO DONATE TO THE FRENCH FAMILY Now, the water is gone, but much of what she owns has been destroyed. Since early Wednesday morning, French, her husband and several neighbors have been removing damaged drywall, tearing out the kitchen and carrying ruined furniture and belongings into the front yard. “You know, you’re sitting there with your house full of water, sitting in the fact that you lost your entire home. But now we can actually move and work instead of think,” French said. While French has begun cleaning up, other residents are still waiting for floodwaters to recede. Susan Destafney, who has lived in the neighborhood for four decades, said she has never experienced anything like it. “We’ve lived in our home for 40 years. We’ve never seen the likes of this,” Destafney said. Community volunteers have also stepped in to help, including Alaura Macpherson, who runs the local group Quit Messen With Jensen. Macpherson said volunteers have been collecting cleaning supplies and other necessities for affected families. She is also organizing a community fundraiser and meal on Nov. 25 to raise money for flood victims. Local restaurants are expected to donate food, while the event will also serve as a resource center connecting residents with contractors, cleanup services and other recovery assistance. “The community is what helps each other. We are a family,” Macpherson said. Martin County officials have opened a Multi-Agency Resource Center at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach to connect flood victims with recovery assistance.
