entry.article_text: What was once a sprawling cattle pasture in western Martin County now looks more like a lake.What residents described as 3 to 4 feet of floodwater currently covers parts of Hungryland Farms in the Trailside community, forcing cattle to wade and swim through submerged pastures in search of dry ground.WATCH REPORT BELOW: But for the families who live and work there, the flooding is more than a natural disaster. They say it's a crisis years in the making — one they warned officials about as far back as 2018.Documents obtained by WPTV show residents raised concerns about drainage problems long before last week's historic rainfall inundated the Treasure Coast.Now, with the rain gone but the water lingering, residents are questioning whether the devastation could have been prevented.Melissa Chirico, who raises grass-fed cattle at Hungryland Farms in the rural Trailside community, says the flooding has transformed her property almost overnight."It feels like Lake Okeechobee," she said.Her cattle, accustomed to grazing freely across the farm, are now navigating deep floodwater. "It's completely covered," Chirico said. they're all underwater."The flooding has left her animals without their primary food source and exposed them to potentially deadly hazards, including drowning, waterborne parasites and electrical dangers.Chirico pointed to an electrical transformer nearly submerged by floodwater, questioning whether her cattle could be electrocuted if they wandered too close.And despite the rain stopping, she said the water isn't draining — it's rising. "We always thought we were through because the rain had stopped, but the water kept rising," she said.For Trailside Homeowners Association President Kyla Shay, the flooding is the culmination of years of unresolved drainage concerns.In a 2018 letter obtained by WPTV, Shay warned homeowners that property south of Trailside had effectively become a reservoir, with water rising as much as 3.5 feet above community roads and breaching a berm — a raised barrier designed to control water flow.That same year, Shay contacted the South Florida Water Management District, warning that blocked drainage had left some pastures under 8 feet of water.She asked for help but says the underlying problems were never resolved."It's a combination of years of 'We'll get to it,' and we never got to it," Shay said.Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton acknowledges the community faces significant drainage challenges.Gorton said a berm breached Monday on the county-owned Elise J Property northeast of Trailside, sending water into a nearby canal, with some water backflowing into the community."We still can't get back to that breach," Gorton told investigative reporter Kate Hussey, explaining that high water levels have prevented crews from accessing the area.But the larger problem, he said, is Trailside's geography.The community is essentially a bathtub, surrounded by berms, hundreds of acres of wetlands and two independent water control districts.Water flows into the area, but there is only one drainage ditch for it to slowly escape."There's no easy way to get that water out except by pump or gravity," Gorton said.WPTV contacted engineer Bob Higgins, who works with both the Pal Mar Water Control District and the Hobe St. Lucie Conservancy District.Higgins said a potential solution had already been designed years ago: an outfall that would allow water to drain through the R G Mitigation Bank Preserve to the south and the neighboring Elise J property, which Martin County acquired in 2026. But that project was never built.When Hussey asked Gorton whether the county had been aware of the proposal, he confirmed officials had discussed it with the property's former owner."We did have some dialogue with the previous owner of Elise J about creating a formal water control structure that could discharge before the berms would breach," Gorton said.According to Gorton, the former owners submitted two permit applications to the South Florida Water Management District, but construction never began.WPTV contacted the former property owners, who said they did not know why the project was never completed.When Hussey reached out to the South Florida Water Management District, the agency said Trailside was outside its jurisdiction.However, Gorton said the district had permitted every property within Trailside and oversaw the proposed drainage project.Hussey followed up with the district, seeking clarification about its jurisdiction and asking why the drainage project was never constructed.The district has not responded to those follow-up questions.Despite the years of delays, Gorton said there may finally be a path forward."The good news is the county purchased that property, and it's our intent to bring that project forward," he said.Gorton said he has already requested the original permit applications in hopes of expediting approval — and construction— of the project.He also plans to return Friday to assess the flooding and determine what immediate relief may be possible."We're looking at ways to get the water out faster," he said.But for residents like Chirico, every additional day underwater carries a cost. "This could be a very costly natural disaster for us," she said.Her cattle still need to eat. Their pastures are submerged. And with no clear timeline for when the water will recede, the future of her farm remains uncertain."I don't have any food," Chirico said to her cows. "I'm sorry."For now, Hungryland Farms is living up to its name — and the families who depend on it are waiting for the water to go down.WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey continues to seek answers from the South Florida Water Management District about the proposed drainage project and why it was never completed.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie to break ground on new 6,000-seat soccer stadium in December
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie is getting closer to welcoming its first professional soccer team , with a groundbreaking ceremony for a new 6,000-seat stadium scheduled for Saturday, Dec. 12. Port St. Lucie Sports Club announced Thursday that construction will begin at Walton One, where the stadium will sit on approximately six acres. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Port St. Lucie to break ground on new pro soccer stadium in December The club is preparing to compete in USL League One in 2027, and the new stadium is expected to serve as more than just a place to watch soccer. Plans call for a year-round destination where families and community members can gather for entertainment and other events. The development group will fully fund construction of the stadium and has entered into an agreement with the City of Port St. Lucie to use the land. 'From day one, we knew this had to be about much more than building a soccer club,' said Gustavo Surez, founder and CEO of Port St. Lucie Sports Club. 'We set out to create something that feels like a true part of this community, a place where families can gather, young players can dream, and new traditions can take shape.' The groundbreaking ceremony will begin at noon on Dec. 12, bringing together club leaders, USL representatives, partners and founding members. A public celebration will follow at 1:30 p.m., featuring food trucks, entertainment and activities for all ages. The club says more details about the event will be announced in the coming weeks.

entry.title: Businesses impacted by Military Trail closure after Learjet crash can apply for grants of up to $5,000
entry.summary: Starting Thursday, Palm Beach County is making $250,000 available to help businesses and nonprofits that lost revenue after the Nov. 1 Learjet crash forced the partial closure of Military Trail near Greenacres. The Palm Beach County Board of County Commissioners approved funding for the Military Trail Business Interruption Grant Program on Tuesday. County Administrator Joseph Abruzzo initially launched the program Nov. 2 under local emergency authority. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Businesses impacted by Learjet crash can apply for $5K grants Eligible businesses and nonprofits can receive a one-time grant of up to $5,000, while funding remains available. County officials said the closure of Military Trail near the crash site disrupted businesses by limiting access for customers and deliveries. The county's Department of Housing and Economic Development will administer the grants. Businesses can use the money for operating expenses including rent, payroll, utilities and essential inventory. PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW: $250K in grants for Palm Beach County businesses impacted by Learjet crash The county will use an applicant's latest filed business tax return to estimate revenue losses based on a 30-day interruption. Grants will be awarded on a first-come, first-served basis until the $250,000 is exhausted or all eligible applicants have been served. Who is eligible? The eligible area stretches along Military Trail from Broadway Street on the south to Kelly Drive and Sussex Avenue on the north. Businesses and nonprofits must have been operating at a physical location within the designated area before Nov. 1. Applicants must also certify that the road closure disrupted their operations or access and that they intend to continue or resume operations. The county will verify addresses using the official program map. How to apply Applications and full program criteria will be available Thursday, Nov. 12, on the Palm Beach County Department of Housing and Economic Development website. Applicants will need to submit: A signed application A W-9 Their latest filed business tax return Proof of the business address Photo identification for the authorized signer Applicable Sunbiz documentation A business tax receipt or documentation showing an exemption Awards are capped at $5,000 for each eligible business or nonprofit.

entry.title: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County rejects plan that could bring nearly 500 homes to low-lying site    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change for a roughly 34-acre property near South 25th Street and West Midway Road that could allow nearly 500 homes. The vote came as residents sought answers about recent flooding and commissioners questioned how the property handles drainage. An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The property sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties. If designated for residential use, the site could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request. See also: 77 homes hit by Martin County flooding. Where to get help now At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate last week’s flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems, and explain how to prevent future flooding. I love my community, but it’s not fair that we’re suffering because nobody has taken the initiative to do what’s right for us, one resident said. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of the neighborhood and surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also asked for a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials. White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. It covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.

entry.title: 'Quit is not an option': Fort Pierce woman loses house for a second time to a storm - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Quit is not an option': Fort Pierce woman loses house for a second time to a storm    WPBF
entry.article_text: A Fort Pierce woman is recovering from devastating flooding that destroyed her childhood home, marking the second time in two years she has lost everything. Terri Polk, who previously lost her home in the Spanish Lakes community to a tornado during Hurricane Milton, moved back into her childhood home to care for her mother, who has Alzheimer’s. Now, that home has been severely damaged by floodwaters. “The heart throb of our whole family is here,” Polk said. Polk shared that the house, built by her parents, has always been a central place for her family. “My mother’s door has always been open to everyone in the family,” she said. “This breaks your heart because I grew up in this house, I actually grew up here.” Last Monday, floodwaters rushed into the home, leaving behind destruction. “In the morning, the water was up to the tops of the beds,” Polk said. By the time the water receded, the damage was done. Polk’s belongings, including her bed and bookcases, now lie in a pile on the front lawn. Polk said she hasn’t slept in days as she tries to process the loss. The home is now filled with dehumidifiers, and Polk’s flood insurance won’t cover all the damages. Despite the challenges, she remains determined to rebuild. “No is not the answer; quit is not an option,” she said. “I’m not going to give up." entry.title: St. Lucie County residents demand action after historic flooding - WPBF
entry.summary: St. Lucie County residents demand action after historic flooding    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie County filled Tuesday night’s Board of County Commissioners meeting, demanding answers and action after last week’s historic flooding. “I lost everything; I’m a 73-year-old widow,” one resident said. Dozens of residents spoke during the public comment period, voicing concerns about the flooding and criticizing the county’s response. Many called for improved retention and drainage systems to prevent future disasters. “We don’t need another explanation on how historic this rainfall was. We need to make sure this never happens again,” another resident said. One woman shared how the flooding has upended her life. “I’ve been living in a motel since last Monday. I was on vacation and had to come home. The meeting also highlighted questions about the school district’s decision to keep schools open during Monday’s flooding. The district is expected to address these concerns at its meeting next Tuesday. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

entry.article_text: Yvette Drucker is beginning a new chapter in public service as Palm Beach County's new Clerk of the Circuit Court and Comptroller, taking over one of the county's most significant constitutional offices.Sworn in Tuesday, Drucker steps into the role following a turbulent period for the clerk's office under former Clerk Mike Caruso. She now oversees approximately 670 employees and an $87.4 million budget while serving as the county's chief financial officer, treasurer and auditor.WATCH REPORT BELOW: In an exclusive interview with WPTV's Joel Lopez, Drucker discussed her leadership priorities, her transition from Boca Raton City Council, questions about her experience and the future of the county's controversial investments in Israel bonds."It's a new day for the clerk's office. It's been a little bit of a challenging time for the individuals that work here. I have a phenomenal staff. They've kept it afloat, so my goal is to really listen, evaluate, and then execute what we can do to make it better," Drucker said.Drucker is the first Hispanic woman to hold the position of Palm Beach County clerk and comptroller.For her, the milestone carries personal significance. Her parents immigrated from Cuba in 1957, and she says her journey represents the American dream."It's really important to me because my parents are immigrants. I still have a living grandmother who's 91, and she's still here, and I am the American dream," she said.Drucker is also the first college graduate in her family. She credits her parents with instilling the values that helped shape her career."My parents didn't really have a lot of schooling. They had good work ethic and integrity. And they respected people, so really important for me to continue to inspire and lead in a way that others can look up to me and that they can also make their impact in the world."Her swearing-in ceremony was an especially meaningful moment, with her parents by her side."My mom held the Bible while I got sworn in. My dad anchored her to the left, and they're just so proud," Drucker said.She described the ceremony as a defining moment in both her professional and personal life."A surreal moment, but I took it all in. I've learned that you have to really be in the moment and be present," she said. "A really defining moment in my career and in my life."Drucker is no stranger to public service. She spent six years on the Boca Raton City Council, serving as deputy mayor and vice chair of the city's Community Redevelopment Agency before reaching her term limit."Six years you were with the City of Boca Raton, so why clerk of courts?" Lopez asked Drucker."I was term limited, so we do have term limits in the city, and after a couple of years, like about one year, a little over one year ago, I was just approached by a former clerk to look at this position," Drucker said. "I was not done with public service. I was born to serve, and I've been doing that since my student government days, back in high school and middle school."She said the clerk's position offered an opportunity to bring together her experience in business, government and community service."I have a background in human resources and out of corporate America, I worked for ADP TotalSource. I did 14 years there, so I also had an advocacy background and then my government. So it's a good way of marrying in my private sector with my public sector and my community service sector all in one," Drucker said.Although her time on the Boca Raton council ended, Drucker made clear that her commitment to public service had not.She said she wanted to finish her responsibilities in Boca Raton before beginning her new role, making sure the work she had started was completed.In the same week, she ended her time with Boca Raton and started with Palm Beach County, a process she said usually takes two months to transition."I pride myself with not missing meetings in six years and attending and participating, and I finished everything that I started," Drucker said.Drucker inherits an office with hundreds of employees and says she wants to build on the experience already in place while identifying opportunities to improve operations.Her message to employees is straightforward: public service must come before politics."This is a new day for this office. This office has been working, but we can make it work better for the people that we serve," she said. "I will stand by what I've been saying all along, people over politics, people over party, and definitely people over power, and that's just kind of the way that I've always led with a lot of heart. And a lot of integrity for the work that I do."Drucker says her first 100 days will focus on understanding how each department operates, reviewing the budget and identifying ways to make the office more efficient."I want to understand every department, their inner workings, the budget. We also have to understand Amendment 3, which obviously passed, and we have to respect the will of the voters and also just like I said earlier, listen, really evaluate and then execute how we're gonna serve the public," she said.She also emphasized the importance of putting the right people in the right positions."This is a public-facing operation. It's really important for me to have the right people in the right places so that we can continue serving the public," Drucker said.While some have questioned whether her background adequately prepares her for the office's court administration, accounting and auditing responsibilities, Drucker acknowledged she does not expect to know everything immediately."We have a chief of legal, runs the operations and we have subject matter experts and I'm not gonna tell you that I know everything on day one," she said. "But the way that I operate and the way that I've conducted myself throughout the city and throughout my career, I will learn as needed and will make changes as needed."She says she plans to rely on the office's existing leadership and experienced employees as she continues the transition. She recently hired her chief of staff and also the executive administrator to the clerk, but those names have not been made public."Also, this office has a deputy clerk who is interim clerk, Ms. Shannon Ramsey-Chessman, who's been incredible, and she has institutional data, and I believe that we're going to be a great team as we, you know, continue to take one day at a time."One of the biggest questions facing Drucker, who identified herself as Jewish, is the county's investment in Israel bonds.Palm Beach County has approximately $1 billion invested in the bonds, making it the largest investor in the world. The investment became a point of controversy during the campaign, and Drucker had previously expressed support for it.Now in office, she says she plans to take another look at the county's investment strategy, particularly following the passage of Amendment 3.Asked whether she still supports the county investing in Israeli bonds, Drucker said investment decisions must ultimately serve taxpayers."So I say to the public, like any investment portfolio, whether you have your own or you're overseeing an investment portfolio of this size, you always have to evaluate and make sure that your investments are aligned with what is best for the taxpayer base," she said.Drucker said the bonds have served the county well up to this point, but that does not mean the investment should go without review."And now with Amendment 3 passing, we really need to evaluate, and that's something that I'm gonna sit with our director of finance and with our county administrator," she said.She stopped short of committing to either maintaining or eliminating the investment."It's not a yes or a no; it's just, does it continue to make sense? Is this something that we have to evaluate and we always have to evaluate how we invest and how we are using the taxpayer dollar is important."When asked whether she would consider reducing or eliminating the investment if it no longer made financial sense, Drucker said the county would have to evaluate that possibility."Is it safe to say if it didn't make sense, you'd be willing to reduce, if not potentially eliminate this investment?" asked Lopez."If it didn't make sense, we would have to evaluate, correct," said Drucker.She also pointed out that Israel bonds make up only part of the county's broader investment portfolio."Even though we have a large amount in Israel bonds, we have a large portfolio. Seventy-five percent of our portfolio is not invested in Israel bonds," she said.For Drucker, the next step is making sure residents understand how the county's investments work and what they mean for the community."I think education is gonna go a long way," she said.She also pushed back on making the issue political, saying the focus should remain on the county's financial interests and the taxpayers who depend on those investments."I think we're going to leave politics out of it. It's not a political discussion. I think it's really, what are the returns to help the county?" Drucker said.She plans to meet with county officials and review the investment portfolio before making any decisions.Drucker says the transition has been busy, but she is encouraged by the employees already in place and the team she is building around her.She has brought on a chief of staff and an executive administrator to help guide her through the responsibilities of the office.She also thanked the voters and supporters who helped bring her into the position, including those who crossed party lines."I'm just really excited to be here. I think that we're gonna have this office is going to continue to produce amazing things for this community. I'm just so honored," she said. "And I'm just so proud to represent this office, and I really look forward to everything that we have to do."As she begins her tenure, Drucker says her commitment is to serve everyone in Palm Beach County, regardless of political affiliation."This office is here to serve everybody regardless of who and what you are; that's my promise to them," she said.And as for what comes next, Drucker has a simple message:"The best is yet to come, and I believe that," Drucker said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Milagro Center and United Way are making holidays brighter in Delray Beach
entry.summary: As families across Palm Beach County prepare for the holidays, the Milagro Center in Delray Beach is working to make the season brighter for children and families struggling financially. The nonprofit is partnering with United Way through WPTV's Season of Hope campaign to help provide food and toys to families in need. For many households, the holidays bring additional financial pressure as the cost of groceries, gas and other necessities continues to stretch already tight budgets. Milagro Center President and CEO Barbara Stark says the extra support can make a meaningful difference. Stark says the organizations mission is to help students succeed in school and prepare for productive, self-sustaining futures after graduation. For students like Ethan, a fourth grader at Morikami Park Elementary School, the center is a place to explore interests, build skills and have fun. 'I love doing art here, and I also love the experiments we do with Mr. C. Its really enjoyable,' Ethan said. Holiday expenses create added pressure for families Stark says the holiday season can be particularly difficult for the families the center serves, many of whom are single-parent households. 'We want to make sure that these underserved, at-risk children succeed in school,' Stark said. 'The holidays are always a very tough time for our families because they struggle financially.' She says rising expenses can make it difficult for parents to provide the holiday experience they want for their children. entry.title: 'It feels like Lake Okeechobee': Martin County community underwater after years of drainage concerns
entry.summary: What was once a sprawling cattle pasture in western Martin County now looks more like a lake. What residents described as 3 to 4 feet of floodwater currently covers parts of Hungryland Farms in the Trailside community, forcing cattle to wade and swim through submerged pastures in search of dry ground. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Martin County community underwater after years of drainage concerns But for the families who live and work there, the flooding is more than a natural disaster. They say it's a crisis years in the making one they warned officials about as far back as 2018. Documents obtained by WPTV show residents raised concerns about drainage problems long before last week's historic rainfall inundated the Treasure Coast. Now, with the rain gone but the water lingering, residents are questioning whether the devastation could have been prevented. 'All of our pastures ... they're all underwater' Melissa, who raises grass-fed cattle at Hungryland Farms in the rural Trailside community, says the flooding has transformed her property almost overnight. 'It feels like Lake Okeechobee,' she said. Her cattle, accustomed to grazing freely across the farm, are now navigating deep floodwater. 'It's completely covered,' Melissa said. 'All of our pastures ... they're all underwater.' The flooding has left her animals without their primary food source and exposed them to potentially deadly hazards, including drowning, waterborne parasites and electrical dangers. Melissa pointed to an electrical transformer nearly submerged by floodwater, questioning whether her cattle could be electrocuted if they wandered too close. And despite the rain stopping, she said the water isn't draining it's rising. 'We always thought we were through because the rain had stopped, but the water kept rising,' she said. Warnings dating back to 2018 For Trailside Homeowners Association President Kyla Shay, the flooding is the culmination of years of unresolved drainage concerns. In a 2018 letter obtained by WPTV, Shay warned homeowners that property south of Trailside had effectively become a reservoir, with water rising as much as 3.5 feet above community roads and breaching a berm a raised barrier designed to control water flow. "It's completely covered," Melissa said. they're all underwater."The flooding has left her animals without their primary food source and exposed them to potentially deadly hazards, including drowning, waterborne parasites and electrical dangers.Melissa pointed to an electrical transformer nearly submerged by floodwater, questioning whether her cattle could be electrocuted if they wandered too close.And despite the rain stopping, she said the water isn't draining — it's rising. "We always thought we were through because the rain had stopped, but the water kept rising," she said.For Trailside Homeowners Association President Kyla Shay, the flooding is the culmination of years of unresolved drainage concerns.In a 2018 letter obtained by WPTV, Shay warned homeowners that property south of Trailside had effectively become a reservoir, with water rising as much as 3.5 feet above community roads and breaching a berm — a raised barrier designed to control water flow.That same year, Shay contacted the South Florida Water Management District, warning that blocked drainage had left some pastures under 8 feet of water.She asked for help but says the underlying problems were never resolved."It's a combination of years of 'We'll get to it,' and we never got to it," Shay said.Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton acknowledges the community faces significant drainage challenges.Gorton said a berm breached Monday on the county-owned Elise J Property northeast of Trailside, sending water into a nearby canal, with some water backflowing into the community."We still can't get back to that breach," Gorton told investigative reporter Kate Hussey, explaining that high water levels have prevented crews from accessing the area.But the larger problem, he said, is Trailside's geography.The community is essentially a bathtub, surrounded by berms, hundreds of acres of wetlands and two independent water control districts.Water flows into the area, but there is only one drainage ditch for it to slowly escape."There's no easy way to get that water out except by pump or gravity," Gorton said.WPTV contacted engineer Bob Higgins, who works with both the Pal Mar Water Control District and the Hobe St. Lucie Conservancy District.Higgins said a potential solution had already been designed years ago: an outfall that would allow water to drain through the R G Mitigation Bank Preserve to the south and the neighboring Elise J property, which Martin County acquired in 2026. But that project was never built.When Hussey asked Gorton whether the county had been aware of the proposal, he confirmed officials had discussed it with the property's former owner."We did have some dialogue with the previous owner of Elise J about creating a formal water control structure that could discharge before the berms would breach," Gorton said.According to Gorton, the former owners submitted two permit applications to the South Florida Water Management District, but construction never began.WPTV contacted the former property owners, who said they did not know why the project was never completed.When Hussey reached out to the South Florida Water Management District, the agency said Trailside was outside its jurisdiction.However, Gorton said the district had permitted every property within Trailside and oversaw the proposed drainage project.Hussey followed up with the district, seeking clarification about its jurisdiction and asking why the drainage project was never constructed.The district has not responded to those follow-up questions.Despite the years of delays, Gorton said there may finally be a path forward."The good news is the county purchased that property, and it's our intent to bring that project forward," he said.Gorton said he has already requested the original permit applications in hopes of expediting approval — and construction— of the project.He also plans to return Friday to assess the flooding and determine what immediate relief may be possible."We're looking at ways to get the water out faster," he said.But for residents like Melissa, every additional day underwater carries a cost. "This could be a very costly natural disaster for us," she said.Her cattle still need to eat. Their pastures are submerged. And with no clear timeline for when the water will recede, the future of her farm remains uncertain."I don't have any food," Melissa said to her cows. "I'm sorry."For now, Hungryland Farms is living up to its name — and the families who depend on it are waiting for the water to go down.WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey continues to seek answers from the South Florida Water Management District about the proposed drainage project and why it was never completed.

entry.title: Martin County firefighters raise staffing concerns after it says hiring class canceled - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County firefighters raise staffing concerns after it says hiring class canceled    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Martin County Firefighters Union is asking county leaders to reconsider canceling a firefighter hiring class planned for January, saying the department is already short-staffed and the loss of new hires could increase pressure on crews. In a Facebook post, the union said the county canceled the class, which was expected to bring about 25 firefighters into Martin County Fire Rescue . The county cited budget concerns tied to Amendment 3 , according to the union. The union said the department is 17 firefighters short now and could be about 25 short by January as employees retire or leave for other departments. Fewer firefighters mean fewer available personnel to respond to emergencies, increased reliance on mandatory and voluntary overtime, and greater demands placed on the firefighters who remain, the union wrote. The union said its members recently agreed to forgo negotiating a new contract that would have taken effect in October, giving up a cost-of-living pay adjustment to help the county address financial challenges. It said members did so after being assured that Fire Rescue would not be affected by hiring freezes tied to Amendment 3. See also: Bobcat rescued after getting caught in barbed-wire fence near Stuart The union also questioned county administrative pay increases, saying administrative employees received 6% raises in October while firefighters face staffing shortages. The post calls on the Board of County Commissioners and county administrator to move forward with the hiring class. The county was not quoted in the union’s post. Martin County is taking a measured approach to hiring as it evaluates its long-term financial outlook and operational needs. With rising operating costs, inflation, and potential revenue impacts following the passage of Amendment 3 and anticipated SAFER Grant repayment obligations in the upcoming budget cycle, the County is being mindful of additional staffing commitments. While the firefighter recruitment class was planned months before Amendment 3 passed, current fiscal considerations have prompted a review of future hiring. The County is currently taking a soft hiring freeze approach, carefully evaluating vacancies and staffing needs. Maintaining public safety remains a priority for Martin County," the County said in a statement.

entry.title: St. Lucie County shelter waives adoption fees after taking in 114 cats from alleged hoarding case
entry.summary: A St. Lucie County animal shelter is urgently seeking homes for cats and kittens after taking in more than 100 animals from a home last month. The Humane Society of St. Lucie County is teaming up with BISSELL Pet Foundation for an emergency 'Empty the Shelters' adoption event on Nov. 13 and 14. Adoption fees will be waived for all cats and kittens during the two-day event. WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County shelter waives adoption fees after taking in 114 cats The shelter says it's facing a capacity crunch after taking in 114 cats from a Port St. Lucie home in October. The cats were rescued from a home at the center of an alleged animal hoarding case that led to a woman's arrest on 29 felony animal cruelty charges. Now, the Humane Society is hoping the adoption event will free up much-needed space so it can continue caring for the animals. All pets available for adoption are spayed or neutered, vaccinated and microchipped. The event runs from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Friday, Nov. 13, and Saturday, Nov. 14, at the Humane Society of St. Lucie County, located at 8890 Glades Cut-Off Road in Port St. Lucie. Anyone interested in adopting can view available pets at hsslc.org .

entry.title: After magical season, Park Vista High School bowling finishes in the top 5 in Florida
entry.summary: In life, we all start somewhere, and for a group of kids, AMF Bowling Alley in Boynton Beach is where it all began. 'I started at a Saturday league here at AMF probably when I was 12,' Jett Kramer, a sophomore bowler at Park Vista High School, said. 'My aunt showed me a youth league here, so I started doing it and have been doing it for five years now,' Mateo Ruiz, a junior bowler at Park Vista High School, said. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Park Vista HS bowling team finishes top five in the state Both young men met at the bowling lanes at AMF as kids and have now forged a deep bond at Park Vista High School. In fact, they're not the only two bowlers from the school who love AMF Bowling; the entire team does. It's their practice court, and it's also the place they knew this year would be special. 'Last year we also had a great team, so I knew our team this year would be just as good if not better,' said Kramer. So, how good were they this year? The team won both the county championship and district championship and qualified for state. 'That was pretty good considering we didn't make it last year; that was pretty much an upset,' co-captain Nate Banks said. 'It was awesome. We all bowled great. We had a phenomenal season; everyone bonded together. It was a phenomenal season,' co-captain Jordan Fein said. The team was on fire all season and finished fifth at state. While it wasn't the finish they'd hoped for, it was a building block for next season. Ruiz finished as a state runner-up. 'It was definitely an amazing moment. I wish I could've gotten first, but I appreciate getting there,' Ruiz said.

entry.summary: Residents of Riviera Beach's Lone Pine community are confronting the aftermath of devastating flooding, with gutted homes, piles of belongings lining neighborhood streets and families struggling to figure out what comes next. A week after floodwaters forced residents from their homes, the damage is becoming clearer, leaving some without flood insurance and questioning whether they can afford to rebuild. The flooding has turned once-familiar homes into cleanup projects and left residents facing the loss of belongings, memories and, in some cases, their sense of security. Thomas walked Hoffman through her damaged home, where much of her belongings had been removed and left in piles along the curb. 'I'm all alone. entry.title: 'Bigger than ourselves': Florida Panthers host military appreciation night
entry.summary: Throughout the season, the Florida Panthers host themed nights at some home games. On Thursday, the Cats hosted the Detroit Red Wings for military appreciation night. Despite trailing most of the game, the Florida Panthers pulled off an epic third-period comeback. The Cats tied it up at 4 apiece, then scored in the final minutes to take the lead and send Detroit home with a loss. Watch report from Eleanor Sheahan: 'Bigger than ourselves': Florida Panthers host military appreciation night The Panthers beat the Red Wings 5-4 for their military appreciation game. Outside Amerant Bank Arena, members of the United States Coast Guard and Army welcomed fans before puck drop. Inside, military members and their families got early access to Pantherland for a first look at military appreciation merch. Then on the rink, the Panthers recognized retired Army veteran Joe St. John as their Heroes Among Us honoree of the night. Another army veteran at the game was Scott Sloane. As you get older and you recognize what you did and people serving today and what it takes to service and the sacrifice it takes and then people appreciating that, that's a warm feeling, that really makes you look back at your life a little bit and your service., Sloane said. Sloane is a part of the Panthers Warriors, a hockey club for disabled us military veterans who have served our country and want to play hockey. When you leave the military, some of us lose that camaraderie, and so we have to bring it back, and we do it through this organization, Sloane said. Panthers Warriors started in 2019. Sloane said they play in tournaments and, over the years, have built a strong community that combines veterans and Panther fans. On Thursday Sloane was among the many veterans cheering on the cats. Thank you for your service as well, like hockey it brings us together. It's a collaborative thing. All the military branches work together so that's what we learned from a young age, a collaborative environment and being a part of something bigger than ourselves, Sloane said. The Panthers Warriors are always looking for more players. To learn more, visit their Instagram @ pantherswarriorshockey . The Florida Panthers begin another road trip; they head to St. Louis to play the Blues.

entry.title: Martin County firefighters raise staffing concerns after it says hiring class canceled - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County firefighters raise staffing concerns after it says hiring class canceled    WPEC
entry.article_text: The Martin County Firefighters Union is asking county leaders to reconsider canceling a firefighter hiring class planned for January, saying the department is already short-staffed and the loss of new hires could increase pressure on crews. In a Facebook post, the union said the county canceled the class, which was expected to bring about 25 firefighters into Martin County Fire Rescue . The county cited budget concerns tied to Amendment 3 , according to the union. The union said the department is 17 firefighters short now and could be about 25 short by January as employees retire or leave for other departments. Fewer firefighters mean fewer available personnel to respond to emergencies, increased reliance on mandatory and voluntary overtime, and greater demands placed on the firefighters who remain, the union wrote. The union said its members recently agreed to forgo negotiating a new contract that would have taken effect in October, giving up a cost-of-living pay adjustment to help the county address financial challenges. It said members did so after being assured that Fire Rescue would not be affected by hiring freezes tied to Amendment 3. See also: Bobcat rescued after getting caught in barbed-wire fence near Stuart The union also questioned county administrative pay increases, saying administrative employees received 6% raises in October while firefighters face staffing shortages. The post calls on the Board of County Commissioners and county administrator to move forward with the hiring class. The county was not quoted in the union’s post. Martin County is taking a measured approach to hiring as it evaluates its long-term financial outlook and operational needs. With rising operating costs, inflation, and potential revenue impacts following the passage of Amendment 3 and anticipated SAFER Grant repayment obligations in the upcoming budget cycle, the County is being mindful of additional staffing commitments. While the firefighter recruitment class was planned months before Amendment 3 passed, current fiscal considerations have prompted a review of future hiring. The County is currently taking a soft hiring freeze approach, carefully evaluating vacancies and staffing needs. Maintaining public safety remains a priority for Martin County," the County said in a statement.

entry.article_text: A Fort Pierce mother is speaking out after watching body camera footage of the night her 19-year-old daughter was fatally shot in Fort Lauderdale near an Airbnb. She believes her daughter was asking police for help and wants to know whether the officers who first responded could have done more. I already knew half of what happened, and to see it and to hear it was heartbreaking, said Alacia Ford-Barron, the mother of Myrah Zeigler. She shared the video with CBS12 News. The body camera video shows officers arriving after an altercation involving two groups of women inside the Airbnb. Officers tell everyone to leave. Ford-Barron says her daughter had been attacked and that belongings, including car keys, were taken. The group needed to retrieve those items from a nearby park. In the footage, Zeigler asks officers to walk with the group to get their belongings. One officer asks whether they have a way to get to the park. Zeigler responds that they can. Ford-Barron says she believed officers were going to help. Minutes later, gunfire erupts nearby. An officer reports that shots were fired two blocks away. Friends can be heard screaming as officers try to revive Zeigler. She later died at a nearby hospital. See also: FDOT reopens all lanes on SR 809 and Military Trail after deadly Learjet 60 crash I wanted to know why they didn't call backup. I wanted to know why she did not listen to my daughter when she was trying to explain to her and asking her to walk down to the park, Ford-Barron said. Larry Lamar Smith was later arrested in connection with Zeigler’s death. Ford-Barron says she appreciates the detectives’ work but still has questions about the initial police response. I have to be my daughter's voice. I know that if I shut down, who's going to speak for my daughter? CBS12 News is waiting to hear back from Fort Lauderdale police.

entry.title: More people, limited freshwater: Treasure Coast plans for water needs through 2050 - WPEC
entry.summary: More people, limited freshwater: Treasure Coast plans for water needs through 2050    WPEC
entry.article_text: As the Treasure Coast prepares for decades of growth, water managers face a critical question: How will the region supply enough freshwater for more people while protecting the farms, waterways and wildlife that also depend on it? Water is a necessity that is being planned for at all times, years in advance. With the explosive growth in population unfolding now, the plan is even more critical. The South Florida Water Management District’s 2026 Upper East Coast Water Supply Plan looks ahead to 2050, outlining future needs in Martin and St. Lucie counties and northeastern Okeechobee County. The district says the region’s limited freshwater resources make conservation and alternative water supplies essential to planning for that growth. What we’re seeing is about a 36-percent increase in the population in the planning area by 2050, said Carolina Maran, Chief of District Resiliency with SFWMD, describing a population approaching three-quarters of a million people. The demand for water, however, is not necessarily increasing at the same rate, Maran says. Demand for water supplied to homes and businesses, along with commercial, landscaping, and recreational uses, is expected to rise. Agricultural water use, which is the region’s largest category, is projected to decline. See also: WPB police ask public for information on sidewalk assault outside Hook Fish and Chicken Meeting the shifting needs will depend on more than population forecasts. It will also require infrastructure, efficient water use, and planning for uncertain conditions, including drought and storms. Inside a University of Florida laboratory in Fort Pierce, Dr. Sandra Guzman and her team study how water moves through soil and across different land uses. Guzman is an Associate Professor of Smart Irrigation and Hydrology with the UF/IFAS Agricultural and Biological Engineering department. A demonstration table with sand and simulated farm fields shows how water’s movement changes depending on the ground beneath it. In another area, there are charts demonstrating how immediate communication can connect area farmers with real-time agriculture and weather data. I always tell my team: water is a blessing and a curse, Guzman said. The challenge is not simply whether water is available. Its quality also determines how it can be used. We suffer from a lot of issues regarding deficit of water because it’s not only the volume of water; it’s also the quality of water, Guzman said. That creates a balancing act: supplying people and farms while protecting the lagoons, estuaries, and wildlife that depend on the region’s water resources. The district’s approach includes alternative water sources, expanded treatment and storage, and conservation. What that means is that investing in reuse, investing in efficient water uses, and also alternative water sources like the Floridan Aquifer, Maran said. Projects described in the plan include reverse-osmosis treatment, reclaimed-water expansions, and stormwater storage. In coming years, some of the infrastructure needed to support future demand must still be built. SFWMD describes the plan as a framework for local governments, utilities, agricultural operations, and other water users to guide water supply decisions. Its recommendations are intended to inform local comprehensive plans, facility work plans and ordinances. Having a plan, however, does not guarantee that every project will be completed on time. Carrying it out will require follow-through by the communities and water providers preparing for growth. On farms, part of the solution is knowing more precisely when crops need water, and how much of it. Guzman’s team works on tools that help farmers measure soil moisture and irrigate more efficiently, directing water where crops need it. The research connects decisions made in the field to the broader challenge of stretching the region’s water supply. So, in this lab, we work for that: every single drop of water that is coming out of whatever aquifer or freshwater system becomes food to your table, Guzman said. As the Treasure Coast grows, its water future will depend both on the infrastructure communities build and on how efficiently people use the supplies already available. They say it's a crisis years in the making — one they warned officials about as far back as 2018.Documents obtained by WPTV show residents raised concerns about drainage problems long before last week's historic rainfall inundated the Treasure Coast.Now, with the rain gone but the water lingering, residents are questioning whether the devastation could have been prevented.Melissa, who raises grass-fed cattle at Hungryland Farms in the rural Trailside community, says the flooding has transformed her property almost overnight."It feels like Lake Okeechobee," she said.Her cattle, accustomed to grazing freely across the farm, are now navigating deep floodwater. "It's completely covered," Melissa said. they're all underwater."The flooding has left her animals without their primary food source and exposed them to potentially deadly hazards, including drowning, waterborne parasites and electrical dangers.Melissa pointed to an electrical transformer nearly submerged by floodwater, questioning whether her cattle could be electrocuted if they wandered too close.And despite the rain stopping, she said the water isn't draining — it's rising. "We always thought we were through because the rain had stopped, but the water kept rising," she said.For Trailside Homeowners Association President Kyla Shay, the flooding is the culmination of years of unresolved drainage concerns.In a 2018 letter obtained by WPTV, Shay warned homeowners that property south of Trailside had effectively become a reservoir, with water rising as much as 3.5 feet above community roads and breaching a berm — a raised barrier designed to control water flow.That same year, Shay contacted the South Florida Water Management District, warning that blocked drainage had left some pastures under 8 feet of water.She asked for help but says the underlying problems were never resolved."It's a combination of years of 'We'll get to it,' and we never got to it," Shay said.Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton acknowledges the community faces significant drainage challenges.Gorton said a berm breached Monday on the county-owned Elise J Property northeast of Trailside, sending water into a nearby canal, with some water backflowing into the community."We still can't get back to that breach," Gorton told investigative reporter Kate Hussey, explaining that high water levels have prevented crews from accessing the area.But the larger problem, he said, is Trailside's geography.The community is essentially a bathtub, surrounded by berms, hundreds of acres of wetlands and two independent water control districts.Water flows into the area, but there is only one drainage ditch for it to slowly escape."There's no easy way to get that water out except by pump or gravity," Gorton said.WPTV contacted engineer Bob Higgins, who works with both the Pal Mar Water Control District and the Hobe St. Lucie Conservancy District.Higgins said a potential solution had already been designed years ago: an outfall that would allow water to drain through the R G Mitigation Bank Preserve to the south and the neighboring Elise J property, which Martin County acquired in 2026. But that project was never built.When Hussey asked Gorton whether the county had been aware of the proposal, he confirmed officials had discussed it with the property's former owner."We did have some dialogue with the previous owner of Elise J about creating a formal water control structure that could discharge before the berms would breach," Gorton said.According to Gorton, the former owners submitted two permit applications to the South Florida Water Management District, but construction never began.WPTV contacted the former property owners, who said they did not know why the project was never completed.When Hussey reached out to the South Florida Water Management District, the agency said Trailside was outside its jurisdiction.However, Gorton said the district had permitted every property within Trailside and oversaw the proposed drainage project.Hussey followed up with the district, seeking clarification about its jurisdiction and asking why the drainage project was never constructed.The district has not responded to those follow-up questions.Despite the years of delays, Gorton said there may finally be a path forward."The good news is the county purchased that property, and it's our intent to bring that project forward," he said.Gorton said he has already requested the original permit applications in hopes of expediting approval — and construction— of the project.He also plans to return Friday to assess the flooding and determine what immediate relief may be possible."We're looking at ways to get the water out faster," he said.But for residents like Melissa, every additional day underwater carries a cost. "This could be a very costly natural disaster for us," she said.Her cattle still need to eat. Their pastures are submerged. And with no clear timeline for when the water will recede, the future of her farm remains uncertain."I don't have any food," Melissa said to her cows. "I'm sorry."For now, Hungryland Farms is living up to its name — and the families who depend on it are waiting for the water to go down.WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey continues to seek answers from the South Florida Water Management District about the proposed drainage project and why it was never completed.

entry.title: One-year emergency contract sets phased MARTY transit return in Martin County - cw34.com
entry.summary: One-year emergency contract sets phased MARTY transit return in Martin County    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Following a brief pause, the Martin County Board of Commissioners announced on Tuesday that the county has reached a resolution to begin phased restoration of MARTY transit services. The county says it has reached a one-year emergency contract with MTM Transit, LLC to begin the phased restoration of public transportation services following an abrupt disruption due to a contract breach by the prior vendor. Last month, MARTY public transit services in Martin County abruptly stopped after its operator withdrew from its contract due to rising operating costs. This left many people without a regular bus service. The county now says it will be taking a phased approach to resuming operations, prioritizing riders who rely on ADA paratransit services, then working towards restoring fixed-route services. See also: Delray Beach says new Florida law will block St. Patrick’s Day, Pride events For those who with disabilities who cannot use regular fixed-route bus services, ADA paratransit services are expected to resume on Thursday, Nov. Details regarding scheduling and reservations are available at 772-463-2822 , the county says. A start date for restoration of full services has yet to be announced. Our priority is to restore public transportation as quickly and responsibly as possible, with particular attention to residents who depend on these services to access essential needs, as well as fiscal responsibility to the taxpayer, said Ash Beecher, Martin County Transit Administrator. We recognize the disruption this has caused for our riders and the broader community, and we are working to reestablish service in a thoughtful, coordinated manner.

entry.title: 'Did its job': Indian River County beaches recovering after erosion from nor’easter and King Tides - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Did its job': Indian River County beaches recovering after erosion from nor’easter and King Tides    WPBF
entry.article_text: Indian River County beaches are recovering after a nor’easter and king tides caused erosion along the coastline, with officials noting improvements in shoreline conditions. Erosion officials said water levels had risen almost as high as a sign at Tracking Station Beach, but the sand has already begun shifting back into place. Waves and high water significantly impacted the county’s coastline. “This is a great example of coastal resistance at work,” officials said. Johnnie Sabin, a coastal specialist with Indian River County’s Department of Natural Resources, said the shoreline at Tracking Station Beach is already showing signs of recovery. “Much of the sand we placed on the beach, while it shifted briefly, has already been returning. I mean, these beaches, these berms, there's a lot more space. They're a little higher, a little wider so folks aren't in jeopardy to visit the beaches anymore,” Sabin said. Sabin explained that Tracking Station Beach experienced five to ten feet of erosion. He credited dune plants for helping hold the sand together and said the county’s Sector Five Beach Restoration Project performed as expected. “Luckily because of the sand being there, it buffered all private properties, the roads, all the infrastructure we care about and it did its job,” Sabin said. While major parks in the central beach area are open, some beach access points remain closed. Sabin advised visitors to check the county’s website before heading out. The county plans to repair beach parks where needed. Beachgoer Erin Dobrinski has noticed some of the damage but it's not stopping her from enjoying the beach. “You know down the Sebastian riverfront area down there there's a part of the sidewalk completely blocked off and if you peep around you can see it's all eroded,” Dobrinski said. Sabin said there are no current plans for another major sand project, but with more king tides expected, the county is closely monitoring the coast. There is good news for sea turtles, as Sabin reported that less than one percent of nests were affected by the erosion event. “They're resilient creatures. This is not their first rodeo. And they're going to continue doing what they do,” Sabin said. Erosion officials are asking the public to help protect the shoreline by picking up trash and debris. entry.title: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes - WPBF
entry.summary: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes    WPBF
entry.article_text: After more than a week of standing floodwater, some residents near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are finally beginning to clean up their homes as water slowly recedes. Martin County began pumping water out of the neighborhood Monday, allowing some homeowners to begin assessing the damage. For Lisa French, the receding water means she can finally begin the difficult work of cleaning out her home. “I mean, we’ve been underwater for a week,” French said. When WPBF 25 News visited French’s home several days ago, water was still standing inside, reaching more than a foot deep in some rooms. CLICK HERE FOR INFORMATION ON HOW TO DONATE TO THE FRENCH FAMILY Now, the water is gone, but much of what she owns has been destroyed. Since early Wednesday morning, French, her husband and several neighbors have been removing damaged drywall, tearing out the kitchen and carrying ruined furniture and belongings into the front yard. “You know, you’re sitting there with your house full of water, sitting in the fact that you lost your entire home. But now we can actually move and work instead of think,” French said. While French has begun cleaning up, other residents are still waiting for floodwaters to recede. Susan Destafney, who has lived in the neighborhood for four decades, said she has never experienced anything like it. “We’ve lived in our home for 40 years. We’ve never seen the likes of this,” Destafney said. Community volunteers have also stepped in to help, including Alaura Macpherson, who runs the local group Quit Messen With Jensen. Macpherson said volunteers have been collecting cleaning supplies and other necessities for affected families. She is also organizing a community fundraiser and meal on Nov. 25 to raise money for flood victims. Local restaurants are expected to donate food, while the event will also serve as a resource center connecting residents with contractors, cleanup services and other recovery assistance. “The community is what helps each other. We are a family,” Macpherson said. Martin County officials have opened a Multi-Agency Resource Center at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach to connect flood victims with recovery assistance. entry.title: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes - WPBF
entry.summary: Community gathers to begin cleanup as Jensen Beach flooding slowly recedes    WPBF
entry.article_text: After more than a week of standing floodwater, some residents near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are finally beginning to clean up their homes as water slowly recedes. Martin County began pumping water out of the neighborhood Monday, allowing some homeowners to begin assessing the damage. For Lisa French, the receding water means she can finally begin the difficult work of cleaning out her home. “I mean, we’ve been underwater for a week,” French said. When WPBF 25 News visited French’s home several days ago, water was still standing inside, reaching more than a foot deep in some rooms. CLICK HERE FOR INFORMATION ON HOW TO DONATE TO THE FRENCH FAMILY Now, the water is gone, but much of what she owns has been destroyed. Since early Wednesday morning, French, her husband and several neighbors have been removing damaged drywall, tearing out the kitchen and carrying ruined furniture and belongings into the front yard. “You know, you’re sitting there with your house full of water, sitting in the fact that you lost your entire home. But now we can actually move and work instead of think,” French said. While French has begun cleaning up, other residents are still waiting for floodwaters to recede. Susan Destafney, who has lived in the neighborhood for four decades, said she has never experienced anything like it. “We’ve lived in our home for 40 years. We’ve never seen the likes of this,” Destafney said. Community volunteers have also stepped in to help, including Alaura Macpherson, who runs the local group Quit Messen With Jensen. Macpherson said volunteers have been collecting cleaning supplies and other necessities for affected families. She is also organizing a community fundraiser and meal on Nov. 25 to raise money for flood victims. Local restaurants are expected to donate food, while the event will also serve as a resource center connecting residents with contractors, cleanup services and other recovery assistance. “The community is what helps each other. We are a family,” Macpherson said. Martin County officials have opened a Multi-Agency Resource Center at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach to connect flood victims with recovery assistance. entry.title: Fort Pierce mom demands answers after video shows moments before daughter’s death - WPEC
entry.summary: Fort Pierce mom demands answers after video shows moments before daughter’s death    WPEC
entry.article_text: A Fort Pierce mother is speaking out after watching body camera footage of the night her 19-year-old daughter was fatally shot in Fort Lauderdale near an Airbnb. She believes her daughter was asking police for help and wants to know whether the officers who first responded could have done more. I already knew half of what happened, and to see it and to hear it was heartbreaking, said Alacia Ford-Barron, the mother of Myrah Zeigler. She shared the video with CBS12 News. The body camera video shows officers arriving after an altercation involving two groups of women inside the Airbnb. Officers tell everyone to leave. Ford-Barron says her daughter had been attacked and that belongings, including car keys, were taken. The group needed to retrieve those items from a nearby park. In the footage, Zeigler asks officers to walk with the group to get their belongings. One officer asks whether they have a way to get to the park. Zeigler responds that they can. Ford-Barron says she believed officers were going to help. Minutes later, gunfire erupts nearby. An officer reports that shots were fired two blocks away. Friends can be heard screaming as officers try to revive Zeigler. She later died at a nearby hospital. See also: FDOT reopens all lanes on SR 809 and Military Trail after deadly Learjet 60 crash I wanted to know why they didn't call backup. I wanted to know why she did not listen to my daughter when she was trying to explain to her and asking her to walk down to the park, Ford-Barron said. Larry Lamar Smith was later arrested in connection with Zeigler’s death. Ford-Barron says she appreciates the detectives’ work but still has questions about the initial police response. I have to be my daughter's voice. I know that if I shut down, who's going to speak for my daughter? CBS12 News did not receive a response from Fort Lauderdale Police before publication. Update : In a statement provided Friday, the department said it remains saddened by the loss of Myrah Zeigler and extends its condolences to her family and loved ones. Police said the lead detective has maintained regular communication with the family and encouraged any concerns about the handling of the case to be addressed directly with the department through its established complaint process. The department declined an interview, citing the active and ongoing investigation.

entry.title: Florida flooding survivors praise heroes who came to their aid
entry.summary: From high-water rescues to the heroes who live next door, people are sharing their stories about the good Samaritans who came to their aid during the recent floods that ravaged our area. Tessie Watts from Riviera Beach says first responders and the mayor of her city pulled her to safety after she fled her home and more than 20 inches of water. WATCH REPORT BELOW: Heroes emerge after historic flooding swamps Palm Beach County, Treasure Coast Nicole Vazquez from Fort Pierce shared with WPTV anchor Hollani Davis that her brother is her hero. She said he helped the family sandbag their home before leaving, then came back by boat to get them out. 'He left, and he came back Tuesday to evacuate us, and then we took shelter with him that night,' says Vazquez. The selfless acts stretched to West Palm Beach, where Miles Bradford and his friend jumped in to help stranded drivers. 'If it was me, I would want someone to get out there and help me,' says Bradford. Long after the water is gone, even though there will undoubtedly be more tough days ahead, it's these acts of kindness that people say they'll remember.

entry.title: FHP trooper-involved shooting incident shuts down I-95 in Indian River County
entry.summary: Interstate 95 in Indian River County is shut down in both directions early Friday morning, creating a major traffic disruption for drivers near the Indian River-St. Lucie County line. On Nov. 12, around 11:20 p.m., FHP said a trooper was involved in a shooting incident on I-95 near mile marker 141. According to FHP, the incident began when the trooper initiated a traffic stop, and the suspect fled, resulting in a pursuit. The pursuit escalated and turned into a gunfire exchange between the trooper and the suspect. Authorities said no troopers were injured during the shooting. FHP said the suspect sustained injuries from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound and was pronounced dead at the scene. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said the highway is closed due to the ongoing investigation. All northbound and southbound lanes of I-95 are closed at this time. The southbound entrance ramp at Oslo Road is also shut down. Northbound drivers were being directed off I-95 at Indrio Road, while southbound drivers were being directed to exit at Oslo Road. The northbound entrance ramp from Indrio Road is also closed. Officials said all body cam and dash cam video will be reviewed during the investigation. The FDLE will take over as the lead on the investigation. WPTV is working to learn more about when the interstate could reopen.

entry.title: Boca Helping Hands aims to provide Thanksgiving meals for more than 4,000 Palm Beach County families
entry.summary: Boca Helping Hands is asking the community to help provide Thanksgiving meals for more than 4,000 Palm Beach County families through its annual Thanksgiving Box Brigade . The nonprofit is asking donors to contribute $29.72, the cost of a Thanksgiving box that helps provide families facing food insecurity with the ingredients for a holiday meal. WATCH REPORT BELOW: What can a $30 Thanksgiving box become? For families already stretching household budgets, Boca Helping Hands CEO Dr. Andrew Hagen said the added cost of Thanksgiving can make the holiday particularly difficult. 'You know this has been a tough year for a lot of people economically, and we want to make sure they have a good Thanksgiving,' Hagen said. Boca Helping Hands plans to distribute turkeys and Thanksgiving meal boxes to current Pantry Bag Program clients Nov. 21 and 22 at five drive-thru locations in East Boca Raton, West Boca Raton, Delray Beach, Boynton Beach and Lake Worth Beach. Volunteers pack thousands of Thanksgiving boxes Preparing thousands of Thanksgiving meals requires plenty of hands. Volunteers gathered at the Boca Helping Hands food center in Boca Raton to pack the boxes, including a group from Vivmark Residential. Hagen credited the volunteers and community supporters with making the effort possible. 'We're going to be able to provide at least 4,000 families with Thanksgiving meals, and that's because of the people here today, thanks to you and thanks to all the people that support Boca Helping Hands,' Hagen said. To demonstrate the work that goes into the effort, volunteers from Vivmark Residential and The Boca Raton (who donated 100 turkeys) turned packing into a friendly competition. Each team packed 12 boxes, ending the challenge in a tie. Turning a Thanksgiving box into dinner The ingredients inside the boxes are intended to give families the foundation for preparing their own Thanksgiving meals at home. Chef Andrew 'Andy' Roenbeck, vice president of culinary operations and group executive chef at The Boca Raton, demonstrated how some additional ingredients families may already have can add new flavors to the meal. Roenbeck added apples to stuffing and Florida orange to cranberry sauce. He topped pumpkin pie with meringue and gave it a toasted finish. And when it came to the stuffing, he offered a simple Thanksgiving philosophy. 'Everything's better with butter,' Roenbeck said. entry.title: Fort Pierce mom demands answers after video shows moments before daughter’s death - cw34.com
entry.summary: Fort Pierce mom demands answers after video shows moments before daughter’s death    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A Fort Pierce mother is speaking out after watching body camera footage of the night her 19-year-old daughter was fatally shot in Fort Lauderdale near an Airbnb. She believes her daughter was asking police for help and wants to know whether the officers who first responded could have done more. I already knew half of what happened, and to see it and to hear it was heartbreaking, said Alacia Ford-Barron, the mother of Myrah Zeigler. She shared the video with CBS12 News. The body camera video shows officers arriving after an altercation involving two groups of women inside the Airbnb. Officers tell everyone to leave. Ford-Barron says her daughter had been attacked and that belongings, including car keys, were taken. The group needed to retrieve those items from a nearby park. In the footage, Zeigler asks officers to walk with the group to get their belongings. One officer asks whether they have a way to get to the park. Zeigler responds that they can. Ford-Barron says she believed officers were going to help. Minutes later, gunfire erupts nearby. An officer reports that shots were fired two blocks away. Friends can be heard screaming as officers try to revive Zeigler. She later died at a nearby hospital. See also: FDOT reopens all lanes on SR 809 and Military Trail after deadly Learjet 60 crash I wanted to know why they didn't call backup. I wanted to know why she did not listen to my daughter when she was trying to explain to her and asking her to walk down to the park, Ford-Barron said. Larry Lamar Smith was later arrested in connection with Zeigler’s death. Ford-Barron says she appreciates the detectives’ work but still has questions about the initial police response. I have to be my daughter's voice. I know that if I shut down, who's going to speak for my daughter? CBS12 News did not receive a response from Fort Lauderdale Police before publication. Update : In a statement provided Friday, the department said it remains saddened by the loss of Myrah Zeigler and extends its condolences to her family and loved ones. Police said the lead detective has maintained regular communication with the family and encouraged any concerns about the handling of the case to be addressed directly with the department through its established complaint process. The department declined an interview, citing the active and ongoing investigation.

entry.title: Wellington man sentenced to 7 years for $2.3 million fraud scheme involving sham cosmetic surgery clinics
entry.summary: A Wellington man has been sentenced to seven years in federal prison for a fraud scheme that prosecutors say used fake cosmetic surgery clinics and the stolen identities of more than 100 people to obtain millions of dollars from medical lenders. Jacquez Dion Tullis, 42, was sentenced Thursday to 84 months in prison after previously pleading guilty to conspiracy to commit bank fraud and aggravated identity theft, according to the U.S. Department of Justice. U.S. District Judge Rodolfo A. Ruiz II sentenced Tullis to 60 months for the bank fraud conspiracy charge and a consecutive 24 months for aggravated identity theft. Tullis was also ordered to serve five years of supervised release and pay more than $2.3 million in restitution. The court also ordered a forfeiture money judgment of more than $2.3 million. Prosecutors detail sham medical clinics According to court documents and Tullis' admissions in his plea, Tullis and his co-conspirators created six sham medical clinics between April 2018 and February 2024. The clinics purported to provide cosmetic surgery and other medical services but provided no actual care, prosecutors said. The conspirators registered the clinics with the Florida Department of State using stolen personal information belonging to practicing doctors and other people without their knowledge or consent, according to the Justice Department. Prosecutors said some doctors were falsely identified as clinic owners in applications seeking approval as merchants with medical lenders. Once the clinics were approved, the conspirators submitted fraudulent credit applications in the names of more than 100 people. The applications sought approximately $3.1 million and falsely claimed the money would pay for cosmetic surgery and other medical services. The people whose identities were used did not authorize the applications or receive treatment, prosecutors said. According to the Justice Department, death records showed some of the purported patients had died before the dates they supposedly received medical care. The scheme ultimately defrauded medical lenders of approximately $2.3 million, according to prosecutors. COVID-19 relief fraud Federal prosecutors said Tullis was also involved in a separate scheme targeting a pandemic-era federal relief program. The court also ordered a forfeiture money judgment of more than $2.3 million.According to court documents and Tullis' admissions in his plea, Tullis and his co-conspirators created six sham medical clinics between April 2018 and February 2024.The clinics purported to provide cosmetic surgery and other medical services but provided no actual care, prosecutors said.The conspirators registered the clinics with the Florida Department of State using stolen personal information belonging to practicing doctors and other people without their knowledge or consent, according to the Justice Department.Prosecutors said some doctors were falsely identified as clinic owners in applications seeking approval as merchants with medical lenders.Once the clinics were approved, the conspirators submitted fraudulent credit applications in the names of more than 100 people.
